title: When Routing Collapses: On the Degenerate Convergence of LLM Routers

review.summary: This paper identifies and characterizes a failure mode termed "routing collapse": as the user cost budget increases, learned LLM routers converge to almost exclusively calling the single most capable (and most expensive) model, even though an oracle policy would still use cheaper models for a large fraction of queries. The authors show this phenomenon empirically on RouterBench and MMR-Bench, and diagnose its cause through (i) a training-set (in-sample) evaluation that rules out train/test generalization gap as a necessary cause, (ii) an analysis of the feasible-set performance margin between the best and second-best models, showing that near-ties are pervasive, and (iii) a controlled noise-injection experiment on oracle labels showing that even unbiased perturbations induce collapse. They further provide a theoretical argument (via a random-utility/argmax analysis) showing that under i.i.d. symmetric noise, the highest-true-performance feasible model is always the most likely arg-max winner, explaining why instability concentrates on the strongest model rather than dispersing across mid-tier models. Building on this diagnosis, they propose EquiRouter, which replaces pointwise scalar-score regression with a pairwise ranking-aware training objective, combined with FiLM-style query-conditioned model embeddings and an interaction-based joint feature construction. They also propose a new evaluation metric, the Routing Collapse Index (RCI), to directly quantify dominated/collapse-prone routing decisions at the per-query level. Experiments on RouterBench and MMR-Bench (plus OOD splits and ablations) show that EquiRouter achieves higher nAUC, lower QNC (cost to reach top-model-level performance), and lower RCI than a fairly comprehensive set of prior routing baselines.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The core empirical observation (routing collapse) is interesting, clearly illustrated (Figs. 1-3), and demonstrated consistently across two different benchmarks and modalities, which strengthens the claim that this is a general phenomenon rather than a benchmark artifact.
2. The diagnostic methodology is fairly thorough: the training-set evaluation experiment to rule out generalization as a necessary cause is a sensible and informative control; the margin analysis and controlled noise-injection experiment provide converging evidence for the small-margin/decision-sensitivity explanation.
3. The theoretical result in Appendix B.4 (that the highest-true-performance model is always the most probable arg-max winner under i.i.d. symmetric noise) is a nice, mathematically clean explanation for why collapse concentrates on the strongest model rather than diffusing across mid-tier candidates.
4. The proposed RCI metric fills a genuine gap: curve-level metrics (nAUC, Ps, QNC) cannot detect per-query dominated decisions, and RCI is well-specified with clear edge cases and illustrative examples.
5. The experimental comparison covers a reasonably broad and current set of baselines (embedding-based, graph-based, IRT-based, causal, clustering-based), and includes ablations (w/o joint feature, w/o ranking loss) and an OOD robustness check, plus a cost-prediction sanity check (Appendix C) ruling out cost-estimation error as a confound.
6. Complexity analysis suggests the method is lightweight and practically deployable.

Weaknesses:
1. Originality of the fix is somewhat limited: the core mechanism of EquiRouter—supervising a pairwise ranking objective rather than pointwise regression—is essentially the classic pointwise-vs-pairwise learning-to-rank distinction (e.g., RankNet-style logistic pairwise loss), which is not discussed or cited despite being directly relevant prior art from the learning-to-rank/IR literature. The paper would be strengthened by explicitly situating its
review.key_questions_for_authors: 1. Can the authors report variance across multiple seeds/runs for the main results in Table 1? Several of the nAUC gaps (e.g., 0.7712 vs 0.7555 for AvengersPro) are numerically modest, and without error bars it is hard to assess whether these differences are statistically meaningful. 2. How does EquiRouter's pairwise ranking objective conceptually and empirically differ from established pointwise-vs-pairwise learning-to-rank methods (e.g., RankNet)? Could a simple RankNet-style baseline applied directly on top of an existing scalar-score router (without the FiLM/joint-feature architecture) already mitigate collapse to a similar degree, isolating the contribution of the architectural components? 3. In the theoretical argument (Appendix B.4), the noise model assumes i.i.d. symmetric perturbations across models. Real learned predictors likely have correlated, model-specific, and possibly non-symmetric biases (e.g., systematically higher variance for weaker models). Does the concentration result still hold, qualitatively or quantitatively, when this idealized noise assumption is relaxed? 4. On MMR-Bench, NIRT achieves a higher Ps than EquiRouter while EquiRouter wins on nAUC and RCI—can the authors clarify this apparent tension and discuss whether there exist settings in which the ranking-first objective might sacrifice peak accuracy for better cost control? 5. Since RCI treats any suboptimal selection as sn=1 regardless of the magnitude of performance loss, could two routers with very different practical quality (one slightly suboptimal vs. one severely suboptimal) receive similar RCI scores? Have the authors considered a magnitude-sensitive variant?
review.limitations: The paper does not include a dedicated limitations or broader societal impact discussion. While cost-aware LLM routing is a fairly benign efficiency-oriented topic, the paper would benefit from explicitly discussing: (1) limitations of the RCI metric (e.g., its insensitivity to the magnitude of performance loss, and its dependence on the availability of ground-truth per-model performance labels, which are expensive to obtain and may not exist for arbitrary future queries), (2) the reliance on offline precomputed instance-model utility benchmarks (RouterBench, MMR-Bench) rather than live deployment, which may not perfectly capture real-world query distributions, and (3) potential negative impacts such as routers being tuned to explicitly game evaluation metrics like RCI rather than true user-perceived quality. These points are not addressed in the current submission and should be added.

title: The Laplacian Keyboard: Beyond the Linear Span

review.summary: This paper proposes the Laplacian Keyboard (LK), a hierarchical framework for reinforcement learning that combines representation-based and behavior-based approaches to zero-shot/task-agnostic RL. During pre-training, the method learns graph Laplacian eigenvectors (via the ALLO objective) from a reward-free dataset, and then trains a Universal Successor Feature Approximator (USFA) conditioned on these eigenvector-based reward weights, yielding a continuous library of "options" indexed by weight vectors. During the downstream phase, a meta-policy learns to select and sequentially compose (stitch) these options via state-dependent weight vectors, allowing the agent to approximate tasks whose reward function lies outside the linear span of the Laplacian basis. The paper provides a theoretical bound (Theorem 3.1) relating the value-function approximation error of a truncated Laplacian basis to the basis size and reward smoothness (graph total variation), building on existing spectral graph theory results (Zhu & Rabbat, 2012) combined with a Bellman contraction argument. Empirically, the paper evaluates LK on the DeepMind Control suite (Cheetah, Quadruped, Walker) and the Item-Collector gridworld, comparing zero-shot performance against Forward-Backward representations (FB) and comparing hierarchical composition gains against a flat TD3 baseline, as well as comparing against a privileged Option-Keyboard-Basis (OKB) method that has access to hand-specified reward features.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper addresses a well-motivated gap: bridging representation-based zero-shot RL methods (limited by linear span) and behavior-based option composition methods (which typically require hand-specified reward features). Using Laplacian eigenvectors to induce both a reward-approximation basis and a task-agnostic behavior library is a sensible and reasonably novel synthesis of existing components (ALLO, USFA, Option Keyboard-style composition).
- The theoretical bound (Theorem 3.1), while derived by fairly directly composing an existing spectral truncation bound with a standard Bellman-contraction argument, is clearly stated, properly proven in the appendix, and empirically validated on a toy domain (Appendix B.3), which is a nice sanity check.
- The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: three DMC domains with three different offline datasets, several basis sizes, and an additional gridworld comparison against a privileged baseline (OKB). The appendix includes many additional plots, per-dataset breakdowns, and a careful investigation (Appendix E) into anomalous behavior in Quadruped, which is commendable transparency.
- The visualizations of the induced Laplacian behavior basis (Figures 5, 11, 16) are informative and support the claim that meaningful, diverse behaviors emerge without hand-crafted priors.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The central selling point of LK — that hierarchical composition of options improves over zero-shot solutions and flat RL — does not hold uniformly. In Table 2, the Quadruped domain shows LK underperforming its own zero-shot baseline in nearly every task and basis size (mostly negative percentages), which directly undercuts the generality of the claimed benefit of hierarchical composition. The explanation offered (the leading eigenvector already captures most task structure) is plausible but is a post-hoc rationalization for a case where the proposed mechanism fails, and it is not clear how a practitioner would know a priori when LK's composition will help versus hurt.
- In Table 1, the flat TD3 oracle (trained with substantially more environment interactions, 2M) outperforms both LK and FB zero-shot solutions on nearly every task by a wide margin, and it is not entirely clear from the main text whether the "Flat TD3" baseline appearing in Figures 6/7 (compared at matched sample budget for sample-efficiency claims) is the same agent as this 2M-step oracle or a separately-trained one with the 200K budget; this ambiguity makes it harder to assess the sample-efficiency claims rigorously.
- The statistical evidence for "LK matches FB" rests on a single sign test with no reported effect sizes/confidence intervals, despite substantial variance across datasets (Table 5) — e.g., LK trails FB by 200+ points on several Cheetah/Walker/RND combinations. A more rigorous statistical treatment (e.g., paired tests with effect sizes, or per-domain breakdown of significance) would make this claim more convincing.
- Each individual component (Laplacian representation learning via ALLO, USFA, hierarchical composition of options as in the Option Keyboard) is drawn from prior work; the novelty is primarily in the specific combination and in deriving Laplacian eigenvectors as a task-agnostic option basis rather than requiring hand-specified reward features. This is a reasonable but incremental contribution.

Presentation:
- The main text is generally clear and logically organized (motivation → Laplacian basis theory → LK framework → empirical validation), and the figures are well constructed and support the narrative.
- However, a large amount of important material (per-dataset results, ablations explaining the Quadruped anomaly, hyperparameter details) is deferred to a lengthy appendix (28 pages), which somewhat obscures the completeness of the main paper's story; a reader relying only on the main text would miss the important caveat about Quadruped's negative results in Table 2 (though this is properly reported and discussed, just not foregrounded prominently in the main narrative/conclusion).

Significance:
- The idea of building a task-agnostic option library directly from the same eigenvectors used for reward approximation, and coupling it with a meta-policy for stitching, is conceptually appealing and could be impactful if shown to scale robustly across more diverse domains. However, given the mixed empirical results across only three (structurally similar) locomotion domains plus one small gridworld, the practical significance and robustness of the approach remain somewhat unproven.

Originality:
- Moderate. The combination of Laplacian representations with USFA-based continuous option libraries and Option-Keyboard-style meta-policy composition, entirely learned from reward-free data (without hand-specified reward features), is a reasonably novel synthesis relative to prior work such as Barreto et al. (2019)'s Option Keyboard (which requires hand-specified features) and Alegre et al. (2025)'s OKB (which uses privileged reward features).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Why does hierarchical composition in LK fail to improve (and often hurt) performance relative to zero-shot in the Quadruped domain, and what practical guidance can be given for anticipating when composition will help versus hurt on a new task/domain?
2. Please clarify the relationship between the "Flat TD3" oracle trained for 2M steps (Table 1) and the "Flat TD3" baseline shown in Figures 6/7 for sample-efficiency comparisons — are these the same trained policy evaluated at different points, or separately trained agents with matched budgets?
3. Beyond the single sign test, can you provide a more detailed statistical analysis (e.g., per-domain paired significance tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals) comparing LK and FB zero-shot performance, given the substantial variance observed across datasets in Table 5?
4. How sensitive are the results to the choice of fixed option-termination horizon t_term, and would learning termination conditions (as suggested in the conclusion) qualitatively change the reported improvements, particularly in the domains where composition currently underperforms?
5. What is the total computational/sample cost (wall-clock or gradient steps) of the full three-stage LK pipeline (Laplacian encoder + USFA + meta-policy) relative to FB and flat TD3, and does this cost meaningfully offset the reported sample-efficiency gains during the downstream phase?
review.limitations: The conclusion discusses some limitations (fixed basis cannot capture all tasks in complex environments; possible extensions to online exploration and learned termination sets), and Appendix E provides a thoughtful post-hoc analysis of why hierarchical composition fails in the Quadruped domain. However, this important negative result is not clearly foregrounded as a limitation in the main text/conclusion, and could be stated more directly (e.g., explicitly noting that composition benefits are not universal and can sometimes hurt performance). The Impact Statement is generic boilerplate ("no potential societal consequences... need not be specifically highlighted") and could be expanded to at least briefly consider the implications of automated skill/option discovery (e.g., safety of emergent behaviors, use in robotics) rather than being dismissed without discussion.

title: Physics-Informed Policy Optimization via Analytic Dynamics Regularization

review.summary: The paper proposes PIPER, a physics-informed reinforcement learning framework that augments the actor's loss with a differentiable "Lagrangian residual" derived from the inverse-dynamics equation M(q)q̈+b(q,q̇)=τ. An "Automated Dynamics Oracle" extracts M(q) and the generalized bias term b(q,q̇) from the MuJoCo XML at runtime using CRBA and RNEA, and an auxiliary PINN Φ_ϕ is trained to predict joint accelerations from (state, action) pairs. The predicted acceleration is plugged back into the inverse-dynamics equation to obtain an "implied torque," and the residual between this implied torque and the policy's chosen action is added as a penalty to the actor's objective (usable with PPO, TD3, SAC, and TQC). The authors further propose task-specific variants of this loss (kinematic, contact/friction, impulse-momentum, and grasp-stability terms) for the Fetch manipulation suite (Reach, Push, Slide, PickAndPlace) with a 7-DOF Franka arm. Experiments report substantial improvements in sample efficiency, precision, and stability over standard baselines across all four tasks and four algorithms.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The idea of grounding a model-free actor's updates in analytically extracted rigid-body dynamics (rather than learned/approximate physics) is a reasonable and potentially useful direction, and the paper attempts to make the approach algorithm-agnostic (PPO/TD3/SAC/TQC).
- The related-work discussion is fairly comprehensive and correctly situates the work relative to Deep Lagrangian Networks, safety layers, residual RL, and PINN-based dynamics learning.
- The task-specific instantiations (impulse-momentum for sliding, work-energy for pushing, force-closure for grasping) show an attempt to tailor the general principle to different contact regimes.

Weaknesses (soundness):
1. Action-space inconsistency: The method is formalized assuming direct joint-torque control (a = τ_θ, Section 3.1), and the whole Lagrangian residual (Eq. 9–10) is built on this assumption. However, the evaluated environments (FetchReach-v4, FetchPush-v4, FetchSlide-v4, FetchPickAndPlace-v4 from Gymnasium-Robotics) are standard mocap/Cartesian-displacement-controlled tasks with low-dimensional (typically 4-D) actions, not 7-DOF joint torques. The paper never explains how this mismatch was resolved (e.g., whether the environments were modified to expose joint torque control), which raises serious doubts about the correctness of the reported physics-residual computation and the validity of the entire empirical section.
2. Circularity in the PINN training objective: The physics residual r(s,a) depends on Φ_ϕ, yet Φ_ϕ's own loss (Eq. 8) includes a term that directly minimizes ‖r(s,a)‖² in addition to the supervised acceleration-fitting term. This creates a self-referential objective whose effect on preventing degenerate solutions (e.g., the PINN learning to trivially satisfy the residual rather than model true dynamics) is not analyzed.
3. Ad hoc, task-specific engineering: Four different loss formulations (Eq. 15–19) are introduced with several additional hand-tuned coefficients (λ1, λ2, λf, λm, λg) per task. This substantially undercuts the paper's claim of an "algorithm-agnostic," "plug-and-play" framework, since a new hand-crafted physics loss is required per task family.
4. Statistical rigor: Despite claiming 5 seeds and 100 evaluation episodes per checkpoint, Tables 2–3 report only point estimates with no confidence intervals, standard errors, or significance tests. The uniformly large improvements (up to 79.5% precision gain, 47% stability gain, 45% efficiency gain) across every metric, every task, and every algorithm are suspicious in the absence of variance reporting.
5. Missing ablations: There is no ablation isolating the contribution of the PINN vs. the analytic M(q), b(s) terms, the energy-conservation term vs. the base residual, or the task-specific augmentations vs. the generic Lagrangian residual. It is therefore unclear which component(s) drive the reported gains.
6. Missing baselines: Despite discussing Deep Lagrangian Networks, PI-MBRL, and HJB-RL at length in Related Work (and even including a qualitative comparison table, Table 1), none of these physics-informed baselines are empirically compared against; only vanilla PPO/TD3/SAC/TQC+HER are used as baselines, understating the significance of PIPER's advantage over prior physics-informed RL work.
7. Practical assumptions: The method requires querying "MuJoCo's contact sensors" for τ_ext at runtime, which may require environment/XML modification, in tension with the claim that "no alterations to existing simulators" are required.

Weaknesses (presentation):
- Multiple naming inconsistencies ("Dynamics Oracle", "Automated Dynamics Oracle (ADO)", "Analytic Dynamics Oracle"; "PINN-RL Training Pipeline" vs. "PIPER").
- Equation 14 encloses the entire energy-violation term in absolute value bars in an unusual way, and its role in the loss (L1 vs L2, how it's weighted) is not stated precisely.
- Some sentences are grammatically incomplete or garbled (e.g., "realistic surface properties faithfully model real-world , utilizing...").
- Figure captions and text sometimes conflict on labeling (e.g., Fig. 5(b) internal labels reference "PINN" vs. text referencing "PIPER-TQC").

Weaknesses (significance/originality):
- The core idea of using PINN-based physics residuals to regularize policy learning is closely related to existing physics-informed RL and Lagrangian-network literature already cited by the authors; the specific combination (analytic M,b extraction + learned acceleration proxy + actor regularization) is incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.
- Evaluation is restricted to a single robot arm (Franka) and four simulated Fetch tasks, limiting generalizability claims ("new paradigm for efficient and physically consistent robotic control").
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. The formalism assumes direct joint-torque actions (a = τ_θ), but FetchReach/Push/Slide/PickAndPlace in Gymnasium-Robotics use low-dimensional Cartesian/mocap displacement actions. Did you modify these environments to expose joint-torque control? If so, please describe the exact action space and simulator modifications used in your experiments.
2. How do you prevent the PINN training objective (Eq. 8) from degenerating, given that it directly optimizes to reduce the same residual r(s,a) that is later used to regularize the policy? Can you show that Φ_ϕ converges to an accurate forward-dynamics model rather than a shortcut that trivially satisfies the residual?
3. Can you provide standard deviations / confidence intervals across the 5 seeds for the metrics in Tables 2 and 3, and statistical significance tests (e.g., paired t-test or bootstrap CIs) supporting the claimed percentage improvements?
4. Please provide an ablation that separates the contributions of (a) the generic Lagrangian residual, (b) the energy-conservation term, and (c) the task-specific losses (impulse-momentum, grasp-stability, etc.), so readers can assess which components matter.
5. Why were no comparisons made against the physics-informed RL baselines discussed at length in Related Work (Deep Lagrangian Networks, PI-MBRL, HJB-RL), especially since Table 1 already positions PIPER against them qualitatively?
review.limitations: The paper includes a brief "Limitations and Trade-offs" paragraph acknowledging reliance on introspectable simulator models and the Sim2Real gap, plus a note on ~15-20% computational overhead. However, it does not discuss the potential action-space/methodology mismatch noted above, lacks discussion of failure cases or negative results, and does not address broader societal impact (e.g., dual-use concerns for physically consistent robotic manipulation). These should be expanded in a revision.

title: Why Depth Matters in Parallelizable Sequence Models: A Lie Algebraic View

review.summary: This paper develops a Lie-algebraic/control-theoretic framework for analyzing why depth matters in parallelizable sequence models (transformers, diagonal SSMs such as Mamba/GLA, and their variants). The authors formalize sequence models as controlled dynamical systems (state-space models) and relate their Lie-algebraic class (abelian, nilpotent, solvable, non-solvable) to order-sensitivity of the tasks they can represent. Building on the Magnus expansion, they define a 'commutator mass' that quantifies approximation error incurred when an order-symmetric (abelian/restricted) model approximates an order-sensitive target system (Theorem 3.2). They then show that stacking layers corresponds to constructing a tower of Lie algebra extensions: an abelian k-layer SSM can exactly simulate any solvable Lie algebra of derived length k (Theorem 3.4), and for non-solvable systems, error decreases doubly-exponentially with depth via nilpotentization (Corollary 3.6). They further derive a logarithmic-depth upper bound (Proposition 3.7) and an exponential state-width lower bound (Corollary 3.8) for simulating bounded-length word problems. Experiments on symbolic word problems (spanning abelian, nilpotent, solvable, non-solvable groups) and a continuous 3D rigid-body rotation task test several architectures (transformer, GLA, signed Mamba, AUSSM, DeltaProduct) at varying depths, generally showing that increased depth mitigates expressivity limitations, though with notable learnability/training-stability issues in deeper models.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper provides a unifying, mathematically rigorous (extensive appendix with full proofs) Lie-algebraic account of depth-dependent expressivity, connecting several previously disparate results (Merrill et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2023; Grazzi et al. 2025; Shakerinava et al. 2026) into a coherent extension-theoretic narrative.
- Unlike prior expressivity work that mostly proves binary (im)possibility results, this paper attempts to quantify *how bad* the approximation error is and how it scales with depth, which is a genuinely useful and underexplored question.
- The theoretical results (Theorem 3.4, Corollary 3.6, Proposition 3.7, Corollary 3.8) are internally consistent, build on standard tools (Magnus expansion, derived/lower-central series, Lyndon word factorization), and yield concrete, falsifiable predictions (e.g., logarithmic depth suffices, exponential error decay).
- Experiments span a reasonably broad set of algebraic classes (C2/C3, D8/H3, S3/S4, A5) and modalities (symbolic word problems and continuous 3D rotation), and honestly report both supporting evidence and disagreements (learnability failures) rather than only favorable results.

Weaknesses (affecting soundness/significance ratings):
- A central gap is that the theorems are *existence* results (there exists a k-layer abelian SSM that approximates/simulates the target), but the paper does not establish that gradient-based training of the actual tested architectures (GLA, Mamba, transformers) converges to such constructions. The experiments repeatedly show this gap in practice (e.g., AUSSM fails on S3/S4 even at 2 layers, deep Signed Mamba/GLA models plateau or degrade), and the authors attribute this to vague 'learnability issues' without a rigorous account, which somewhat undercuts the practical predictive power the abstract/discussion claims for the theory.
- Remark 3.9 (used to explain several experimental discrepancies, e.g., AUSSM's failure to learn solvable WPs with 2 layers) is stated as an unproven conjecture. Using a conjecture to post-hoc explain negative results is a soundness concern, since it is unclear whether the failures are due to the conjectured algebraic obstruction or simply optimization/architecture-specific issues (numerically, the paper itself notes Signed Mamba outperforming AUSSM despite a more restricted eigenvalue range, suggesting non-algebraic factors dominate).
- The theory operates on continuous-time, piecewise-constant-input SSMs with linear/affine generators, while the tested architectures include gating, softmax normalization, and other nonlinear/discrete components not fully captured by the linear generator abstraction. The mapping from theory to the specific tested architectures (e.g., how softmax attention or GLA gating exactly correspond to 'restricted' SSMs) is asserted rather than rigorously derived in the main text.
- The quantitative predictions (e.g., specific exponential decay rate O(ε^{2^{k-1}+1})) are not directly validated numerically in the experiments; the comparisons in Section 4 are largely qualitative (does depth help, does the max length match the log-depth curve) rather than a direct fit of predicted vs. observed error-scaling constants.
- Presentation: the paper is dense with heavy Lie-theoretic and control-theoretic formalism front-loaded in Section 2, which may reduce accessibility for a general ICML audience; important intuition (e.g., why the commutator mass approximates order-sensitive error, why nilpotentization gives the specific error order) is deferred to appendices.
- Sample size for experiments (3 seeds) combined with visibly large variances at higher depths (Figure 3) limits the strength of quantitative claims about depth-error trends in the harder regimes.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can you clarify the relationship between your existence-type theorems (3.4, Corollary 3.6, Prop 3.7) and learnability via gradient descent? Is there any theoretical or empirical evidence that trained models converge near the constructed cascade decomposition?
2. Remark 3.9 (restricted k-layer SSMs cannot simulate solvable algebras of derived length k+1) is left as a conjecture but is used to interpret key experimental failures (e.g., AUSSM on S3/S4). Can you provide partial evidence, a proof sketch, or at least clarify how confident you are that observed failures are due to this algebraic obstruction rather than optimization/architecture-specific issues?
3. How rigorously does the continuous-time affine-generator SSM framework map onto the actual discrete, gated architectures tested (softmax attention, GLA gating, Mamba's selective mechanism)? What assumptions/approximations are needed, and how sensitive are your bounds to violations of them?
4. Could you provide a more direct quantitative test of the predicted error-decay rate (e.g., fitting observed simulation error vs. depth to the O(ε^{2^{k-1}+1}) form) rather than only qualitative trend comparisons?
5. Given the notable training instability of deep models (e.g., only marginal gains from 5→8 layers in Signed Mamba on A5), what concrete practical guidance do you believe the theory currently offers for architecture/depth selection in real applications?
review.limitations: The paper discusses some limitations in the Discussion/Future Directions section (finite-precision arithmetic sensitivity, unresolved learnability/optimization issues, training instability of deep models) and acknowledges that its bounds are worst-case/existence results. However, the existence-vs-learnability gap and the reliance on an unproven conjecture (Remark 3.9) to interpret experimental failures deserve more explicit and prominent discussion as core limitations rather than being framed mainly as 'future directions.' The Impact Statement is boilerplate with no substantive discussion of societal impact, which is acceptable for a primarily theoretical contribution but could be expanded slightly (e.g., implications for trust/reliability of deployed sequence models on order-sensitive tasks).

title: FaithRL: Learning to Reason Faithfully through Step-Level Faithfulness Maximization

review.summary: This paper proposes FaithRL, an RL framework designed to make LLM reasoning more "faithful" (i.e., grounded strictly in the evidence needed to answer a question) in multi-hop QA settings. The authors formalize three optimization objectives over trajectory space (maximize correctness, minimize hallucination, maximize "reasoning faithfulness") and argue theoretically that the first two lead to degenerate behavior (over-confidence or over-conservativeness) while the third stabilizes the refusal rate at a level consistent with model capability. To instantiate the faithfulness objective, they introduce (1) a "geometric reward" whose coefficients are derived from an offline-estimated baseline correctness/hallucination rate (motivated by maximizing the Truthful Helpfulness Score, a signed-area metric), and (2) a Faithfulness-Aware Advantage Modulation (FAAM) mechanism that reweights token-level GRPO advantages according to whether an LLM-judged verifier deems each reasoning step supported by required evidence. Experiments on 2WikiMultiHopQA-Full, HotpotQA-Full, and MuSiQue-Full (synthetically extended with unanswerable samples for the first two) with Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B backbones show that FaithRL improves THS, correctness, and hallucination rate relative to a range of refusal-aware SFT, confidence-based, RLVR, and factuality-driven RL baselines. The paper additionally reports OOD generalization to GSM8k/MATH500, training dynamics of the "faithful step ratio," ablations on the two components and the α hyperparameter, and a computational cost analysis showing modest (~14%) overhead versus GRPO.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The problem (aligning reasoning faithfulness rather than just outcome correctness) is well-motivated and topical, and the paper situates itself carefully against refusal-aware SFT, confidence calibration, and factuality-driven RL literature.
- The geometric reward derivation from the Truthful Helpfulness Score is an elegant way to make the correctness/hallucination trade-off adaptive to a model's baseline capability rather than using arbitrary fixed weights, and Theorem 4.2's algebraic identity (that this specific reward makes expected return proportional to THS) is correct given the reward's construction.
- The empirical evaluation is broad: two backbones, three in-domain benchmarks with fine-grained answerable/unanswerable breakdowns (Appendix H.1), OOD generalization checks, ablations of both components, hyperparameter sensitivity for α, and a reasonably thorough compute-cost analysis. The consistency of gains across backbones and benchmarks is a point in favor of the practical utility of the method.
- The qualitative case studies (Appendix J) are illustrative of the intended mechanism (rejecting spurious steps, refusing under missing evidence).

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The theoretical results (Theorems 4.1, 4.3, and the associated proofs in Appendices C and F) are largely informal comparisons of expected one-step rewards for discrete actions (Refuse vs. Attempt) rather than rigorous analyses of policy-gradient/RL training dynamics (which would need to account for function approximation, non-tabular policies, clipping, and finite-sample stochasticity). Labeling these as "Theorem"/"Proof" somewhat overstates their rigor; they are essentially motivating arguments, valid at an intuitive level but not full proofs of asymptotic convergence for the actual optimization procedure (GRPO with clipping) used in the paper.
- Theorem 4.2's "geometric alignment with THS" is a direct algebraic consequence of how the reward was constructed (reward y0/0/–x0 chosen so that its expectation equals 2×signed area); presenting it as a theorem, while technically correct, is closer to a design verification than a novel theoretical insight.
- The entire pipeline (reward computation, faithfulness verification, evaluation) leans heavily on an LLM judge (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct). The empirical "validation" of Assumptions 3.3/3.4 in Appendix B is performed using the same class of LLM judge, which is somewhat circular—it does not establish ground-truth correctness of the assumptions independent of the judge's own biases, and there's no human-agreement or judge-robustness analysis.
- The construction of the "Full" unanswerable variants of 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA (evidence pruning + Best-of-32 filtering with the same backbone family used for training) could introduce dataset-specific artifacts that favor the proposed method's ability to detect these particular synthetic gaps, and may not transfer to naturally-occurring unanswerable questions.
- No variance/multiple-seed reporting is provided for the main results; given RL training's known instability, some measure of seed variability or confidence intervals would strengthen the empirical claims.
- The framework's applicability is inherently limited to settings with well-defined evidence sets K(q)/E(q) (retrieval-augmented, multi-hop QA); the OOD experiments on GSM8k/MATH500 use inference-only evaluation, not further RL training, so they demonstrate transfer of faithfulness metrics rather than of the training procedure itself to non-evidence-based domains.
- Minor: the reference list appears to duplicate the same paper as both Chen et al. (2025b) and Chen et al. (2025c) with identical titles and arXiv IDs, suggesting a citation bookkeeping error.

Presentation:
- Overall clear and well organized, with a good balance of main text and appendix detail. The framing of "Objective A/B/C" and Figure 1-3 illustrations aid understanding.
- The dense notation (multiple assumptions, corollaries, and theorem statements) sometimes obscures that the core mechanism is fairly intuitive (reward shaping + advantage masking by an evidence-overlap check); tightening the theoretical exposition or being more explicit about the informal nature of the arguments would improve rigor-transparency.

Significance/Originality:
- The combination of adaptive (capability-dependent) reward shaping and step-level advantage modulation via evidence verification is a reasonably novel synthesis, though each individual ingredient (process reward models, refusal-aware training, factuality-driven step rewards) exists in prior work the paper cites. The contribution is more of a careful engineering synthesis with an appealing motivating narrative than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How exactly is the offline baseline (x0, y0) estimated (e.g., per-query, per-dataset, fixed once at the start of training)? Does it remain static throughout RL training, and if so, could staleness of this estimate destabilize the geometric reward as the policy improves?
2. How sensitive are the main results to the judge model used for reward computation and step verification? Have you measured judge-human agreement, or judge self-consistency, to rule out systematic biases propagating into both the reward signal and the reported hallucination/faithfulness metrics?
3. Can you clarify whether Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 are meant as formal convergence results for the actual GRPO-based optimizer used, or as intuitive one-step reward comparisons? If the latter, could you soften the claims (e.g., "illustrative argument" rather than "Theorem"/"Proof")?
4. How would FaithRL extend to settings without an explicit, enumerable evidence set (e.g., open-ended generation, general chat, or tasks where "evidence" is not naturally decomposable into discrete documents)? Is the method fundamentally tied to retrieval-augmented multi-hop QA?
5. Could you report variance across multiple training seeds for at least a subset of the main table, to establish that the reported gains are not within noise given known RL training instability?
review.limitations: The paper includes a limitations section (Appendix A) acknowledging dependence on process-level evidence annotations and the added computational cost of the external verifier. However, the discussion could be extended to cover: (a) potential reward hacking risks in the step-level verifier (e.g., models learning to produce superficially evidence-aligned but logically vacuous steps), (b) reliance on LLM-judge quality for both reward computation and evaluation metrics, and (c) applicability boundaries for domains lacking well-defined evidence sets. No explicit societal impact/negative-impact discussion beyond a brief, largely positive Impact Statement is provided; a brief discussion of misuse risk (e.g., faithfulness metrics being gamed, or judges being biased in ways that systematically disadvantage certain question types) would be a useful addition.

title: Rel-MOSS: Towards Imbalanced Relational Deep Learning on Relational Databases

review.summary: This paper addresses the class imbalance problem in relational deep learning (RDL) over relational databases, which the authors claim has not been previously studied. The proposed method, Rel-MOSS, comprises two components: (1) Rel-Gate, a relation-wise gating controller that uses attention-style estimation to modulate neighborhood messages per relation type based on their estimated likelihood of belonging to the minority class, mitigating what the authors term 'minority information collapse'; and (2) Rel-Syn, a relation-guided minority synthesizer that extends SMOTE-style over-sampling to heterogeneous entity graphs by incorporating structural 'relational signatures' (e.g., entity-type histograms, fan-in/fan-out distributions) into the distance metric used for identifying interpolation neighbors, plus an auxiliary MSE reconstruction loss on these signatures. The paper provides informal theoretical propositions motivating both components, evaluates on 12 RelBench entity classification datasets against RDL baselines and classic imbalance-handling techniques (SMOTE, GraphSMOTE, Focal loss, GraphSHA, ReVar), and includes ablations, qualitative visualizations (t-SNE, distance radar charts), extensive hyperparameter sweeps, backbone-agnosticism experiments (HGT, RelGNN), and runtime analysis.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The problem is well-motivated and practically relevant: RDL is an emerging area and class imbalance in entity classification is indeed a realistic and underexplored complication given the examples provided (fraud detection, churn prediction).
2. The empirical evaluation is broad, covering 12 diverse RelBench datasets, multiple baselines spanning both classic imbalance techniques and graph-specific methods, and multiple backbones (GraphSAGE, HGT, RelGNN), which supports some generality of the proposed approach.
3. The ablation studies (w/o Rel-Gate, w/o Rel-Syn) and qualitative analyses (representation distance radar charts, t-SNE visualization of synthetic samples) provide some support that each component contributes to performance, and that Rel-Syn's synthetic samples appear visually more consistent with the true minority manifold compared to SMOTE/GraphSMOTE.
4. Extensive hyperparameter and efficiency analyses (memory bank scale, batch size, latent dimension, runtime) are provided in the appendix, which aids reproducibility understanding.

Weaknesses:
1. Soundness of theoretical claims: Proposition 4.1 and 4.2 are presented with heavy formalism (contraction mapping, Lipschitz bounds) but rest on strong simplifying assumptions (ignoring nonlinearity, WLOG single entity type, i.i.d.-like decompositions) that are not clearly connected to the actual heterogeneous, multi-hop, non-linear GNN architecture used in practice. The propositions largely restate the well-known observation that skewed aggregation dilutes minority signal (already established for homogeneous imbalanced GNNs, e.g., GraphSMOTE's motivation) rather than deriving something novel specific to relational structure. Proposition 4.2 is essentially a conceptual claim/definition dressed as a
review.key_questions_for_authors: 1. Could you clarify how baselines were adapted to the heterogeneous, multi-table RDB setting — in particular, how SMOTE and Focal Loss (originally designed for flat feature vectors or single-graph node classification) handle multiple entity/relation types, and whether hyperparameters (k-nearest-neighbors, focal loss gamma) were tuned per dataset for fair comparison? 2. Table 1 shows some baselines (e.g., RDL, RDL-HGT, RelGNN) with exactly 0.5000/0.0000 and no standard deviation reported — does this indicate a single run, or that variance was truly zero across all runs? If the former, why were multiple seeds not run for these baselines while they were for others? 3. How exactly is B-Acc/G-Mean computed for RDL, RDL-HGT, RelGNN given that these are presumably trained with a single (not class-balanced) loss and a default threshold of 0.5 — did you also tune the decision threshold for baselines, or is the reported degenerate performance simply an artifact of an untuned threshold rather than genuine model failure? 4. Can you report a proper significance test (e.g., paired t-test or Wilcoxon) across datasets, given that many improvements over the best baseline are within 1 standard deviation? 5. Why was RDL-HGT/RelGNN with focal loss, GraphSHA, or ReVar with relation-wise weighting not included as stronger, more comparable baselines, given that GraphSHA/ReVar are designed for homogeneous graphs and might be structurally disadvantaged in the heterogeneous RDB setting used here?
review.limitations: The paper includes a limitations section (Appendix F) which appropriately identifies extensions to entity regression and use of advanced generative models as future work, and briefly notes an unverified conjecture about foundation models' resistance to imbalance. However, the discussion does not address more immediate limitations of the current work, such as: the reliance on informal/loosely justified theoretical propositions, the sensitivity of results to several hyperparameters (as shown in the extensive appendix sweeps, e.g., γ, ω, batch size, latent dimension all show large performance swings), the lack of statistical significance testing despite reporting standard deviations, and the additional complexity/hyperparameter tuning burden introduced by Rel-MOSS relative to simpler baselines. The impact statement is brief and mostly promotional; it does not discuss potential negative societal impacts, such as risks of over-sensitizing models to minority classes leading to increased false positives (e.g., wrongly flagging legitimate users as fraudulent) or the environmential/computational cost of the additional memory bank and interpolation search process at scale. I recommend the authors add discussion of these points.

title: Provably Efficient Algorithms for S- and Non-Rectangular Robust MDPs with General Parameterization

review.summary: This paper studies robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) with s-rectangular and non-rectangular uncertainty sets under general (non-tabular) policy parameterization, in both discounted and average-reward settings. The key technical contributions are: (1) an entropy-regularized discounted reduction that restores strong duality for average-reward RMDPs, which otherwise lack a minimax saddle point; (2) new Lipschitz/smoothness bounds for entropy-regularized robust value functions with respect to both general policy parameters and a linearly-parameterized transition kernel, with constants independent of state-space size (enabling extension to infinite/continuous state spaces); (3) a multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) gradient estimator for the infinite-horizon gradient that improves sample complexity by a factor of O(ε^-2) relative to fixed-horizon truncation methods; and (4) two algorithms built on these tools—a projected gradient descent (PGD) method for s-rectangular sets (O(ε^-5) sample complexity) and a Frank-Wolfe method for non-rectangular sets (O(ε^-4) discounted, O(ε^-10.5 H^5.5) average-reward). The paper claims to be the first to give end-to-end sample complexity guarantees for RMDPs with general parameterization beyond (s,a)-rectangularity, and the first such guarantees in the average-reward regime.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Addresses a genuine and recognized gap: extending sample-complexity guarantees for robust MDPs beyond (s,a)-rectangularity and beyond tabular/linear policies, and providing the first end-to-end guarantee for average-reward robust MDPs.
- The entropy-regularized discounted reduction to restore strong duality in the average-reward setting is a sensible and technically appropriate device, building on but non-trivially extending Mai & Jaillet (2021) and the discounted-reduction technique of Wang et al. (2022).
- The MLMC gradient estimator addressing infinite-horizon bias/variance tradeoffs is a reasonable and well-motivated technical tool, with a careful (if dense) analysis using median-of-means for robustness.
- The paper is thorough in its theoretical exposition; nearly all claimed results are proven in the appendix with detailed derivations (Lipschitz bounds, Danskin's theorem application, gradient dominance lemmas, convergence proofs for PGD and Frank-Wolfe).
- Comparison Table 1 clearly situates the contribution relative to prior work (Li et al. 2023, Wang et al. 2025, Ghosh et al. 2025, Chen & Huang 2024), which aids interpretability of the claimed improvements.
- The Limitations section (Appendix H) is unusually candid, acknowledging the very large polynomial exponents in the final bounds, the residual gap δ_Ξ from non-rectangularity, and dependence on the span H, along with concrete directions for improvement.

Weaknesses (affecting soundness/significance more than correctness per se):
- No empirical validation whatsoever. For a paper introducing several new algorithms (PGD, Frank-Wolfe, MLMC estimator), even small-scale synthetic experiments verifying the qualitative behavior of the estimator or algorithm convergence would substantially strengthen confidence in practical relevance and correctness of the pipeline.
- The claimed "general parameterization" is asymmetric: while the policy class is genuinely general (subject to Fisher non-degeneracy and log-policy smoothness), the transition kernel/uncertainty set must be linearly parameterized (Section 3.4) to make the machinery tractable. This is a significant restriction that somewhat undercuts the generality claimed in the title/abstract for the uncertainty-set side, though the authors do partially address this via the Wasserstein approximation argument (Assumption 3.4).
- The final sample complexity bounds are extremely high order in ε (e.g., O(ε^-5(1-γ)^-18) for PGD, O(ε^-10.5 H^5.5) for average-reward Frank-Wolfe). While the paper presents these as improvements over prior work, in absolute terms they are impractically large, and no lower bounds are given to contextualize how far from optimal these rates might be.
- Several key quantities (distribution mismatch coefficient D, curvature constant C_f, non-rectangularity gap δ_Ξ, and the span H in the average-reward reduction) are treated as given constants without concrete bounds or examples showing they are well-behaved in practice; this makes it hard to assess real-world tightness or applicability of the guarantees.
- Assumption 3.2 (unique optimality up to equivalence classes), which is essential for invoking Danskin's theorem, is asserted with limited independent justification beyond a footnote claim of being the "weakest" assumption enabling gradient-based optimization; this deserves more rigorous discussion or citation support.
- The core duality-restoration idea (entropy regularization for s-rectangular MDPs) is explicitly borrowed from Mai & Jaillet (2021), and the discounted-to-average-reward reduction is from Wang et al. (2022); combined with MLMC methodology from Blanchet et al. (2019), the technical novelty largely lies in stitching together and extending these tools to the new general-parameterization, non-rectangular setting, rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

On the specific rubric dimensions:
- Soundness (3/4): The overall proof architecture appears internally consistent and the various lemmas/theorems build logically on each other; however, several assumptions are strong and under-justified, and I did not exhaustively verify all algebraic steps in the lengthy appendix proofs.
- Presentation (3/4): The paper is dense with heavy notation and many forward references between text and appendix, which makes it hard to follow without careful cross-referencing; the comparison table and structured related work sections help mitigate this.
- Significance (3/4): The problem addressed (average-reward RMDPs with general parameterization) is important and underexplored, but the resulting bounds are so loose that practical impact in the near term is limited; the lack of experiments further limits demonstrated significance.
- Originality (3/4): The combination of ideas is novel for this specific problem setting, though individual components (entropy regularization for duality, MLMC estimators, gradient dominance arguments, Frank-Wolfe for non-convex constrained problems) are drawn from existing literature.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can you clarify how restrictive the linear transition-kernel parameterization (Section 3.4) is in practice? Does the framework meaningfully apply to genuinely non-rectangular uncertainty sets in high/infinite-dimensional continuous state spaces beyond toy linear-mixture examples?
2. How large can the distribution mismatch coefficient D and the non-rectangularity gap δ_Ξ be in realistic settings? Are there natural problem classes where these are provably small/bounded, to give readers intuition about when the theoretical guarantees are meaningful?
3. Given the very high polynomial order in ε for the final bounds (e.g., O(ε^-10.5H^5.5)), do you have any lower bound or hardness argument suggesting these rates are close to unavoidable for this problem class, or is there reason to believe substantial improvement is achievable?
4. Could you provide even a small numerical illustration (e.g., a toy MDP) validating that the MLMC estimator and PGD/Frank-Wolfe algorithms behave as predicted, to increase confidence in the practical correctness of the pipeline?
5. How sensitive are the final guarantees to misspecification of the span H in the average-reward reduction, and how practical is the adaptive H-estimation procedure discussed in Appendix F for real applications?
review.limitations: The authors include a dedicated Limitations section (Appendix H) that candidly discusses (i) the reliance on the ergodicity assumption and possible relaxation to unichain settings, (ii) the irreducible approximation error δ_Ξ arising from non-rectangularity and its unavoidability due to duality failure, and (iii) the very large polynomial dependence on ε and H in the average-reward bounds, along with proposed directions (direct average-reward analysis, improved reductions, adaptive discount schemes) for future improvement. This is a thoughtful and appropriately honest limitations discussion. However, the paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts (the Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not engage with any specific considerations), which is a minor omission given ICML's expectations, though the theoretical nature of the work makes concrete societal impacts less immediate.

title: ARGOS: Automated Functional Safety Requirement Synthesis for Embodied AI via Attribute-Guided Combinatorial Reasoning

review.summary: The paper proposes ARGOS, a two-stage LLM pipeline for automatically synthesizing Functional Safety Requirements (FSRs) for embodied AI robots operating on open-ended natural language instructions. Stage I (Attribute-Guided Hazard Discovery) parses instructions into semantic units (via spaCy), retrieves associated physical attributes from a curated rule base using BGE embedding similarity, and prompts an LLM to combinatorially reason over these attributes to produce hazard descriptions. Stage II (Scenario-Anchored Requirement Synthesis) conditions FSR generation on retrieved regulatory text (e.g., ISO 13482) and a robot hardware/capability profile to produce testable, hardware-consistent requirements. The authors evaluate the framework on 48 curated seed scenarios expanded into 365 hazard scenarios, comparing against Vanilla LLM and Physics-Aware CoT baselines using LLM-as-judge (Gemini) and a human evaluation study, plus a latent semantic topology analysis and an FSR-quality ablation study (w/o ISO, ISO-only, Vanilla, full ARGOS). Results show ARGOS scores higher on physical reliability, long-tail risk discovery, and FSR quality metrics, and the paper reports interesting findings about LLM-judge calibration bias and a 'verbosity trap' in CoT reasoning uncovered by human reviewers.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The motivation is clear and well-grounded in the literature: traditional HARA's reliance on enumerable function lists is a genuine mismatch for the open-ended instruction space of embodied AI, and the paper situates itself carefully against related work on LLM-based hazard analysis, requirements engineering, and the symbol grounding problem.
- The two-stage decomposition (attribute grounding, then regulatory/hardware-conditioned synthesis) is a sensible design, and the qualitative examples (rose/balloon, hot soup delivery) illustrate the intended benefit of attribute grounding over generic collision-based reasoning.
- The evaluation methodology goes beyond single-metric LLM-as-judge scoring: it includes a human evaluation study explicitly designed to check for LLM-judge bias, and the authors honestly report a discrepancy (LLM favoring CoT's verbose but redundant scenarios while humans penalize them) — this kind of self-critical evaluation is commendable.
- The latent semantic topology analysis (Effective Rank, Centroid Shift, Aligned Variance, CSE, Directional Similarity) is a thoughtful attempt to disentangle genuine diversity/long-tail discovery from semantic hallucination/drift, and the ablation study in Stage II isolates the separate contributions of attribute injection versus regulatory grounding.
- Appendices provide substantial transparency: full prompt templates for all conditions, a sample rule base, and detailed robot hardware specifications used for grounding.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The evaluation scale is modest (48 seeds → 365 scenarios; 108 samples used for human evaluation) for a paper claiming "extensive experiments," and no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests, confidence intervals beyond SD) is reported despite several score differences being small relative to reported standard deviations (e.g., CC score for w/o-ISO and full ARGOS is identically 8.56).
- The core evaluation instrument is an LLM-as-judge (Gemini), which is somewhat circular for judging LLM-generated hazard text; although a human study is included, only 108 scenarios and 3 reviewers were used, and no inter-rater agreement statistic (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha) is reported despite being promised ("we analyze inter-rater agreement... in Section 4.2" — this analysis does not appear quantitatively).
- The retrieval threshold τattr = 0.7 and other hyperparameters are stated without justification or sensitivity analysis.
- Although the paper emphasizes k-factor combinatorial reasoning up to k≤3, all detailed prompt templates and reported quantitative results (Tables 2–5) appear to focus on dual-factor (k=2) interactions; no explicit results are shown isolating single-, dual-, and triple-factor performance, leaving this claim under-supported.
- The Combinatorial Hazard Inference formalism (Eq. 2, the ⊗ operator) is essentially notational dressing for a prompt-construction step rather than a well-defined computational operation, and similarly for other equations (Eqs. 1, 3, 4); this raises concerns about whether the technical contribution is primarily prompt engineering with retrieval augmentation rather than a new algorithmic or learning-based method, which is a consideration for ICML's technical bar.
- Comparisons are only made against self-designed Vanilla/CoT baselines using the same backbone; no comparison is made to the actual prior LLM-based hazard-analysis systems discussed in Related Work (e.g., Aegis, Co-Hazard Analysis, Nouri et al.), which limits the ability to assess genuine advancement over the existing literature.
- The rule base underpinning attribute retrieval is expert-curated; while the authors argue this is a one-time cost that decouples atomic constraints from scenarios, there is no analysis of coverage/generalization to attributes or entities outside the curated rule base, which is somewhat in tension with the paper's central claim about solving the "infinite functional space" scalability problem.
- Physical plausibility of generated hazards/FSRs is validated only through LLM/human textual judgment, not through any simulation or physical validation, so the term "physically plausible" is judged by narrative coherence rather than verified physics.

Presentation: The paper is generally clearly written and organized, with helpful running examples, though the mathematical notation in Section 3 is somewhat superficial relative to its apparent rigor, and some empirical claims (e.g., inter-rater agreement analysis, k=3 results) are promised but not clearly delivered in the main text.

Significance: The problem — safety requirement synthesis for embodied AI — is practically important, and the framework could be a useful engineering tool, but the current evidence (small-scale, self-constructed baselines, LLM-judge-centric evaluation) limits confidence in the claimed "extensive" validation and the degree of advance over existing automated hazard analysis approaches.

Originality: The specific combination of attribute-based entity decomposition, combinatorial hazard reasoning, and regulatory/hardware-conditioned FSR synthesis for embodied AI is a reasonably novel application-level contribution, building on established ideas (RAG, attribute grounding, chain-of-thought) rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques.
review.key_questions_for_authors: 1. The paper claims to support k-factor coupled risk reasoning up to k≤3, but the reported experiments and prompt templates in the appendix focus on dual-factor interactions. Can you provide explicit quantitative results comparing single-, dual-, and triple-factor reasoning performance? 2. How sensitive are the results to the retrieval similarity threshold τattr = 0.7, and was this value tuned or chosen a priori? 3. Since the rule base is expert-curated, how does the pipeline behave when encountering entities/attributes not covered by the rule base (e.g., truly novel household objects)? What is the empirical coverage/failure rate in such cases? 4. Could you compare ARGOS against existing LLM-based hazard-analysis frameworks cited in your related work (e.g., Aegis, Nouri et al.) rather than only self-designed Vanilla/CoT baselines, to substantiate claims of advancing the state of the art? 5. Could you report inter-rater agreement statistics for the human evaluation study (promised in Section 4.1 but not shown quantitatively), and statistical significance tests for the score differences reported in Tables 2–5, especially where means are very close (e.g., the identical CC scores for w/o-ISO and full ARGOS)?
review.limitations: The conclusion briefly acknowledges that rigid adherence to current standards (e.g., ISO 13482:2014) may constrain reasoning and positions ARGOS as a human-in-the-loop assistant rather than a standalone replacement, which is a reasonable acknowledgment of scope. However, the paper does not discuss: (1) potential negative societal impacts of over-reliance on automatically generated safety requirements in real deployments (e.g., false sense of assurance, liability implications if LLM-generated FSRs miss critical hazards); (2) the risk of adversarial or out-of-distribution instructions causing silent failures in the attribute retrieval step; (3) computational/latency costs of the pipeline at scale; and (4) generalization limits of the expert-curated rule base to truly novel objects/entities. I recommend the authors add a dedicated limitations/broader impact discussion covering these points.

title: ReTabSyn: Realistic Tabular Data Synthesis via Reinforcement Learning

review.summary: The paper proposes ReTabSyn, a pipeline for tabular data synthesis that fine-tunes an autoregressive language-model generator (GReaT/GPT-2 backbone) with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Motivated by a theoretical utility-gap decomposition (Xu et al., 2023) that separates feature-marginal mismatch from conditional (P(y|X)) mismatch, the authors argue that in low-data regimes it is more important to preserve the conditional distribution than the full joint distribution. They construct oracle-free, rule-based preference pairs by perturbing either the target (Type I) or correlated feature pairs (Type II) of real/augmented rows, and use these chosen/rejected pairs to fine-tune the generator with a DPO-Positive objective. A SMOTE-like data augmentation step is used to initialize training before DPO fine-tuning. The method is evaluated across 10 tabular datasets under three challenging regimes (small sample size, class imbalance, distribution shift), compared against SMOTE, TVAE, TabSyn, GReaT, and RL-based baselines PTA and SynRL, using downstream-utility (AUROC/PR-AUC), fidelity (α-precision/β-recall, marginal/correlation similarity), and privacy (membership-inference) metrics. Ablations examine the two-stage training pipeline, oracle vs oracle-free preference construction, the DPO/SFT budget split, and augmentation size, plus a small case study on domain-constraint satisfaction.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is grounded in a clear theoretical motivation (utility decomposition into feature vs. conditional mismatch), which is used to justify design choices (target vs. feature perturbations, sampling ratio, and the SFT/DPO staging).
- The idea of oracle-free, schema-based perturbation for constructing DPO preference pairs is a reasonably novel and practical adaptation of preference optimization to structured/tabular data, avoiding the need for an external reward/classifier model used in prior RL-based tabular methods (PTA, SynRL).
- Empirical evaluation spans three realistic and practically important regimes (small-N, class imbalance, distribution shift) across 10 datasets, with a reasonably comprehensive set of baselines and metrics (utility, fidelity, privacy).
- Ablations are fairly thorough: they isolate the contribution of augmentation vs. DPO, oracle vs. oracle-free supervision, the target/feature perturbation ratio, and the SFT/DPO budget trade-off, which supports the internal consistency of the design.
- The extension to domain-constraint enforcement (Appendix H) is a nice illustration of controllability, and the reported 0% violation rate versus 1-3% for baselines is a meaningful practical benefit.

- Statistical rigor is limited: although experiments are repeated over 10 seeds, no variance/standard deviation or significance testing is reported in the main tables (Tables 2–5), making it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 0.906 vs. 0.891 PR-AUC) are statistically meaningful given the small absolute margins.

title: When Actions Go Off-Task: Detecting and Correcting Misaligned Actions in Computer-Use Agents

review.summary: This paper studies the problem of detecting and correcting "misaligned actions" in computer-use agents (CUAs) — actions that deviate from a user's authentic intent, whether due to external attacks (e.g., indirect prompt injection) or internal agent limitations (e.g., reasoning errors). The authors propose an intent-centric definition of action alignment and identify three categories of misaligned actions: Malicious Instruction Following, Harmful Unintended Behavior, and Other Task-Irrelevant Behavior. They construct MisActBench, a benchmark of 558 trajectories with 2,264 human-annotated, action-level alignment labels, combining trajectories from existing adversarial CUA benchmarks with synthetically injected unintended-subgoal trajectories for benign settings. They then propose DeAction, a runtime guardrail with a two-stage detection pipeline (lightweight fast check followed by structured systematic analysis conditioned on narrative history summaries) and an iterative correction loop that provides structured feedback to guide the agent toward aligned actions. Extensive offline experiments on MisActBench and online experiments on RedTeamCUA (adversarial) and OSWorld (benign) show that DeAction outperforms adapted baselines (Task Shield, InferAct) in detection F1, substantially reduces attack success rate while preserving/improving task success rate, and does so with moderate latency overhead, which the authors further mitigate via component substitution with lighter models.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The reframing from policy/safety-centric guardrails to an intent-centric notion of "action alignment" is a useful and practically motivated perspective, addressing a real gap (non-malicious but task-irrelevant or reasoning-driven deviations) not well covered by prior safety-policy guardrails.
- MisActBench is carefully constructed with a hybrid pipeline (real attack-induced trajectories from four established adversarial benchmarks + synthesized internal-failure trajectories), with a rigorous two-phase human annotation process and high inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa 0.84).
- The DeAction design is practical: the two-stage fast-check/systematic-analysis pipeline, narrative-summary history conditioning, and iterative structured feedback are all reasonable engineering choices, each backed by ablations (history representation, latency-performance tradeoff, model substitution for cost efficiency).
- Evaluation is extensive: offline detection across 4 backbones, online evaluation across 3 different CUAs (open- and closed-source) in both adversarial and benign settings, comparison against 4 diverse baselines, and detailed runtime/error analysis in the appendix categorized by pipeline component. This breadth strengthens confidence in the practical significance of the results.
- The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a very thorough appendix (annotation guidelines, prompts, per-category breakdowns, qualitative error examples) that aids reproducibility and transparency.

Weaknesses (soundness/originality-related):
- A substantial portion of MisActBench's "Harmful Unintended Behavior" and other internally-arising misalignment examples are synthetically constructed by having an LLM select risk primitives and injection points and merging a separately executed subgoal trajectory into a benign one. While manually validated for plausibility, this procedure could introduce artificial distributional biases (e.g., more clear-cut deviation points, primitive-driven behaviors) that may not represent the natural long-tail distribution of real internally-arising failures, potentially inflating detection performance relative to real deployment.
- The core technical components (two-stage screening, iterative self-correction with structured feedback, narrative history summarization) are largely combinations of existing ideas from the LLM-agent guardrail literature (e.g., Task Shield, InferAct, narrative summarization from Gonzalez-Pumariega et al.) rather than fundamentally new techniques; the novelty is more in the benchmark/taxonomy and CUA-specific integration than in core methodology.
