title: Proact-VL: A Proactive VideoLLM for Real-Time AI Companions

review.summary: This paper presents Proact-VL, a framework for building proactive, real-time video-LLM based AI companions, instantiated in two gaming applications: live commentary (solo and co-commentary) and player guidance. The authors construct the Live Gaming Dataset (561 hours across 12 games) with a dedicated data pipeline (ASR + speaker ID, paralinguistic labeling, domain-specific polishing for commentary; query synthesis + frame description + GPT-4.1 rewriting for guidance; persona mining), and derive a benchmark (Live Gaming Benchmark and a Streaming variant) with new metrics for both text quality (CC/LiveU/FinalQ) and proactivity timing (TimeDiff/PAUC/F1). The core method introduces a chunk-wise input schema for streaming video, a lightweight “decide-then-generate” proactive response mechanism using a special <FLAG> token and a response head that predicts a per-second speaking probability, and a training objective combining a transition-aware weighted classification loss with a stability/rate regularizer. An infinite-inference mechanism based on a dual KV-cache with a reverse-RoPE re-basing trick is also proposed to support long streaming sessions under fixed context budgets. Extensive experiments compare against offline (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro), proactive (VideoLLM-online, MMDuet, LiveStar), and real-time (LiveCC, StreamingVLM) baselines, along with ablations on losses, prompts, thresholds, window size, different backbones, judge robustness, a user study, and case/failure analysis.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper tackles a concrete and underexplored problem (fine-grained proactive timing + short, controlled utterances for streaming companions) and backs it with a large, carefully engineered dataset and multi-faceted benchmark (three scenarios, in-domain/out-of-domain/general splits, and a long-form streaming test set).
- The proactive mechanism (a decision anchor token decoupled from text generation, thresholdable score, transition-aware classification loss, and rate/consistency regularization) is a sensible and well-motivated design that explicitly addresses the failure modes of prior proactive/real-time baselines (over-triggering, jitter, or excessive silence). The ablation in Table 6 supports the necessity of both loss terms.
- The experimental section is unusually thorough for the space allotted: main results across three tasks and two metric families, common/general/out-of-domain generalization (Ego4D, Black Myth Wukong), long-horizon streaming stability, judge-robustness checks (different judges, repeated runs), a human user study, per-game breakdowns, hyperparameter sensitivity (threshold, window size), inference-efficiency profiling, and honest failure-case analysis (HUD OCR/arithmetic errors, repetitive fillers under visual clutter).
- The infinite-inference reverse-RoPE re-basing for a sliding KV-cache is a nice, algebraically clean and practically useful engineering contribution for unbounded streaming under bounded context.
- Limitations are explicitly and non-trivially discussed (weak visual grounding/hallucination, low FPS/resolution constraints, entity/version-update brittleness), rather than being a token paragraph.

Weaknesses (soundness/fairness of comparison):
- The comparison against proactive baselines (VideoLLM-online, MMDuet, LiveStar) is questionable: these models achieve near-degenerate F1 scores (e.g., MMDuet F1 = 0.05–0.32, LiveStar F1 ≈ 0.1–0.24 in several tables), which is far below what one would expect from reasonable systems even under domain shift. It is unclear whether these baselines were fine-tuned on any in-domain data, whether their thresholds/decoding hyperparameters were tuned fairly, or whether the evaluation harness (metrics, temporal binning) disadvantages them systematically. Without this clarification, the magnitude of Proact-VL's advantage over this baseline category is hard to interpret.
- Proact-VL is trained on the newly constructed 128k-sample in-domain dataset, while several proactive/real-time baselines appear to be evaluated largely out-of-the-box (zero-shot) on this domain. This conflates gains attributable to the proposed proactive mechanism/losses with gains attributable simply to in-domain supervised fine-tuning. The multi-backbone ablation (Table 9) partially helps (showing consistent improvement of “Proact-VL_backbone” over the corresponding vanilla backbone), but it does not isolate the proposed proactive-decision mechanism from the effect of chunk-wise SFT on the new data itself; an ablation that trains a baseline proactive method (e.g., MMDuet's own policy head) on the same corpus would strengthen the causal claim.
- Different response thresholds are used for main results (τ=0.3) versus ablation and hyperparameter studies (τ=0.5), without justification of why the “main” number was chosen at a different operating point than everywhere else; this raises a (likely unintentional) risk of selecting the threshold that yields the most favorable numbers for the primary tables.
- Text-quality and proactivity metrics rely heavily on LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-5.1, Gemini) scoring, including a metric (“CC”) computed as win-rate against one of the very baselines being compared (Gemini 2.5 Pro); while judge-robustness checks are provided (Appendix D), potential stylistic bias of the judge toward the fine-tuned model's output style (which was itself partly distilled from DeepSeek/GPT-4.1/Qwen3-Omni during data construction) is not discussed.
- Scope/significance: despite framing as “AI companions” broadly, all experiments, data, and evaluation are specific to gaming commentary/guidance; the generality of the proposed mechanism to other streaming-companion domains (e.g., live sports, general video chat) is asserted but not demonstrated.
- Presentation: the main paper is dense and defers most technical and empirical substance to a very long appendix; a few notational choices (e.g., R vs script R for RoPE rotation matrices in Appendix A.3) are slightly inconsistent. The persona/system-prompt construction pipeline relies on multiple LLM stages (DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-4.1, Qwen3-Omni/VL) without discussion of potential compounding of biases/errors across the pipeline.
- IP/licensing: the dataset is built from scraped YouTube professional broadcast and influencer commentary; the impact statement addresses content-safety filtering but not copyright/consent issues for redistributing derived speech/persona data or a trained model that mimics identifiable commentator styles.

Overall, the soundness of the core technical design is reasonable and the ablations for the proposed loss are convincing, but the fairness and interpretability of the headline comparisons against proactive baselines, and the disentanglement of “data effect” vs “method effect,” are the main soundness concerns.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Were the proactive baselines (VideoLLM-online, MMDuet, LiveStar) and real-time baselines fine-tuned on the Live Gaming training set, or evaluated zero-shot/off-the-shelf? If zero-shot, can you provide a controlled comparison where these baselines' policy/response heads (or the full models, if feasible) are fine-tuned on the same data, to disentangle gains from the proposed proactive mechanism versus gains from in-domain supervision?
2. Can you explain why the main results (Tables 1–3, Sec. 5.2–5.4) use τ=0.3 while all ablation/hyperparameter analyses (Sec. 5.5–5.6, Appendix I) use τ=0.5? Were baseline thresholds/hyperparameters tuned with comparable effort, and how sensitive are the relative rankings in Tables 1–3 to this choice?
3. The F1 scores for MMDuet and LiveStar are near zero across nearly all scenarios (e.g., 0.05–0.32). Could you clarify the exact protocol used to run these baselines (checkpoints, prompts, decision thresholds) and provide qualitative examples of their outputs to rule out an implementation or evaluation-harness issue that unfairly disadvantages them?
4. How much of the improvement in Table 9 (fine-tuning different backbones with Proact-VL) is attributable to the proposed proactive decision head/losses versus simply performing supervised chunk-wise fine-tuning on the new dataset (e.g., is there a variant that fine-tunes the backbone with only the causal LM loss and a naive silence-token/binary head, without the transition-aware weighting and regularizer)?
5. Could you comment on licensing/consent considerations for training on scraped professional broadcast and influencer commentary, particularly regarding style/persona mimicry of identifiable individuals, and whether the released dataset/model will include any usage restrictions?
review.limitations: The paper includes a dedicated limitations discussion (Appendix L) covering weak visual grounding/hallucination in generated commentary, constraints from low FPS/resolution sparse sampling relative to real gaming content (HD, 120+ FPS), and brittleness in entity/character recognition as games update over time; it also includes a societal-impact statement addressing misinformation/bias risks and describes data-cleaning steps taken. This is a reasonably candid treatment. However, the authors do not discuss (a) potential copyright/consent issues in using scraped professional/influencer commentary and persona-mimicking synthetic data, or (b) the risk that a system trained to mimic human commentator styles could be used to impersonate or replace human commentators/streamers without attribution—these points would strengthen the impact discussion.

title: A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities

review.summary: This paper introduces NeuroCognition, a benchmark suite built from three established neuropsychological tests (Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices for abstract/relational reasoning, Spatial Working Memory for maintenance/search, and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test for cognitive flexibility) adapted into text and image variants at multiple difficulty levels for evaluating LLMs. The authors design process-aware metrics (e.g., Sswm penalizing illegal/repeated/no-box moves, Swcst with perseverative-response and failure-to-maintain-set rates) rather than raw accuracy, and evaluate ~10 recent proprietary and open-weight multimodal LLMs. Key findings include: models perform much better on text than image inputs and degrade with increased task complexity; explicit chain-of-thought reasoning is not uniformly beneficial (sometimes hurting RAPM MC performance); simple human-like assistance (pattern hints, note-taking) yields mixed/limited but sometimes consistent gains (especially note-taking on WCST); models show relatively strong cognitive flexibility (WCST) compared to abstract reasoning (RAPM) or complex working memory (hard SWM). The paper also performs an exploratory factor analysis on 156 models across 10 standard benchmarks, finding a single dominant "general capability" factor, and correlates aggregate NeuroCognition scores with external benchmarks (Long HotPotQA, ARC-AGI-2, LLM Task Interference) to argue the new benchmark captures both shared and distinct cognitive signal relative to standard evaluations. Extensive appendices detail item-generation algorithms, prompts, and full per-model results.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The combination of three complementary, well-established neuropsychological constructs (fluid reasoning, working memory, cognitive flexibility) into one coherent, multimodal, scalable benchmark is a useful and reasonably novel framing relative to prior single-task/single-modality cognitive-test adaptations for LLMs.
- Metric design is thoughtful: rather than naive accuracy, the SWM and WCST scores explicitly account for structurally unjustified moves, partial completion, and rule-adherence dynamics (PR, FMS), giving more process-level insight into model behavior than typical benchmarks.
- The experimental scope is broad: 10 SOTA models, multiple modalities, difficulty levels, and several targeted ablations (reasoning on/off, pattern hints, note-taking/cognitive offloading).
- The factor analysis over 156 models and correlation study with external benchmarks is a nice complementary analysis that helps contextualize NeuroCognition relative to "general capability" and situates the new benchmark within the broader evaluation landscape.
- Reproducibility support is strong: detailed generation algorithms (Appendix A/B), full prompts (Appendix F), qualitative failure-case tables, and complete per-model, per-run results with standard deviations in the appendix.
- Interesting, somewhat counterintuitive findings (e.g., reasoning sometimes hurts performance, models are more "human-like" on WCST than RAPM) that could be useful diagnostic signals for the community.

Weaknesses (Soundness):
- Many statistical claims rest on small sample sizes (N=4–10 models) with correspondingly weak power; several ablations report and interpret non-significant p-values (e.g., pattern hints, note-taking on SWM) while still drawing qualitative conclusions from the trends, and there is no correction for the sizeable number of hypothesis tests conducted across tables 4–7 and Figure 2.
- The "human worst-case" baselines used for SWM and WCST are analytically derived idealized bounds rather than empirically measured human performance, which is a departure from standard neuropsychological practice of comparing to normed human data; this weakens the strength of claims that models "exceed" or "align with" human performance, since the comparison point is not an actual human distribution.
- For RAPM text, human performance is not established at all (only image RAPM has a literature-reported human baseline), leaving one of the two primary modalities without any human anchor, which is acknowledged but still limits the interpretability of "human alignment" claims for text.
- The correlation analysis uses "best" leaderboard scores for ARC-AGI-2 that may reflect different reasoning/testing conditions than those used to generate the paper's own NeuroCognition scores, potentially confounding the correlation estimates.
- Reasoning was disabled only for RAPM (for models with "overthinking" issues) but not necessarily consistently handled elsewhere, introducing some methodological inconsistency across tasks when comparing reasoning effects.
- Related work section is largely a list of citations without deep comparative discussion of how NeuroCognition differs from or improves upon the most closely related concurrent cognitive-benchmark efforts.

Presentation:
- Overall structure and tables are clear and results are well organized, but the visible manuscript is riddled with unresolved "(?)" citation placeholders throughout the text (likely an anonymization/compilation artifact), which materially hampers the ability to verify claims attributed to prior work (e.g., specific human RPM performance figures, specific benchmark provenance).
- Figures (heatmap in Fig. 2) are informative but dense; some finer distinctions (e.g., which correlations are truly meaningful vs. spurious given small N) could be presented more cautiously.

Significance/Originality:
- The benchmark is a genuinely useful diagnostic contribution and the process-based scoring is a nice methodological advance over simple accuracy-based cognitive tests for LLMs.
- However, the paper stops short of demonstrating that NeuroCognition can meaningfully improve model training (as speculated in Future Work) or that it captures constructs not already partially covered by existing agentic/long-context benchmarks; the correlation evidence for "distinct but related" cognitive abilities is suggestive rather than conclusive given sample sizes.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Why was an idealized "human worst-case" (rather than empirically measured human performance) used as the baseline for SWM and WCST, and how would conclusions change if compared against actual human subject data instead?
2. Given the small sample sizes (often N=4 to N=10 models) underlying many of the ablation and correlation analyses, how do you address the risk of overinterpreting non-significant or marginally significant trends, and did you apply any correction for multiple comparisons?
3. For the programmatically generated RAPM text items, was item difficulty balanced or controlled across the different attribute-based rule types, and how might the random sampling of 200 items affect fairness across model comparisons?
4. The ARC-AGI-2 scores used in the correlation analysis are drawn from the public leaderboard's best results; were these obtained under comparable reasoning/inference settings to those used for the NeuroCognition scores in this paper? Could mismatched settings confound the reported correlations?
5. Why was reasoning disabled only for RAPM (for models exhibiting "overthinking") and not similarly investigated/adjusted for SWM/WCST, and could this asymmetry bias the reasoning-related conclusions drawn across tasks?
review.limitations: The authors include an explicit Limitations section acknowledging (1) cost-constrained sample sizes for RAPM, (2) the unresolved question of whether neuropsychological tests standardized on humans validly transfer to LLMs (construct/psychometric validity), and (3) the assumption that these well-established human tests remain valid and reliable when applied to LLMs without further psychometric validation. This is a reasonably thorough and honest limitations discussion. However, the authors could further discuss statistical power/multiple-comparison concerns in their many ablation studies and correlation analyses, and could more explicitly caveat the use of idealized "human worst-case" baselines rather than empirical human data. A brief societal impact statement is provided, disclaiming claims of LLM consciousness or human-equivalent cognition, which is adequate.

title: Stochastic Gradient Variational Inference with Price's Gradient Estimator from Bures-Wasserstein to Parameter Space

review.summary: This paper studies the theoretical gap between Wasserstein Variational Inference (WVI, optimizing over Bures-Wasserstein space) and Black-Box Variational Inference (BBVI, optimizing over Euclidean parameter space) for Gaussian variational families. Prior work showed WVI (via SPBWGD) achieves better iteration complexity than BBVI (via SPGD with the reparametrization gradient). The authors show that this gap is due to the choice of gradient estimator rather than the underlying geometry: WVI traditionally uses a Hessian-based estimator derivable via Price's theorem/Stein's identity, while BBVI traditionally uses the reparametrization gradient (first-order only). The paper (1) derives a refined, tighter analysis of SPBWGD with Price's gradient, improving the previous complexity bound by Diao et al. (2023) by a factor of κ in the log term and log(1/ε) in the asymptotic term via using a Bregman-divergence-based variance bound instead of a Wasserstein-distance-based one; (2) shows that BBVI with SPGD can also use an analogous Price/Hessian-based gradient estimator for the scale parameter, achieving matching iteration complexity to WVI, thus closing the previously observed gap; (3) provides a symmetric proof technique for both algorithms based on Bregman divergences and a generalized Lyapunov/two-stage step-size analysis (extending Gower et al. 2019 and Stich 2019) that gives any-time convergence guarantees with improved dependence on both target accuracy ε and initialization distance Δ; (4) empirically validates on 12 real posteriorDB benchmarks that switching to Price's Hessian-based gradient estimator (rather than switching geometry) is the primary driver of the performance gains previously attributed to WVI over BBVI.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The central conceptual contribution—disentangling the effect of geometry (Bures-Wasserstein vs Euclidean parameter space) from the effect of gradient estimator (Price/Hessian-based vs reparametrization)—is a genuinely interesting and clarifying insight in the theory of gradient-based VI. It resolves an apparent puzzle in the literature (why would BW space intrinsically be superior?) with a satisfying explanation.

- The technical execution is solid: the refined variance bound using Bregman divergences (Lemma 3.4/3.5, building on Lemma C.5) is a genuine, nontrivial improvement over Diao et al. (2023)'s approach, and it is used consistently to obtain matching bounds for both SPBWGD and SPGD. title: Beyond Global Alignment: Fine-Grained Motion-Language Retrieval via Pyramidal Shapley-Taylor Learning

review.summary: This paper proposes Pyramidal Shapley-Taylor (PST) Learning, a framework for fine-grained motion-language retrieval that goes beyond the common practice of aligning entire motion sequences with global text embeddings. Motivated by an analogy to human motion perception (joint → segment → holistic), the method decomposes motion into body joints and temporal segments and aligns them progressively with word/phrase-level text tokens across three stages (joint-wise, segment-wise, holistic). To capture context-dependent cross-modal correspondence, the authors adapt the Shapley-Taylor Interaction (STI) index from game theory, quantifying the marginal contribution of a motion-text token pair under random permutations of the joint token set, and use a lightweight learned STI Estimation Head to approximate this expensive computation via distillation. Token compression from joint/word level to segment/phrase level is performed with a KNN-DPC-based compressor. A self-distillation loss further encourages joint-wise similarity distributions to guide segment-wise ones. Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT-ML under both
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The problem (fine-grained motion-language alignment) is well-motivated and clearly framed relative to prior global-alignment approaches.
- The adaptation of Shapley-Taylor Interaction to cross-modal token alignment is an interesting and relatively novel idea, distinct from typical contrastive or attention-based fine-grained alignment schemes.
- Experiments span two standard benchmarks (HumanML3D, KIT-ML) under two evaluation protocols (All / Small Batch), with consistent improvements over multiple recent baselines (TEMOS, T2M, TMR, MotionPatch, Lyu et al.).
- Reasonably thorough ablations on the distillation losses (λS, λD), compression ratio, and motion representation choice.
- Good qualitative visualizations at joint-wise and segment-wise granularities, plus an appendix exploration of LLM-driven part-level text augmentation (PST++), showing further gains.
- The paper is generally well organized, with clear figures illustrating the pyramidal pipeline and the STI concept.

Weaknesses (Soundness):
- The ablation studies do not include a critical baseline: removing the joint-wise and/or segment-wise alignment stages entirely (i.e., holistic-only or two-stage pyramids) to isolate how much of the improvement stems from the pyramidal multi-scale contrastive design itself versus the STI/self-distillation losses. Without this, it is hard to attribute gains specifically to fine-grained alignment.
- The λS=0 and λD=0 ablations remove only the STI distillation and self-distillation losses, but the joint-wise/segment-wise contrastive losses remain active in all settings; thus the specific contribution of the STI mechanism (as opposed to simply having multi-scale contrastive losses) is not cleanly isolated.
- No variance/standard deviation or multiple-seed results are reported, despite the Small Batch protocol relying on random partitioning and the overall gains over the closest baseline (Lyu et al., 2025) being moderate (e.g., R@1 12.45 vs 11.80 on HumanML3D All). This makes it difficult to assess statistical significance of the improvements.
- The theoretical justification for applying Shapley-Taylor Interaction—originally designed for feature attribution/explainability in a single coalition game—to a bipartite cross-modal alignment setting (concatenating motion and text tokens into one coalition and computing a k=2 interaction index) is somewhat ad hoc; a more rigorous grounding or discussion of why this specific adaptation is principled would strengthen the soundness claims.
- The framework heavily depends on the pre-existing MotionPatch representation and ViT encoder from Yu et al. (2024); the core novelty is thus more about the training/alignment scheme than the motion representation itself, though this is reasonably disclosed.
- Related recent baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., CAR, MoRAG, SGAR) are not compared in the main experimental tables (SGAR appears only in an appendix table), weakening the completeness of the empirical comparison.
- Minor: notation inconsistency in the appendix derivation of Equation 3 (K vs. T used interchangeably in Eq. 12), which could confuse readers verifying the derivation.

Presentation:
- Overall clear writing and figures, though the method section (particularly Sec 3.2–3.3) is dense with notation that could benefit from a running example or clearer connection to Figure 1/2.
- The main paper does not report training/inference computational overhead of the STI estimation head relative to baseline retrieval training, despite emphasizing that exact STI computation is "prohibitively expensive"; a wall-clock or FLOPs comparison would clarify practical cost trade-offs.

Significance and Originality:
- The paper addresses a meaningful problem in a growing sub-area (motion-language retrieval) and shows consistent, if moderate, gains over strong recent baselines.
- The combination of pyramidal decomposition + Shapley-Taylor-inspired interaction modeling + self-distillation is a reasonably original synthesis of ideas, though each individual component (multi-scale alignment, token compression, KL self-distillation) has precedent in other cross-modal retrieval literature (e.g., vision-language fine-grained alignment).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can you provide an ablation removing the joint-wise and/or segment-wise alignment branches entirely (holistic-only, or two-stage variants) to isolate how much performance gain is attributable to the pyramidal multi-scale design itself, independent of the STI/self-distillation losses?
2. How sensitive are the reported gains to random seed / batch partitioning (especially under the Small Batch protocol)? Could you report mean ± std over multiple runs?
3. Can you clarify how the STI Estimation Head is used at inference time—i.e., does test-time retrieval rely purely on the contrastively-trained embeddings, with STI serving only as an auxiliary training signal? If so, please state this explicitly and discuss what fraction of the gains stem from STI distillation versus the base pyramidal contrastive objective.
4. What is the additional computational/training-time overhead introduced by the STI Estimation Head and Monte Carlo STI sampling compared to a standard multi-scale contrastive baseline without STI?
5. Could you elaborate on the theoretical justification for treating motion and text tokens as players in a single coalition game for computing Shapley-Taylor interactions, given that Shapley values were originally designed for attributing a single scalar outcome to a set of cooperating features/players within one model, not typically for cross-modal alignment scoring?
review.limitations: The paper includes a brief limitations discussion in the conclusion (local bias toward common/frequent poses, difficulty with rare/complex motions) and mentions future work toward open-vocabulary understanding. However, the discussion does not address broader potential limitations such as computational overhead of the STI mechanism, sensitivity to random seeds/batch composition, or potential negative societal impacts (e.g., misuse of fine-grained motion-language retrieval for surveillance or biometric profiling). Adding a brief discussion of computational cost trade-offs and any societal implications of precise human-motion analysis technology would strengthen this section.

title: HuPER: A Human-Inspired Framework for Phonetic Perception

review.summary: The paper introduces HuPER, a modular, cognitively-inspired framework for phonetic (phone-level) transcription. The system consists of (i) HuPER-Recognizer, a WavLM-Large CTC phone recognizer trained with a self-training procedure in which a learned Corrector converts G2P-derived canonical phoneme sequences into acoustically-grounded 'realized' phone pseudo-labels, justified through a doubly-robust risk-correction (DRRC) analysis borrowed from the missing-data/causal-inference literature; (ii) HuPER-Perceiver, a WFST-based phone-to-word decoder that composes phone lattices with lexicon/LM constraints; and (iii) HuPER-Scheduler, a distortion-score-based controller that routes between pure bottom-up decoding and top-down, reference/hypothesis-constrained (Dysfluent-WFST) decoding depending on estimated evidence quality. The authors report state-of-the-art phonetic feature error rate (PFER) on five English phone-recognition benchmarks using only ~100 hours of training data, competitive zero-shot transfer to 95 unseen languages (VoxAngeles), and improved robustness on a small disordered-speech (PPA) corpus using the adaptive scheduler and reference-guided decoding. Additional analyses probe representational geometry (RSA against PanPhon distinctive features and EMA/acoustic references) and emission-level canonical-restoration behavior.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The central motivation—supervising phonetic models with acoustically-realized phone sequences instead of canonical G2P targets, and modeling perception as an adaptive combination of bottom-up/top-down evidence—is well grounded in the psycholinguistic literature and clearly articulated.
- Task 1 results are compelling: HuPER-Recognizer attains the best average PFER across five English variation benchmarks while using orders of magnitude less labeled/training data than the baselines, and all baseline numbers are reportedly reproduced under a unified pipeline, which strengthens the comparison.
- Zero-shot multilingual evaluation on 95 languages (VoxAngeles) is a nice large-scale generalization test, and the English-only model is shown to be competitive with strongly multilingual-trained baselines.
- The paper includes a thoughtful and unusually transparent failure-case analysis (Appendix E) categorizing when top-down refinement helps or hurts, which is valuable both scientifically and for practitioners.
- The theoretical component (Theorem 3.1 / Appendix B) is a clean, technically self-contained doubly-robust identity for a proxy-label correction procedure.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The link between the theoretical DRRC estimator (Eq. 3–4, which explicitly involves a propensity function g and an inverse-propensity-weighted correction) and the actually implemented self-training recipe (Algorithm 1, which just alternates teacher prediction + Corrector-based relabeling) is not made explicit. No propensity model gˆ is estimated or used at training time in Algorithm 1, so it is unclear in what precise sense the practical procedure
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How exactly does the practical self-training procedure in Algorithm 1 correspond to the doubly-robust corrector Cg(W) analyzed in Theorem 3.1? Is a propensity function g(z, ŷ) ever estimated/used in practice, or is the Corrector C(·) meant to play a different theoretical role? Please clarify the mapping between theory and implementation.
2. In Table 2 and Fig. 6b, is the reported τ* selected on the same nfvPPA data used for evaluation (i.e., no held-out split)? If so, how do the results change under a proper train/validation/test split or cross-validation over speakers, given the very small size of the dataset (1h1m12s, 35 speakers)?
3. What exactly constitutes the '100 hours' of training data reported in the abstract and Table 1 — is this the size of the LibriSpeech subset used for self-training pseudo-labeling (in addition to TIMIT), or a different quantity? A precise breakdown of labeled vs. pseudo-labeled hours at each stage would help contextualize the efficiency claim.
4. Can you provide an ablation removing the Corrector/DRRC-style correction (i.e., naive self-training with raw G2P labels or raw teacher pseudo-labels) to isolate how much of the PFER improvement is attributable specifically to the proposed correction step versus generic self-training/backbone choice (WavLM-Large)?
5. For the canonical-restoration diagnostic (Sec. 8.2, Appendix F.2), how confident are you that TTS-synthesized audio faithfully reproduces the acoustic cues associated with natural glottalization/flapping/cluster reduction, rather than reflecting artifacts of the particular TTS system used to generate the 10 phrases per category?
review.limitations: The paper includes a limitations paragraph acknowledging the small amount of human-verified phone labels, the heuristic/rule-based nature of the scheduler, and the fact that only a subset of human perceptual pathways is modeled. However, it does not discuss: (1) the risk of overfitting/threshold-tuning on the very small nfvPPA evaluation set used for the multi-path scheduler experiments, (2) potential confounds in the TTS-based canonical-restoration diagnostic, or (3) societal/ethical considerations specific to using clinical speech data (PPA patients) beyond a generic impact statement. I would suggest the authors add explicit discussion of these points, particularly the validity of tuning/reporting τ* on the same small evaluation corpus, and any privacy/consent considerations for the PPA speech data used.

title: Multi-Agent Teams Hold Experts Back

review.summary: This paper studies whether self-organizing, equal-status teams of LLM agents can achieve "strong synergy" (matching or exceeding their best individual member), a concept borrowed from organizational psychology on human teamwork. Using both classic human-team decision tasks (NASA Moon Survival, Lost at Sea, Student Body President) with controllable, injected expertise, and five frontier ML benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, SimpleQA, GPQA-Diamond, HLE, MATH-500) with naturally distributed model expertise, the authors show that unstructured multi-agent LLM deliberation systematically fails to reach the performance of the single best team member, even when the expert's identity is explicitly revealed via carefully tuned prompts (relative synergy gaps of 8–38%). Through controlled ablations comparing "Expert Not Mentioned" vs. "Reveal Expert" conditions, they argue the bottleneck is expertise *leveraging* rather than *identification*. An LLM-based (Gemini) conversational coding scheme, validated against human annotators, shows that non-expert agents tend to engage in "integrative compromise" (averaging opinions) rather than "epistemic deference" to the identified expert, and that this compromise behavior worsens with team size and correlates with worse team performance. Finally, they show the same consensus-seeking mechanism confers some robustness to an adversarial saboteur agent, suggesting a trade-off between alignment/agreeableness and expertise utilization. The paper releases an evaluation harness for measuring team synergy.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The framing borrowed from organizational psychology (strong vs. weak synergy, expertise identification vs. leveraging) is a clean, principled lens for evaluating self-organizing multi-agent systems, distinct from most prior work that studies fixed roles/workflows or pure ensembling.
- The experimental design is fairly comprehensive: two complementary settings (controllable psychology tasks and realistic ML benchmarks), multiple information conditions (No Info, Expert Not Mentioned, Reveal Expert, Best Individual), concentrated vs. distributed expertise, and team-size sweeps (2/4/8 agents).
- The identification-vs-leveraging decomposition is a nice methodological contribution and the
review.key_questions_for_authors: 1. The ML benchmark results rest on only 100 problems and 2 seeds per benchmark; how robust are the reported relative synergy gaps (e.g., via bootstrap confidence intervals), and could the 8–38% range shrink or reverse-order under more extensive sampling? 2. Team compositions for ML benchmarks were explicitly chosen to maximize variance in individual model accuracy, which mechanically increases the 'at least one correct' upper bound and the apparent gap. How do results change with more homogeneous, realistic team compositions (e.g., similarly-capable frontier models)? 3. The final answer is produced by a single randomly-selected agent after discussion; how do you rule out that this elicitation step (rather than the deliberation itself) is responsible for some of the observed leveraging gap, e.g., if the selected agent mis-summarizes an otherwise expert-aligned consensus? 4. Could you elaborate on the prompt-tuning process for the 'Reveal Expert' condition (how many variants were tried, what criteria were optimized) and address the possibility that different (perhaps more directive/forceful) prompt designs could substantially close the gap? 5. The attribution of integrative-compromise behavior to RLHF/alignment procedures is central to the discussion but is explicitly acknowledged as correlational; do you have any preliminary evidence (e.g., differences across model families with different alignment recipes, or base vs. instruction-tuned variants) that would support or contradict this hypothesis?
review.limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge two limitations in Section 5.3: (1) the attribution of consensus-seeking behavior to alignment/RLHF is correlational, without a base-vs-aligned model comparison, and (2) the benchmark suite, while spanning multiple tasks, is still a small subset relative to real-world multi-agent deployments. These are reasonable but could be extended: the paper does not discuss (a) the potential sensitivity of ML-benchmark findings to the small 100-problem/2-seed sample sizes, (b) the appropriateness of the 'at least one correct' oracle as an upper bound versus more realistic ensembling baselines (e.g., majority voting, mixture-of-agents), or (c) potential circularity/bias risks from using an LLM (Gemini) to code conversational transcripts, despite the human-agreement check. A broader impact statement is present but generic; given the paper's implications for deploying autonomous multi-agent systems in high-stakes settings, a slightly more substantive discussion of risks (e.g., over-reliance on self-organizing teams in safety-critical domains) would strengthen this section.

title: Tabula RASA: Exposing and Breaking the Relational Bottleneck in Transformers

review.summary: The paper studies why transformers struggle with multi-hop relational reasoning over knowledge graphs. It restates known circuit-complexity results (transformers are TC0, TC0 cannot solve graph connectivity) to argue that Ω(k) layers are necessary for k-hop reasoning, and gives an informal proof sketch of this claim via a reduction to layered-graph connectivity. Building on this motivation, the authors propose RASA (Relation-Aware Sparse Attention), which (1) masks attention to only graph-adjacent positions and (2) adds learnable per-relation-type scalar biases to attention scores. They argue this reduces the combinatorial space of possible attention patterns from O(2^(n^2)) to O(2^m) for a graph with m edges. RASA is instantiated on top of a DistilBERT encoder with a 3-layer GNN and evaluated on the MetaQA multi-hop KGQA benchmark, where it is reported to reach 97.7% accuracy on 3-hop questions, exceeding EmbedKGQA's 94.8% on the same split. An attention-entropy analysis is also presented, showing that RASA's attention distributions have lower entropy than a standard transformer's.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The motivation connecting circuit complexity (TC0, graph connectivity) to the empirical difficulty of multi-hop KGQA is a reasonable and intuitive narrative, and the paper is organized in an easy-to-follow way (theory → method → experiments → discussion).
- The proposed architectural change (adjacency masking + relation-specific attention bias) is simple, easy to implement, and cheap.
- The paper is honest about certain limitations, e.g., that RASA does not change the asymptotic depth requirement, and includes some discussion of when the method is/is not useful.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The central empirical claim is misleading. Table 1 shows that NSM (He et al., 2021) achieves 98.9% on 3-hop, which is *higher* than RASA's 97.7%, and NSM also strictly dominates RASA on 1-hop and 2-hop (97.1% vs 85.6%, 99.9% vs 81.8%). The abstract, main results section, and conclusion repeatedly emphasize beating
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. NSM outperforms RASA on every single split in Table 1 (including 3-hop: 98.9% vs 97.7%), yet the abstract/conclusion exclusively highlight beating the weaker EmbedKGQA baseline. Why is NSM not treated as the primary point of comparison, and how do you justify the paper's framing given this result?
2. Can you provide ablations isolating the individual contributions of (a) sparse adjacency masking alone and (b) edge-type biases alone, versus the full RASA model and a vanilla transformer/GNN baseline with the same backbone/hidden size?
3. Why was one seed excluded from the 1-hop results due to "training instability," and was the same exclusion protocol (with the same warmup schedule) applied consistently to the 2-hop and 3-hop experiments? Please report results from all seeds without exclusion.
4. Given the large standard deviations reported (e.g., ±3.6 for 2-hop), what is the statistical significance of the reported 3-hop improvement over EmbedKGQA (94.8 vs 97.7), and how many seeds were used for that number?
5. Can you provide evidence beyond MetaQA (e.g., other multi-hop KGQA or synthetic graph-reachability benchmarks) to support the generality of the claim that RASA's advantage "grows with reasoning depth"?
review.limitations: The paper lists some limitations (need for explicit graph structure, unchanged asymptotic depth requirement, benefits concentrated on complex queries), which is a reasonable start. However, it does not discuss the reliability of the reported numbers given the small number of seeds, the exclusion of an outlier seed, or the fact that a stronger baseline (NSM) outperforms RASA throughout. There is no discussion of broader societal impact, but given the technical nature of the contribution this is a minor omission compared to the methodological limitations noted above.

title: Seeing Is Believing? A Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models on Visual Illusions and Anomalies

review.summary: The paper introduces VIA-Bench, a benchmark of 1,004 multiple-choice question-answer pairs designed to test whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can correctly perceive and reason about visual illusions and anomalies (color, motion, gestalt, geometric/spatial, general visual illusions, and biological/structural anomalies). The dataset is built through a multi-stage, human-in-the-loop pipeline (taxonomy design, data collection from web sources and existing datasets such as TET, filtering, QA annotation with debiasing, and quality verification). The authors evaluate over 20 MLLMs (proprietary, open-source, and reasoning-enhanced/'thinking' models) using both rule-based matching and LLM-as-a-judge protocols, averaged over five runs. Key findings include: (1) a large gap between human accuracy (93.3%) and the best model (69.2%); (2) inconsistent performance across categories and model families, with no single model dominating; (3) a 'CoT paradox' where explicit chain-of-thought prompting (zero-shot or manually crafted) generally fails to improve, and often degrades, accuracy on illusion/anomaly tasks, attributed to hallucination reinforcement and overthinking rather than correction of initial misperception; and (4) qualitative case studies illustrating failure modes such as visual misperception, self-negation under uncertainty, and repetitive/self-contradictory reasoning traces in long CoT outputs.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Addresses a timely and underexplored question: whether MLLMs actually perceive visual evidence versus pattern-matching to canonical priors, using illusions/anomalies as a diagnostic lens.
- Broad empirical coverage: 20+ models spanning proprietary, open-source, and reasoning-enhanced categories, with two independent scoring protocols (regex match and LLM-judge) and 5-run averaging to reduce noise.
- The taxonomy is grounded in established cognitive-psychology literature and is reasonably comprehensive (six well-motivated categories).
- The 'CoT paradox' finding is interesting and reinforced with both quantitative results (Table 2, Fig. 5) and detailed qualitative case studies (Appendix H) that make the failure modes concrete and legible (e.g., overthinking loops, self-negation, hallucination reinforcement).
- A 'blind' (vision-disabled) baseline is included, which is a valuable sanity check, and its results (revealing that pure text priors can already solve some categories at reasonably high accuracy) are honestly reported.
- Reasonably transparent reproducibility details (model versions, prompts, regex matching rules, judge prompts) are provided in the appendix.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The human-evaluation methodology is under-specified: the number of annotators, their expertise/independence from the dataset curators, and inter-annotator agreement are not reported, which is important since human accuracy (93.3%) is the benchmark's headline reference point and a potential source of circularity if annotators overlap with dataset creators.
- The blind (text-only) baseline is only reported for one model (GPT-4-Turbo) and one 'Random Choice' control, yet the finding that this blind model reaches 87.95% on Motion Illusions and 61.11% on Geometric/Spatial Illusions raises a serious question about how much of the benchmark can be solved via language-only shortcuts despite the stated debiasing effort; this is not investigated systematically across all models/categories, weakening the paper's core claim that VIA-Bench isolates visual perception.
- Per-category sample sizes are quite small (e.g., Gestalt Illusions is only ~11.7% of 1,004, roughly 117 items), yet fine-grained per-category rankings and claims (e.g., 'no model performs well across all aspects') are drawn from these small subsets; combined with visible run-to-run variance (Appendix Table 5), the statistical reliability of category-level comparisons is questionable, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported in the main tables.
- Details of the ground-truth verification and disagreement-resolution process (e.g., how many items were rejected/revised in cross-verification) are not quantified, limiting confidence in dataset quality assurances beyond a qualitative description.
- The dataset construction heavily aggregates existing web images and datasets (e.g., TET); the underlying stimuli are largely not novel, and originality mainly lies in aggregation, taxonomy, and QA formulation rather than new illusion content, which somewhat limits methodological originality.

Weaknesses (significance/originality):
- Several closely related benchmarks already probe similar territory (HallusionBench, Illusory VQA, GVIL, TET, ZeroBench) and prior literature has already observed that CoT can hurt performance on counter-intuitive tasks (as the authors themselves cite, e.g., Liu et al. 2025). VIA-Bench's contribution is best framed as a broader, more current, and more systematically curated aggregation/extension of this research direction rather than a fundamentally new methodological or conceptual advance. A direct comparison table against these closest prior works (dataset size, categories, models tested, findings) would strengthen the positioning.
- The paper is purely evaluative; no mitigation strategies (e.g., fine-tuning, visual grounding-augmented reasoning, tool use) are explored to test whether the identified bottleneck is addressable, which limits the actionable impact of the work beyond diagnosis.

Weaknesses (presentation):
- The related work section is dense with citations but offers limited direct, structured comparison (e.g., a comparison table) against the most relevant prior benchmarks.
- No dedicated 'Limitations' section is provided in the main text; the Impact Statement is generic ('We do not foresee major ethical or social concerns') and does not discuss dataset size, potential memorization of web-sourced illusion images by pretrained models, or the constraints of a multiple-choice format.
- Minor readability issues: heavy reliance on color-coded tables (dark/light green highlighting) that may not be robust for colorblind readers or grayscale printing, ironic given the paper's own focus on color illusions.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How many human annotators contributed to the reported 93.3% human-accuracy baseline, what was their background/expertise, and were any of them also involved in dataset curation or ground-truth verification (potential circularity)?
2. Given that a vision-disabled GPT-4-Turbo scores surprisingly high on some categories (e.g., 87.95% on Motion Illusions, 61.11% on Geometric/Spatial Illusions) purely via textual priors, can you report blind-model baselines systematically across all models and categories to quantify how much of VIA-Bench is solvable without visual input, and discuss how this affects the benchmark's claim of isolating visual perception?
3. What is the inter-annotator agreement rate during ground-truth verification, and how many candidate QA pairs were rejected or revised during the 'Assurance & Debiasing' stage?
4. Given the small per-category sample sizes (e.g., ~117 for Gestalt Illusions) and visible run-to-run variance (Appendix Table 5), how robust are the fine-grained per-category rankings and claims in Table 1? Could you report confidence intervals or variance for the main results table?
5. Have you considered any mitigation experiments (e.g., visual-grounded CoT, fine-tuning on illusion-augmented data, iterative image re-inspection) to test whether the identified perceptual bottleneck can be alleviated, beyond pure evaluation?
review.limitations: The paper lacks a dedicated Limitations section; the Impact Statement is brief and generic, stating no foreseeable ethical/societal concerns without discussing concrete limitations such as: (1) the relatively modest and imbalanced per-category dataset size that limits statistical robustness of fine-grained comparisons, (2) potential data contamination/memorization since many illusion images are sourced from public web content that may overlap with model pretraining corpora, (3) reliance on a closed multiple-choice format that cannot fully capture nuanced open-ended reasoning failures, and (4) insufficiently detailed human-annotation methodology (number/expertise of annotators, agreement rates). I recommend the authors add an explicit Limitations subsection addressing these points and briefly discuss possible negative impacts (e.g., benchmark gaming, overclaiming of AGI-relevance) alongside constructive mitigation suggestions.

title: PRISM: A 3D Probabilistic Neural Representation for Interpretable Shape Modeling

review.summary: This paper proposes PRISM, a framework for statistical shape modeling that combines implicit neural representations with an information-geometric treatment of uncertainty. Shapes are represented as covariate-conditioned displacement fields from a shared template, and the conditional distribution of the displacement is modeled as a heteroscedastic Gaussian whose mean and covariance are parameterized by a coordinate-based MLP trained with an NLL objective. Building on this probabilistic field, the authors derive a closed-form Fisher Information expression (decomposed into a mean-trajectory term and a covariance-evolution term) that, together with a Cramér–Rao bound, yields an analytic estimate of local temporal uncertainty computable via automatic differentiation. An amortized inverse encoder is trained to map (template point, displacement) pairs to an estimated intrinsic developmental time without per-subject test-time optimization. The framework is instantiated for several downstream tasks: population mean shape reconstruction, global/local intrinsic time inference, personalized longitudinal shape forecasting, and unsupervised OOD detection (illustrated on pediatric airway obstruction). Experiments are conducted on two synthetic Starman variants (global and spatially-local temporal uncertainty), a synthetic parametric human-body dataset (ANNY), and a real pediatric airway CT dataset, with A-SDF and NAISR used as deterministic baselines.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper targets a genuine and underserved problem: propagating population-level, covariate-conditioned uncertainty directly onto anatomical space, rather than in a diffeomorphism/momentum parameter space that requires costly numerical integration/resampling to visualize.
- The derivation of the closed-form Fisher Information for the heteroscedastic Gaussian field (Appendix A.2) is thorough and appears mathematically correct (score function derivation, vanishing cross term via Isserlis' theorem, Cramér-Rao bound proof); this is a clean theoretical contribution that ties implicit representations to classical estimation theory.
- The framework is evaluated on a diverse and reasonably well-designed set of tasks (mean trajectory reconstruction, global/local intrinsic time estimation, temporal uncertainty calibration, personalized forecasting, OOD detection), and the Starman(L) experiment nicely demonstrates a capability (spatially heterogeneous time modeling) that the deterministic baselines cannot represent at all.
- Qualitative validation of the uncertainty estimates against ground truth on synthetic data (Fig. 3) and sanity checks on real clinical data (Fig. 4, Fig. 7) add some credibility to the calibration claims.
- The clinical application (subglottic stenosis detection as OOD) is compelling and clinically meaningful, and the ablation between global vs. local scoring (Table 5) is informative.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The framework rests on strong, largely unvalidated modeling assumptions: (1) displacement at each point is Gaussian (unimodal, no skew) — this may not hold for anatomical growth processes with more complex marginal distributions; (2) the population mean intrinsic time equals chronological time (E[τ|p,t]=t), which is asserted as a “standard” assumption but is not tested for the real airway dataset, where ground-truth τ is fundamentally unavailable; any secular bias in the data would directly invalidate the Cramér-Rao-based interpretation of σ_τ.
- Point correspondence, which underlies literally all quantities in the paper (µ, Σ, τ estimates), is delegated to a separate template-registration network described only in the appendix as “not our primary contribution.” Yet errors in this correspondence propagate directly into the estimated displacement field and hence into all downstream uncertainty claims. No quantitative accuracy assessment of the registration/correspondence quality is reported.
- The OOD score formula (Eq. 17) contains an apparent notational inconsistency (τ̂_max defined via g(q,p) rather than g(q,d)), raising minor concerns about care in the final derivations/writing.
- Only one real clinical dataset is used, and even there the intrinsic-time-based evaluation must fall back to chronological age as a surrogate ground truth, which weakens the strength of the “uncertainty is clinically meaningful” claim; the paper acknowledges NAISR outperforms PRISM on global time estimation and on personalized shape prediction on this dataset, meaning the method’s main proposed advantage (uncertainty quantification) is convincingly shown only on synthetic data.
- Baselines are limited to two deterministic methods (A-SDF, NAISR) retrofitted with test-time optimization for time/uncertainty tasks; no comparison is made against other probabilistic shape/implicit models (e.g., probabilistic DeepSDF variants, GP morphable models, or the classical hierarchical diffeomorphic models discussed at length in Related Work) despite these being natural uncertainty-aware baselines that the introduction explicitly critiques.

Weaknesses (presentation):
- The main text is generally readable, but heavy notational/derivational content (Sec. 4.3, App. A.2) could be more concisely summarized, with intuition foregrounded and full derivations kept exclusively in the appendix.
- Several figures (e.g., Fig. 7) are extremely dense and hard to parse in the given format.
- No error bars / variance across runs are reported for the quantitative tables, making it hard to assess whether differences between PRISM and NAISR/A-SDF (which are often small, e.g., Table 1 Starman(G)) are statistically meaningful.

Weaknesses (significance / originality):
- While the specific closed-form Fisher-Information-for-implicit-shape-fields combination appears new, each individual ingredient (heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL training, Fisher information for multivariate normal families, Cramér-Rao bound, amortized inverse mapping) is well-established; the novelty is primarily in the assembly and application domain rather than fundamentally new estimation theory.
- The claim of being “the first implicit neural representation framework for uncertainty-aware statistical shape analysis” is strong and should be moderated given related probabilistic implicit representation literature not directly compared against.
- Practical significance is somewhat constrained by the single scalar covariate (age) assumption acknowledged by the authors as a limitation; many clinically relevant covariates are multivariate.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How is the accuracy of the template-based point correspondence (Appendix A.1) validated, and how sensitive are the reported µ/Σ/uncertainty estimates to correspondence errors, especially on the real airway dataset where anatomical variability is higher than in synthetic data?
2. The assumption E[τ|p,t] = t underlies the Cramér-Rao-based interpretation of temporal uncertainty. On the real airway dataset, since ground-truth τ is unavailable, how do you justify/validate that this unbiasedness assumption approximately holds, and how would violations affect the reported uncertainty calibration in Fig. 4?
3. Could you clarify the OOD score definition in Eq. (17), specifically whether τ̂_max should depend on g(q, d) rather than g(q, p), and confirm this is not a typo affecting reported results?
4. Why were more directly comparable probabilistic baselines (e.g., Gaussian Process Morphable Models, or a probabilistic/VAE-based implicit shape model) not included, given that Related Work explicitly discusses their limitations relative to PRISM?
5. On the airway dataset, NAISR outperforms PRISM on global intrinsic time estimation (Table 2) and personalized shape prediction (Table 4). Could you provide more insight into why the proposed probabilistic framework underperforms a deterministic baseline on real data specifically, and whether this suggests overfitting to the synthetic assumptions (Gaussian, unbiasedness)?
review.limitations: The authors provide a reasonable Limitations section acknowledging the restriction to a single scalar covariate and the challenge of long-term forecasting under increasing stochasticity in degenerative conditions. However, the discussion does not address: (1) the potential negative societal impact of an automated anomaly/pathology detector for pediatric airway conditions being deployed without extensive clinical validation (e.g., risk of false negatives/positives influencing clinical decisions); (2) limitations related to the strong parametric (Gaussian, unbiasedness) assumptions underlying the uncertainty quantification, which could produce overconfident or miscalibrated uncertainty estimates if violated on real, more heterogeneous clinical populations; (3) the dependency of all results on the accuracy of a separately-trained, unvalidated point-correspondence/registration module. I would suggest the authors expand the limitations discussion to cover these points.

title: Omni-fMRI: A Universal Atlas-Free fMRI Foundation Model

review.summary: The paper presents Omni-fMRI, a self-supervised foundation model for fMRI that operates directly on voxel-level signals rather than relying on predefined ROI parcellations. To make voxel-level modeling with a standard ViT+MAE architecture computationally tractable, the authors introduce (1) a dynamic patch tokenization scheme that removes background voxels and adaptively assigns coarse or fine patches based on a local spatiotemporal intensity-variance complexity score, (2) a dual-path multi-scale embedding module that fuses low- and high-frequency information from heterogeneous patch sizes via a zero-initialized residual MLP, and (3) a scale-aware MAE reconstruction objective with per-scale decoding heads and loss normalization to avoid coarse patches dominating the loss. The model is pretrained on ~49,497 sessions across 9 datasets and evaluated on a newly assembled benchmark of 11 datasets / 16 downstream tasks spanning demographic prediction, disease diagnosis, image retrieval, emotion detection, and brain-state classification. Extensive experiments (fine-tuning, linear probing, few-shot, scaling analysis, ablations, and Neurosynth-based interpretability) show consistent improvements over existing voxel-level (SwiFT, NeuroSTORM) and ROI-based (BrainLM, Brain-JEPA, BrainMass) foundation models, along with substantially reduced pretraining wall-clock time.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation of current fMRI foundation models (atlas dependency) and proposes a coherent technical pipeline (adaptive tokenization + dual-path embedding + scale-aware reconstruction) tailored to the specific structure of 4D fMRI data.
- Very extensive empirical evaluation: many datasets/tasks (demographics, diagnosis, retrieval, emotion, state prediction), linear probing, few-shot data-efficiency curves, scaling analysis (model size and data), and an interpretability analysis using Neurosynth meta-analytic maps.
- Substantial and well-documented ablations (complexity metric choice, patch normalization, mask ratio, self-supervised objective choice, threshold sensitivity), which lend some support to design decisions.
- Reported computational efficiency gains are compelling (32 GPU-hours vs. 13 days for NeuroSTORM), which if reproducible would be a meaningful practical contribution enabling larger-scale pretraining.
- The benchmark suite itself, with released logs and subject IDs, could be a useful community resource for standardizing fMRI foundation model evaluation.

Weaknesses (Soundness):
- Statistical rigor is limited: most results are based on n=3 runs, with Cohen's d effect sizes reported instead of significance tests; for a paper claiming consistent state-of-the-art performance across 16 tasks, this is a fairly thin evidentiary basis, especially for disease-diagnosis tasks with small sample sizes (e.g., PPMI n=331, ADNI n=497).
- Some ablation gaps are small (e.g., threshold ablation differences of ~1-3 accuracy points on a single run) and lack error bars, making it hard to assess robustness of the specific hyperparameter choices (τ=0.25, background threshold, etc.).
- Fairness of baseline comparisons is unclear: the paper states baselines received “necessary hyperparameter searches” but provides limited detail on search budgets, and different baselines use very different backbones/compute regimes, which complicates isolating the source of gains (architecture vs. tokenization vs. data scale vs. tuning effort).
- Potential subject/session leakage: for Type II datasets, pretraining and downstream splits share the same underlying subject pool (70/30 split), and it's not entirely clear whether splits are subject-disjoint across all uses (pretraining vs. fine-tuning vs. testing), which could inflate performance if any leakage occurs.
- The complexity score (temporal intensity variance) is heuristic and static; while ablated against a few alternatives, the theoretical justification is somewhat informal, and it is unclear how sensitive performance is to interacting hyperparameters (base patch size, background threshold, and τ) as a joint search rather than independent ablations.

Weaknesses (Originality):
- The core techniqal ingredients — adaptive/dynamic patch sizing, dual-path multi-scale embedding with zero-initialized residual branches, and scale-conditioned decoding — are closely adapted from existing computer vision literature (Choudhury et al. 2025; Rao et al. 2021; Havtorn et al. 2023). The novelty here lies primarily in the domain adaptation to voxel-level fMRI (e.g., background pruning, variance-based complexity, scale-normalized MAE loss for 3D+T patches) rather than in fundamentally new methodology.

Weaknesses (Presentation):
- The introduction contains a clear typographical/editing error (the “contributions” paragraph is duplicated verbatim), suggesting the manuscript needs another proofreading pass.
- The main paper is quite dense with many tables and results deferred to the appendix; while the appendix is thorough, in-text summaries occasionally lack pointers to exact locations, and some claims (e.g., “brain state prediction… 100% supervision” sentence cut off) appear incompletely edited (“under full supervision (100” cut off in Appendix B.3).
- Overall notation is reasonably clear, and figures (Fig. 2, 4, 5) are helpful, though some (Fig. 1) are difficult to parse at a glance due to dense radial layout.

Weaknesses (Significance):
- The significance is somewhat tempered by the fact that gains, while consistent, are often modest in some tasks (e.g., HCP sex classification: 95.54 vs. 94.17 for NeuroSTORM) and very large in others (e.g., 23-way HCP task few-shot), which is an interesting but not fully explained pattern — a discussion of why gains vary so much across tasks would strengthen the paper.
- The scalability argument (32 hours vs. 13 days) is compelling, but such wall-clock comparisons across different GPU types (A10G vs. A6000 vs. V100) do not control for compute/FLOPs, which weakens the strength of the efficiency claim as an apples-to-apples comparison.
review.key_questions_for_authors: 1. Can you provide statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals) in addition to Cohen's d effect sizes, particularly for the smaller disease-diagnosis datasets (PPMI, ADNI) where n=3 runs may not sufficiently characterize variance? 2. For Type II datasets (ABCD, ABIDE, HCP rest, PPMI) that are split 70/30 between pretraining and downstream tasks, can you confirm the split is strictly subject-disjoint (not merely session-disjoint), and clarify whether any subjects appear in both the general pretraining corpus and downstream test sets across other datasets? 3. What hyperparameter search budget (e.g., number of trials, search space) was used for each baseline model, and were all baselines fine-tuned for a comparable number of GPU-hours/epochs to ensure fairness relative to Omni-fMRI? 4. Can you report FLOPs-normalized or GPU-hour-normalized training cost comparisons (rather than wall-clock across different GPU architectures) to substantiate the efficiency claims relative to NeuroSTORM and BrainMass? 5. How sensitive is the model to the background-removal threshold and complexity threshold τ when varied jointly (rather than independently), and could an inappropriate combination of thresholds inadvertently discard clinically relevant signal in specific patient populations (e.g., atrophied brain regions in AD)?
review.limitations: The paper includes a limitations paragraph acknowledging that the complexity-based dynamic tokenization is heuristic rather than fully learned/differentiable, and suggests future work on learned patch selection. However, the discussion of limitations is fairly narrow. The authors should also discuss: (1) the limited statistical power given small n (3 runs) and small clinical datasets; (2) potential risks of atlas-free voxel-level models for clinical interpretability/adoption compared to ROI-based approaches favored in clinical neuroimaging workflows; (3) generalization to different scanner protocols, TRs, and preprocessing pipelines not covered in the 11-dataset benchmark; and (4) more specific societal impact considerations regarding potential misuse of subject-level brain decoding (e.g., NSD image retrieval) beyond the generic impact statement provided. Expanding this discussion would strengthen the paper's treatment of limitations and societal impact.

title: AnchorWeave: World-Consistent Video Generation with Retrieved Local Spatial Memories

review.summary: The paper introduces AnchorWeave, a memory-augmented video diffusion framework aimed at improving spatial consistency in long-horizon, camera-controllable video generation. The key idea is to replace a single globally fused 3D point-cloud memory (used by prior works such as SPMem/Spatia/MagicWorld) with a collection of per-frame *local* point-cloud memories, each paired with its own camera pose. Because these local memories are never fused across views, they avoid the cross-view misalignment/ghosting artifacts that accumulate in global reconstructions. Given a target camera trajectory, the method performs a coverage-driven greedy retrieval that selects a compact, complementary set of local memories per temporal chunk (maximizing newly visible coverage), renders them into anchor videos, and integrates up to K anchors into the diffusion backbone through a 'multi-anchor weaving controller' composed of ControlNet-style blocks with shared cross-anchor attention and pose-guided fusion. The system runs in an iterative update–retrieve–generate loop for arbitrarily long video generation, and is instantiated on two backbones (CogVideoX-5B and Wan2.2-5B). The authors evaluate on RealEstate10K and DL3DV under a partial-revisit protocol, comparing against several camera-controllable and memory-augmented baselines (ViewCrafter, Gen3C, TrajCrafter, EPiC, SEVA, and reimplemented Context-as-Memory and SPMem), reporting PSNR/SSIM and VBench-style perceptual metrics. Ablations examine global vs. local memory, pose-guided vs. averaged anchor fusion, joint vs. separate attention, and the number of retrieved anchors, along with qualitative long-horizon open-domain generation examples (including 360° exploration and zero-shot third-person game scenarios).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The core motivation is clearly articulated and intuitively convincing: fusing multi-view depth/pose estimates into a single global point cloud accumulates alignment error that propagates into rendered anchors and then into generated hallucinations, whereas per-frame local point clouds sidestep this fusion step entirely. Figure 1 nicely illustrates the problem.
- The coverage-driven retrieval formulation (greedy visibility-coverage maximization with FoV-based candidate filtering) is a sensible, well-explained algorithmic contribution, and the multi-anchor weaving controller (shared attention + pose-guided importance weighting) is a reasonable mechanism for reconciling multiple, potentially conflicting anchor renderings.
- The empirical evaluation is fairly broad: quantitative comparisons against 7 baselines spanning different memory paradigms (single-anchor V2V methods, implicit multi-view conditioning, and global-memory methods), on two datasets, with two different diffusion backbones, plus a dedicated camera-controllability comparison (rotation/translation error) and several targeted ablations (Table 2, Table 3, Figure 5) that isolate the contribution of local vs. global memory, pose-guided fusion, and joint attention.
- Qualitative results (Figures 4, 6, 9–12) support the quantitative claims and additionally demonstrate promising long-horizon behavior, including 360° panoramic consistency and unexpected zero-shot generalization to dynamic third-person game scenes, despite training only on static scene datasets.

Weaknesses (affecting soundness/significance ratings):
- Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to a cluster of very similar, contemporaneous works cited by the authors themselves (SPMem, Spatia, MagicWorld, Context-as-Memory). The core technical differentiator is largely: (1) skip point-cloud fusion, keep per-frame point clouds, and (2) use attention-based fusion instead of naive rendering/cross-attention on keyframes. These are reasonable engineering choices but the overall system (retrieval + anchor rendering + ControlNet-style conditioning) closely follows the established paradigm from the compared baselines.

title: Privacy Amplification by Missing Data

review.summary: This paper studies an underexplored connection between missing data and differential privacy (DP). The authors formalize a randomized algorithm operating under incomplete data as the composition of a missing-data mechanism D (following the classical MCAR/MAR/MNAR taxonomy of Rubin) and a downstream (ε,δ)-DP algorithm A, yielding a composite mechanism A_D. Their main technical results are: (1) a general amplification theorem (Thm 3.2) showing that for any MAR (hence MCAR) missing mechanism, A_D satisfies (ε′,δ′)-DP with ε′ = ln(1+p*(e^ε−1)) ≤ ε and δ′ ≤ p*δ, where p* is the probability that the differing record between two neighboring datasets is at least partially observed; (2) a tightness result showing that when p*=1 no amplification can be guaranteed in general; and (3) refined amplification results for a newly introduced class of "feature-wise Lipschitz" (FWL) queries (which includes histograms, linear queries, clipped means, and covariance queries) combined with Laplace/Gaussian mechanisms, showing that amplification can still occur even when p*=1, driven instead by the fraction ρ of observed features per sample. The proofs rely on α-divergence formulations of DP and explicit coupling arguments in the spirit of privacy amplification by subsampling (Balle et al., 2018). The paper is purely theoretical, with no empirical experiments, and it closes with an honest discussion of limitations (MNAR is not covered, and independence of the masking mechanism across samples is assumed) and future directions.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper identifies a genuinely interesting and underexplored angle: treating missingness as a potential privacy amplification source rather than purely a nuisance for utility. This connects two literatures (DP and missing-data theory) that have mostly been studied separately (as acknowledged in the related work), and generalizes the closest prior work (Mohapatra et al., 2023, MCAR-only, Bernoulli subsampling framing) to the MAR setting with a general, algorithm-agnostic bound.
- The technical machinery (α-divergence composition, explicit coupling constructions distinguishing a shared component vs. dataset-specific components) is a careful and non-trivial adaptation of amplification-by-subsampling proof techniques to the missing-data setting.
- The introduction of the FWL query class, together with closure properties (Lipschitz post-processing, linear combination) and concrete instantiations (histograms, linear queries, coordinate-wise clipped means, covariance queries) is a nice bridge from the abstract p*-dependent bound to concrete, practically relevant mechanisms (Laplace, Gaussian), and it demonstrates that amplification can occur even in the

title: SimuScene: Training and Benchmarking Code Generation to Simulate Physical Scenarios

review.summary: This paper introduces SimuScene, a new benchmark and training pipeline for evaluating and improving LLMs' ability to generate Python code that simulates physical scenarios described in natural language. The authors build an automatic data generation pipeline (GPT-4o for scenario/question generation, DeepSeek-R1 for quality refinement) covering 52 physical concepts across 5 domains (mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, fluid mechanics, thermodynamics), yielding 7,659 scenarios (334 human-verified test examples). They propose a Code-Video-VLM evaluation pipeline: an LLM writes code, the code is executed to render a video, and a VLM judges whether the video is consistent with several verification questions about the scenario. They benchmark 10 frontier LLMs, finding even the best model (DeepSeek-R1-0528) reaches only 21.5% Avg@8 accuracy. They then propose a Code-Video-Judge RL training approach (SFT + GRPO with VLM-based visual rewards) to improve smaller models (7B, 32B), showing substantial gains (e.g., 7B: 0%→11.1% Avg@8 Acc, 32B: 11.1%→36.9%). They also show that mixing their SFT data with a general instruction dataset (OpenThoughts) improves coding benchmarks without hurting math/physics performance, and provide analyses on VLM-human judge agreement, reward variants, and reward hacking mitigation.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The task (code-based simulation of dynamic physical scenarios) is a novel and interesting combination of physical reasoning and code generation, distinct from existing static physics QA benchmarks or vision-based physics benchmarks.
- The data construction pipeline is reasonably thorough, using multi-stage generation, plausibility filtering, and independent cross-model review (GPT-4o + DeepSeek-R1), with human verification of the test set and quality inspection of training subsets.
- The VLM-as-judge evaluation is validated against human annotation (87.8% agreement) and compared against an LLM-as-judge (text-only) ablation, showing meaningfully higher fidelity for VLM judges — this is a useful validation of the evaluation methodology.
- The RL training results are substantial: 7B and 32B models show large improvements from base to SFT to RL, and the 32B RL model surpasses larger untrained models on Pass@8, which is a compelling demonstration that the proposed data/training pipeline works.
- Efforts to check for reward hacking (multi-question aggregation, ensemble VLM voting during training, train-test VLM separation, human evaluation post-training) are appreciated and add some credibility to the RL results.
- Extensive appendix analyses (domain distributions, response length, error taxonomy of VLM disagreements, reward variant ablations) add depth.

- The core

1) The 'Accuracy' metric requires ALL verification questions (4-12 per scenario, generated automatically by GPT-4o and revised by DeepSeek-R1) to be answered TRUE. Given that the VLM judge itself has ~12-16% disagreement with humans per question, how does this affect the reliability of pass/fail labels for scenarios with a large number of questions? Have you computed how the false-negative rate scales with question count, and could you report per-question or partial-credit agreement to disentangle metric harshness from actual model failure?
