title: Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric

review.summary: The paper proposes TEB, a visual reinforcement learning method that couples task-relevant representation learning with exploration bonuses through a single "predictive bisimulation metric." The key idea is to replace the raw environment reward differential in classical π-bisimulation metrics with a differential computed from a learned Gaussian reward predictor. The authors argue (Theorem 3.3) that this predictive term prevents the metric from collapsing to zero in sparse-reward regions, since the predictor's residual noise has strictly positive variance. Building on this non-degenerate metric, the paper defines a potential function anchored to a batch-averaged pseudo-state, and derives a potential-based intrinsic reward from the metric (Eq. 12–14) that is proven to preserve the optimal policy (Theorem 3.5, essentially Ng et al.'s reward-shaping invariance instantiated with this potential). A value-difference bound (Theorem 3.4) links the metric to policy value gaps, motivating its use for exploration. Experiments are run on six visual MetaWorld manipulation tasks (with distractors and sparse rewards) and seven Maze2D layouts (low-dimensional, reward-free), comparing against strong visual RL baselines (DrM, CTRL-SR, RAP) and a wide set of intrinsic-motivation/skill-discovery baselines (ICM, CeSD, LBS, RND, Disagreement, ProtoRL, BeCL, LSD, DIAYN, SMM). TEB is reported to outperform all baselines on most tasks, and ablations examine the contribution of the representation module, the intrinsic reward module, the anchor-selection strategy, and the effect of predicted vs. ground-truth rewards on metric-based representation learning.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The core idea of unifying task-relevant representation learning and exploration bonus construction under a single behavioral metric is conceptually elegant and well-motivated relative to prior work that treats representation and exploration separately or that relies on ground-truth/low-dimensional states for skill discovery.
- The paper provides a fairly complete theoretical package: contraction/fixed-point existence for the predictive operator, a non-degeneracy guarantee under sparse reward, a value-difference bound, and policy invariance of the shaping term. Even though some of these results are relatively direct adaptations of existing machinery (Kemertas & Aumentado-Armstrong; Chen & Pan; Ng et al.'s potential-based shaping), they are assembled coherently to support the design choices.
- The empirical evaluation is broad: six visual manipulation tasks with strong recent baselines (DrM, CTRL-SR, RAP) plus many exploration/skill-discovery baselines on Maze2D, along with ablations isolating the representation module, intrinsic module, and anchor-selection strategy, plus a targeted study on predicted vs ground-truth rewards.
- Visualizations of maze coverage are a nice qualitative complement to the quantitative coverage numbers.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- Theorem 3.3's non-degeneracy guarantee, while technically correct, is a comparatively weak/almost tautological statement: any reward predictor with strictly positive residual variance Σ will produce a strictly positive expected metric diameter of order sqrt(Σ). The interesting empirical question—whether the learned Gaussian predictor's σθ actually remains meaningfully large in sparse-reward regions during training, rather than shrinking toward the enforced floor σmin (set to 1e-4 in the hyperparameters)—is not analyzed. title: Reversible Lifelong Model Editing via Semantic Routing-Based LoRA

review.summary: This paper introduces SoLA, a method for lifelong (sequential) model editing that assigns each individual edit its own dedicated LoRA module together with a semantic "key" derived from the last-token hidden representation of the edit's input. Once trained, both the LoRA module and its key are frozen, and at inference time an input is routed to the corresponding LoRA module via nearest-neighbor matching against the stored keys (similar in spirit to GRACE's discrete codebook, but storing a LoRA adapter instead of a value vector). Because assignment is discrete and keys/LoRAs are never updated after being frozen, the authors argue this avoids the semantic drift caused by evolving cluster centroids (as in MELO) and the catastrophic forgetting caused by parameter sharing (as in MoE-based ELDER). A further claimed benefit is that deleting a stored key allows a specific edit to be exactly and selectively "rolled back," restoring the base model behavior for that instance without affecting other edits or requiring retraining. The paper also proposes folding module-activation decisions into the first edited layer itself (a "master decision mechanism") to avoid needing a separate auxiliary router network as used in prior LoRA-routing works. Experiments on SCOTUS, zsRE, and hallucination-correction benchmarks (with BERT, T5, GPT2-XL, and additionally LLaMA-3-8B/DeepSeek-R1-8B/Qwen2-7B on UniEdit/WikiBigEdit) show modest but fairly consistent improvements over MELO, ELDER, GRACE and other baselines, along with ablations on edit-layer depth and LoRA rank, an illustrative rollback demonstration on zsRE, and a t-SNE visualization of learned representations.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The high-level motivation—freezing per-edit modules and keys to prevent drift/forgetting caused by continual updates—is intuitive and the empirical analysis in Fig. 2 (linking cluster-center updates in MELO to increased mismatches and degraded ERR/TRR) is a nice diagnostic that motivates the design.
- The experimental evaluation is reasonably broad: three task types, multiple backbones (including larger 7-8B models), several strong lifelong-editing baselines (GRACE, MELO, ELDER) plus classic continual-learning baselines (EWC, CMR, CLEAR) and static-editing baselines (MEND, SERAC, ROME). Ablations on edit-layer location and LoRA rank, plus a rollback case study and t-SNE visualization, add some depth.
- Reported gains, while modest, are fairly consistent across datasets and backbones (Tables 1–2).

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea is essentially GRACE's discrete key-value routing/frozen-codebook mechanism, but replacing the value vector with a full LoRA adapter. The paper does not clearly delineate what is fundamentally new beyond this substitution, and does not compare storage/complexity trade-offs against GRACE directly.
- The claim that "reversible rollback editing" is "the first to be achieved in existing literature" is likely overstated: given that the method already stores a discrete, non-overlapping key-module mapping (much like GRACE's codebook), removing an entry to "undo" an edit is a fairly natural/expected property of any hard-routed, non-parameter-shared memory system, not obviously a novel algorithmic contribution. The paper does not explain what specific technical obstacle other discrete-memory methods (e.g., GRACE) would face in supporting the same rollback behavior.
- Equation 3 and the surrounding description of the "master decision mechanism" are internally inconsistent/confusing: the first line defines d = He(argmin_i dist(q,k_i)), i.e., d appears to be an output of He, yet the following equation redefines He as a function of comparing d to α. It's unclear whether d is a scalar distance, an index, or a decision output, and how exactly the mechanism differs functionally from simply doing a threshold-based nearest-neighbor lookup inside the layer versus outside it (as in prior work). This undermines confidence in the technical description.
- Scalability/storage overhead is not discussed: since every edit gets its own independent, permanently-stored LoRA module and key (never merged or compressed), the total stored parameter/memory footprint grows linearly and unboundedly with the number of edits — a concern the paper explicitly criticizes memory-based baselines (SERAC, CLEAR) for having, but does not analyze for its own method. Fig. 1 reports only "trainable parameters" per edit, not cumulative storage, which could be misleading regarding true resource costs for lifelong editing at scale (e.g., >>1000 edits).
- The threshold α=0.01 is stated without justification or sensitivity analysis, and there is limited discussion of how routing accuracy/mismatch rates for SoLA itself scale as the number of edits grows large (an analog of Fig. 2's mismatch analysis is shown for MELO but not directly for SoLA at larger scale, beyond the 1000-edit curve in Fig. 4).

Weaknesses (presentation):
- Several grammar/phrasing issues throughout (e.g., "most of the existing... suffer," "we employs," "whther delete") reduce readability, though the overall structure is followable.
- Notation in the master decision mechanism section is confusing (see above), and some symbols (R ∈ R^M, He) are not clearly defined before use.
- The related work discussion of MELO/ELDER limitations is repeated almost verbatim in both the main text and the appendix, adding redundancy without additional insight.

Weaknesses (significance/originality):
- The performance gains over the strongest baseline (MELO) are generally modest (e.g., +0.02 Avg on SCOTUS, +0.01 on zsRE in Table 1), and on hallucination correction SoLA does not always achieve the best result (e.g., MELO wins ARR in Table 1; various methods trade off best ERR/TRR/ARR across backbones in Table 2).
- Because the fundamental mechanism (frozen discrete per-edit key-value/module memory) is closely related to GRACE, the paper's originality rests mainly on (1) substituting a LoRA module for a value vector, and (2) integrating routing decisions into the edited layer rather than an external network — both are relatively small architectural changes rather than a new algorithmic paradigm.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How does total stored parameter/memory footprint (not just trainable parameters per edit) scale with the number of edits compared to GRACE, MELO, and ELDER, especially for lifelong editing with thousands of edits? Does storage become a practical bottleneck?
2. Could you clarify the notation and computation in Eq. 3 (the master decision mechanism)? Specifically, what exactly is 'd' — a distance value, an index, or a binary decision — and how is dist(q,k_i) computed and compared with α across layers?
3. What is the fundamental technical difference between SoLA's rollback capability and simply deleting an entry from GRACE's discrete codebook? Why is this rollback property presented as a novel capability rather than a natural consequence of any hard-routed, non-shared-parameter memory architecture?
4. As the number of stored edits grows very large (e.g., beyond the 1000 edits tested in Fig. 4), what happens to routing accuracy/mismatch rates for SoLA itself (analogous to the MELO analysis in Fig. 2)? Is there a risk that semantically similar edits collide in key space?
5. How was the threshold α=0.01 chosen, and how sensitive are ERR/TRR results to this hyperparameter across different datasets and backbones?
review.limitations: The paper's limitations discussion is minimal; the "Impact Statement" is a generic positive framing (safety/reliability/sustainability benefits) without acknowledging concrete limitations such as unbounded storage growth with the number of edits, potential routing/mismatch failures at very large edit counts, or the possibility of the rollback mechanism being misused (e.g., an adversary or malicious actor deleting safety-relevant edits to restore harmful base-model behavior). I recommend the authors add an explicit limitations section discussing storage scalability, routing failure modes at scale, and the dual-use risk of the rollback feature.

title: Box Thirding: Anytime Best Arm Identification under Insufficient Sampling

review.summary: This paper proposes Box Thirding (B3), a new anytime best-arm-identification (BAI) algorithm intended for the regime where the sampling budget T is smaller than (or comparable to) the number of arms N (the “data-poor” regime). The algorithm organizes arms into a hierarchy of “boxes” of size three; whenever a box fills, the best of the three arms is promoted (and receives additional pulls), the median is deferred to a sibling box for future comparison, and the worst is permanently discarded. The authors show that, in aggregate, this ternary rule implements an implicit halving procedure reminiscent of Successive Halving (SH), while remaining fully anytime and free of externally chosen tuning parameters (aside from a closed-form optimal base rate r0). The main theoretical contribution is a decomposition of the total mis-identification probability into a “non-inclusion” term (probability the true best arm is never retained as a viable candidate under limited screening) and a “misidentification” term (error conditional on the best arm being retained). Using this decomposition, the authors derive simple-regret and (ε,δ)-sample-complexity bounds for B3, and compare these against Uniform Sampling (US), bracketed SH (BSH), and SH itself (with known T), showing that B3 attains a candidate-set size Θ(T) (matching US and improving on BSH’s Θ(T/log²T)) while matching SH’s within-candidate-set error rate up to constants, all without knowledge of T. They additionally provide a refined (tighter) worst-case bound for SH itself, improving on a previous bound in Zhao et al. (2023) that could exceed 1. Empirically, B3 is compared to US, BUCB, and BSH on the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest dataset under various synthetic noise models (Gaussian at two variance levels, deterministic, Bernoulli, power-law), plus additional experiments in the data-rich regime against SH and UCB-E.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The core idea—a hierarchical ternary comparison scheme inspired by the “remedian” estimator from robust statistics—is a genuinely interesting and reasonably novel way to obtain an anytime, tuning-parameter-free elimination algorithm that implicitly implements halving without needing to know the horizon T in advance.
- The error decomposition into non-inclusion vs. misidentification is conceptually clean and provides a principled diagnostic tool; the paper backs this decomposition with matching empirical behavior across a spectrum of noise levels (deterministic to high variance), which is a nice validation of the theoretical framework.
- The theoretical contributions are extensive: candidate-set-size characterizations for US/BSH/B3, non-inclusion probability bounds, misidentification bounds within the candidate set, and derived corollaries for simple regret and sample complexity. The authors also derive an improved worst-case bound for vanilla SH relative to prior work, which is a valuable side contribution.
- The empirical study covers multiple noise regimes (Gaussian at two variances, deterministic, Bernoulli, power-law) as well as a data-rich sanity check against fixed-budget algorithms (SH, UCB-E) that have privileged knowledge of T, and the results are broadly consistent with the theory.

Weaknesses (affecting soundness/presentation/significance ratings):

- Presentation: the algorithmic description (Section 3, Algorithm 2) is dense and would benefit from a fuller worked example beyond the single toy trace in Section 4.1; parameters like L, J_l, D, and the interplay between the “top-down sweep” and “base-level replenishment” phases are difficult to parse without repeated reading and cross-referencing with the (very long, 30+ page) appendix. Key technical claims in the main text (e.g., Theorem 4.3, Proposition 4.8) are stated tersely with all substantive derivation deferred to appendices; a reader cannot verify the technical soundness of central claims without working through very long proofs, which limits accessibility.
- Soundness: several of the derivations rely on order-of-magnitude/Θ(·) approximations chained across multiple steps, and the paper does not provide a lower bound tailored specifically to B3 (only appeals to the generic Carpentier & Locatelli fixed-budget lower bound as an approximate comparator). The optimality claims (“B3 achieves optimal screening capacity up to constant factors”) are therefore somewhat informal.
- Experimental scope: the empirical evaluation is essentially a single real dataset (one NYCCC contest, N=5,513) with synthetic reward models layered on top of it; no other real-world crowd-sourced or clinical-trial-like datasets are used, which limits generalizability claims. The comparison in the data-rich regime (Appendix B.2, Tables 1–2) shows B3 sometimes noticeably underperforming SH (which is given the true T), and this gap is not deeply analyzed beyond the qualitative “still competitive” framing.
- Some implementation-level considerations are not discussed: memory/storage overhead of maintaining a growing hierarchy of boxes for very large N, and the practical computational cost of running B3 relative to simpler baselines (US, UCB-E) are not addressed.
- The claim of “no tuning parameters” is slightly overstated, since B3 still relies on the closed-form optimal r0 derived by minimizing a specific (SH-inherited) upper bound; this is a minor terminological point but worth softening.
- The Impact Statement and Limitations discussion in the main text are essentially boilerplate; the paper would benefit from an explicit discussion of the practical limitations of the method (e.g., reliance on 1-sub-Gaussian assumption, discarding sampled information for deferred arms as acknowledged briefly in the Conclusion, and unclear scalability to very large N in terms of storage of the box hierarchy).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How does B3’s memory and computational overhead (number of active boxes, bookkeeping for levels/deferment counts) scale with N, especially for very large N in the data-poor regime where c0 = Θ(T) can still be large?
2. In the data-rich experiments (Appendix B.2, Tables 1–2), SH with known T notably outperforms B3, and the gap appears to grow with N/T. Given both are theoretically Θ(Tε²/N), can you clarify how large this constant-factor gap can become in practice, and whether it is expected to vanish asymptotically?
3. The choice of r0 depends on the assumed schedule shape (e.g., Tl = r^l vs. (l+1)r^l), yet B3 as actually run is fully anytime with L growing dynamically. How exactly is r0 = 1.728 justified/derived for the anytime version of B3 in Algorithm 2, given that this optimality was derived for the fixed-budget SH-style schedule in Proposition 4.11?
4. Could you provide additional evidence (theoretical or empirical) on whether the sub-Gaussian-based concentration bounds remain meaningful for the heavy-tailed power-law/Kumaraswamy experiments in Appendix B.1, or should those results be interpreted purely as an empirical robustness check outside the formal guarantees?
5. Do you have results on additional real-world datasets beyond NYCCC contest 893 that would strengthen the external validity of the empirical claims?
review.limitations: The paper’s discussion of limitations is minimal: the Conclusion notes that B3 discards samples from previous levels when arms are promoted/deferred and suggests sample-reuse (à la Kone et al., 2024) as future work, but this is the only limitation explicitly raised. The “Impact Statement” is generic boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential negative societal impacts (e.g., misuse of BAI-based screening algorithms in domains like clinical trials or hiring/crowdsourcing where miscalibrated ε-best-arm guarantees could have consequences). I would encourage the authors to add: (1) a discussion of computational/memory scalability limitations for very large N, (2) an acknowledgment of the informal nature of some Θ(·)/Ω(·) optimality claims (no B3-specific lower bound), and (3) a more substantive discussion of when/where the method might fail (e.g., strongly correlated arms, non-sub-Gaussian rewards, adversarial arm orderings) or have unintended consequences if deployed in high-stakes selection settings.

title: UniG2U-Bench: Do Unified Models Advance Multimodal Understanding?

review.summary: This paper introduces UniG2U-Bench, a large-scale diagnostic benchmark designed to study whether and when the generative capability of unified multimodal models (UMMs) improves their understanding/reasoning performance (the "Generation-to-Understanding", G2U, direction, as opposed to the more commonly studied Understanding-to-Generation direction). The benchmark aggregates ~3,000 curated samples from existing sources (e.g., MMSI-Bench, IllusionBench, Geometry3K, PhyX, ChartQA, Uni-MMMU, RealUnify, VSP, BabyVision) into 7 high-level cognitive categories and 30 fine-grained subtasks. The authors evaluate over 30 models (base VLMs, native unified models, and agentic tool-use systems) under two protocols — Direct inference and Generate-then-Answer (GtA) — and strictly pair each unified model with its purported base VLM to compute a "G2U Gain" (Δ). They introduce two GPT-4o-judged diagnostic metrics, Reasoning-to-Visual Alignment (RA) and Answer-to-Visual Alignment (AL), to assess intermediate generated visuals during GtA. Through this framework the paper reports: (1) unified models generally underperform their base VLMs and GtA often underperforms Direct inference; (2) exceptions occur in spatial-intelligence, illusion, and multi-step state-tracking tasks, where generation seems to help; (3) task-level and model-level correlation analyses of Δ suggest generation-understanding coupling induces systematic, base-model-dependent inductive biases rather than random noise. Extensive appendices provide ablations for edit-untrained models, a failure-case taxonomy for generated intermediates, and full prompt/rubric specifications.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The research question (does generation help understanding, and under what conditions) is timely, well-motivated, and complementary to the more common evaluation direction (does understanding help generation).
- Scale of evaluation is substantial: >30 models spanning AR, diffusion, flow, discrete-diffusion, and agentic paradigms, with a taxonomy (E2E/decoupled/agentic) that is clearly articulated in Section 3.2 and Fig. 2.
- The explicit decomposition of ΔDirect vs ΔGtA (Eq. 6) and the strict base-model pairing protocol is a reasonable methodological framework for trying to isolate causal G2U effects from confounds of backbone scale.
- The RA/AL diagnostic metrics are a useful addition that attempts to explain *why* GtA succeeds or fails (fidelity vs. redundancy vs. error propagation), and the correlation analysis (Fig. 10) linking task-level and model-level Δ patterns is an interesting higher-order finding.
- Extensive appendices (failure-case taxonomy, OOD ablations for edit-untrained models, full prompt templates) add transparency and reproducibility value.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- Per-subtask sample sizes are often small (e.g., Chart & Table = 100 samples total across the whole category; several MMSI/illusion subtasks likely have on the order of tens of examples), yet fine-grained deltas (Table 5, Table 10) are reported without confidence intervals or significance testing, making some of the
review.key_questions_for_authors: See below.
review.limitations: See above.

title: VideoAfford: Grounding 3D Affordance from Human-Object-Interaction Videos via Multimodal Large Language Model

review.summary: The paper introduces a new task—grounding 3D object affordance from human-object-interaction (HOI) demonstration videos—together with a large-scale dataset, VIDA (38K HOI videos, 16 affordance types, 38 object categories, 22K point clouds), collected from public HOI video corpora and captioned/labeled with the help of VLMs (GPT-4o) followed by manual verification. Building on VIDA, the authors propose VideoAfford, a baseline that couples a frozen video MLLM (Video-LLaVA/LanguageBind) with a frozen latent action encoder (RenderNet) and a frozen 3D point encoder (Uni3D), fine-tuned with LoRA. Following the LISA paradigm, a special <AFF> token's hidden state is projected and fed to a lightweight cross-attention decoder together with dense point features to predict an affordance mask. A modified, spatially-weighted Dice loss (
review.strengths_and_weaknesses: ) + Ls_dice loss ("spatial loss") is introduced to encourage locally compact predictions. Experiments compare VideoAfford against several adapted image/language-based affordance-grounding baselines on seen/unseen splits, along with ablations on the action encoder, spatial loss, and number of sampled frames.
review.key_questions_for_authors: 1) Since videos and 3D point clouds in VIDA are generally not the same physical object instance (one video can be paired with many point clouds sharing only object category and affordance label), how does the model actually learn to transfer the *specific* spatial/temporal interaction pattern seen in a video onto the geometry of an unrelated 3D instance? Doesn't this reduce the task largely to affordance/category classification-conditioned segmentation rather than genuine video-grounded 3D localization? Can you provide evidence (e.g., attention/heatmap visualizations tied to video content, or an ablation replacing the real video with a random video of the same category/affordance) that the video content beyond its category label materially improves localization? 2) Section 5.1 states that IAGNet, GREAT, and AGILE are used as baselines, but Table 2 lists XMF, PFusion, IAGNet, LASO, GREAT, Seqafford, and LMAfford3D*. Please clarify which baselines were actually run, how
review.limitations: The Impact Statement is boilerplate ("there are many potential societal consequences... none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted") and the paper does not discuss important limitations: (i) the weak video-to-point-cloud correspondence (different physical instances) that may undermine the central motivating claim that dynamic video cues improve *fine-grained* 3D grounding rather than just category/affordance classification; (ii) potential noise/bias introduced by VLM-generated captions and affordance labels despite manual verification (no inter-annotator agreement or error-rate statistics are reported); (iii) dataset provenance and licensing issues from scraping YouTube and other public video sources; (iv) safety and reliability concerns of deploying an MLLM-based affordance predictor on real robots (hallucination, distribution shift, failure modes). I recommend the authors add a substantive limitations discussion covering these points and quantify annotation quality/agreement, as well as discuss deployment risk given reliance on frozen foundation models and LoRA fine-tuning on a still noisy, VLM-curated dataset.

title: The Truncation Blind Spot: How Decoding Strategies Systematically Exclude Human-Like Token Choices

review.summary: This paper proposes the "truncation blind spot" hypothesis: standard likelihood-based decoding strategies (top-k, nucleus sampling, beam search, contrastive search) systematically exclude tokens that a human writer would select for communicative appropriateness but that are statistically rare, and this mismatch is a mechanistic driver of the detectability of LLM-generated text. The authors formalize a taxonomy of token inclusion/exclusion under model vs. human selection (Table 1), and operationalize the blind spot through two measurable proxies—predictability (average log-likelihood under a reference LM) and lexical diversity (n-gram uniqueness). Using over 1.8M generated texts across 8 language models (Transformer, Mamba, RWKV, and two proprietary APIs), 5 decoding strategies, and 53 hyperparameter configurations, the paper reports: (1) 8–18% of human tokens fall outside typical truncation sets (RQ1); (2) simple classifiers (RF/LR/NB) using only predictability and diversity achieve AUC-ROC of ~0.97–0.98 (RQ2); (3) detectability correlates far more strongly with decoding/truncation parameters than with model scale or architecture (RQ3); and (4) configurations that achieve low detectability often do so by producing incoherent rather than natural text, i.e., a detectability-quality dissociation (RQ4). An extensive appendix adds analyses of cross-model token-set overlap, POS-level composition of excluded tokens (showing content words are disproportionately excluded), and results for proprietary models.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Addresses an interesting and underexplored question ("why" is machine text detectable, not just "how to detect it"), which is a valuable reframing relative to the mostly detector-engineering literature.
- Very large-scale, systematic experimental design spanning many models, decoding strategies, hyperparameters, and datasets, which lends robustness to the qualitative trends reported (e.g., truncation strictness vs. detectability).
- The finding that detectability depends primarily on decoding configuration rather than model scale/architecture is a useful, actionable insight, as is the demonstrated dissociation between low detectability and text quality (Table 4, Section 6).
- Extensive supplementary analyses (POS composition of the blind spot, cross-model truncation-set overlap, proprietary model results, hyperparameter heatmaps) add depth and partially substantiate the main claims.
- The paper is generally well organized around four clear RQs, with tables and figures that make the empirical trends easy to follow.

Weaknesses (soundness/originality):
- The causal story is under-supported: the paper largely demonstrates correlational relationships between decoding parameters and (a) exclusion rate, and (b) detector AUC, but does not clearly establish that the blind spot specifically (as opposed to generic effects of restricting to high-probability tokens, already documented by Holtzman et al. 2020, Su & Collier 2023, and used implicitly by perplexity-based detectors such as GPTZero) is the operative mechanism. The predictability/diversity signals used here largely reproduce well-known text-degeneration statistics rather than directly measuring "intent-driven selection" or "communicative appropriateness," which the theoretical framework in Section 2 centers on. This leaves a substantial gap between the psycholinguistically motivated theory and what is actually measured.
- The heavy formal apparatus in Section 2 (ergodic theorem, stationarity assumptions, information-theoretic framing) does not appear to generate testable predictions beyond the intuitive claim that truncation excludes low-probability tokens; it reads as over-engineered relative to the empirical contribution.
- No direct comparison to established zero-shot or trained detectors (DetectGPT, GPTZero, supervised classifiers) is provided, which would strengthen the claim that predictability+diversity indeed "explain" existing detectability results rather than merely correlate with them.
- Methodological details on the classifier train/test protocol (e.g., whether splits are within-configuration or across configurations/models, which would materially affect how the reported AUC-ROC should be interpreted) are not fully specified in the main text.
- The RQ4 quality-detectability dissociation claim relies on a weak, non-significant Spearman correlation (ρ=0.097, p=0.092, n=300) drawn from a previously published human evaluation (self-citation reuse); a non-significant result is a fairly thin basis for claiming "dissociation" rather than simply an underpowered test.
- The RQ3 architecture/scale regression (Appendix A.8) is under-specified (model form, sample sizes per family, potential confounds) for a claim as strong as "architecture, not scale, matters," and is relegated entirely to the appendix.
- Overall originality is moderate: while the "blind spot" naming/taxonomy and the systematic combination of decoding sweep + simple classifier + POS analysis are a nice synthesis, the underlying statistical primitives (perplexity/predictability, n-gram diversity as detection signals, decoding-strategy effects on text statistics) are largely already established in prior literature.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How do you distinguish the specific contribution of the "blind spot" (human tokens excluded from the model's truncation set) from the already well-documented general effect that truncation increases predictability and decreases diversity (e.g., Holtzman et al. 2020)? Could an ablation isolate exclusion-specific effects from these more generic distributional shifts?
2. What is the exact train/test protocol for the classifiers in Table 2/3 (Section 4.5)? Are splits stratified within a single decoding configuration, or do train and test sets span different configurations/models/datasets to test generalization? This materially affects interpretation of the reported AUC-ROC values.
3. How does your predictability+diversity classifier compare empirically (same texts, same setup) to established detectors such as DetectGPT, GPTZero, or a simple perplexity-only baseline? This would help substantiate that your proposed mechanism captures something beyond what existing detectors already exploit.
4. Given the non-significant correlation reported in Section 6 (ρ=0.097, p=0.092, n=300), what is the statistical justification for concluding a genuine "dissociation" between detectability and quality, rather than an underpowered/null result? Do you have additional or larger-scale human evaluation data to support this claim?
5. For the architecture/scale regression in Appendix A.8, how many models/configurations underlie each family-specific regression, and were confounds (e.g., training data, tokenizer, alignment procedure) adequately controlled? Could you provide the full model specification and diagnostics?
review.limitations: The authors include an explicit Limitations section acknowledging that (1) predictability/diversity proxies do not capture contextual appropriateness, (2) intent-driven selection is a theoretical construct inferred indirectly from text, (3) the analysis is limited to English, three domains, and short (≤256 token) sequences, and (4) exclusion-rate analyses rely on only five open-source models. This is a reasonably candid treatment. However, the authors could further acknowledge the correlational (rather than causal) nature of the connection between the blind spot and detectability, and the reliance on previously published, possibly underpowered human-evaluation data for the quality-detectability dissociation claim. The Impact Statement briefly addresses dual-use concerns (that understanding detectability could aid evasion) but this discussion is fairly cursory and could be expanded, e.g., regarding implications for watermarking and adversarial paraphrasing already flagged as effective evasion strategies in cited related work (Krishna et al. 2023).

title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

review.summary: The paper introduces Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP), a method for stochastic Lipschitz black-box optimization that maintains an explicit active set At defined by a Lipschitz UCB envelope Ut(x) and a global LCB-based lower bound ℓt. The authors argue that classical zooming/adaptive-discretization algorithms (Kleinberg et al., Bubeck et al., Munos, Valko et al.) implicitly perform the same pruning but do not expose it as a first-class, computable, anytime-valid certificate. Under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension α, the paper proves a shrinkage bound on Vol(At) and derives sample complexity O~(ε^-(2+α)), matching a stated minimax lower bound. Three extensions are proposed: CGP-Adaptive (a doubling scheme to learn an unknown Lipschitz constant with O(log T) overhead), CGP-TR (trust-region variant with certified restarts to scale to d>50), and CGP-Hybrid (switches to GP-UCB refinement within At when a local/global Lipschitz ratio ρ indicates local smoothness). Twelve benchmarks (d∈[2,100]) are used to empirically compare CGP variants against 9 baselines, with reported wins for CGP-Hybrid across all benchmarks tested, plus ablations, wall-clock comparisons, and certificate-based early-stopping demonstrations.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The idea of exposing a computable active-set certificate with an explicit volume/gap-based stopping rule is a nice practical framing, and the writing lays out the mechanism (Ut, ℓt, At) clearly with an illustrative figure.
- The theoretical development (containment theorem, shrinkage theorem, sample complexity, matching lower bound) is internally consistent and the proof sketches in the main text and appendix follow standard confidence-bound plus Lipschitz-propagation arguments correctly as far as I can check.
- The paper considers three practically relevant extensions (unknown L, high dimension, and local smoothness), which is a reasonable applied contribution if properly validated.
- Ablations (Table 9), wall-clock comparisons (Table 8) and margin-condition validation (Table 10) are appreciated additions that go beyond simple regret comparisons.

Weaknesses (soundness/originality/significance):
1. Novelty concerns: Table 1 explicitly shows CGP's sample complexity is identical, O~(ε^-(2+α)), to prior zooming algorithms. The claimed innovation is that the pruning is made "explicit" rather than an "implicit analysis artifact." This is a valid engineering/interpretability contribution, but it is a comparatively thin theoretical advance: the underlying mechanism (UCB/LCB comparison against a global lower bound) is mathematically the same tool already used (often explicitly, e.g., in DOO/SOO/HOO's node elimination rules) in the cited prior work. The paper does not clearly establish what new technical difficulty is solved beyond repackaging.
2. Citation integrity concerns: Several citations attributed to "Shihab et al." are used to support specific technical claims (e.g., "the implicit pruning is an analysis artifact not exposed to the user," "safe robotics where certificates enable stopping," "sample complexity results under margin conditions," "lacks certificate guarantees") but the actual titles of these references (proxy-gaming detection in RL/LLM alignment, sparse-reward structure, LLM constraint propagation, LLM compression via Fisher diagnostics) appear entirely unrelated to Lipschitz optimization or bandit margin conditions. One citation ("Shihab et al., 2026") is dated in the future relative to the review period. This pattern raises serious concerns about citation fabrication, citation-stuffing, or unchecked LLM-generated references, which undermines confidence in the paper's overall rigor and trustworthiness.
3. The empirical results are suspiciously uniform: CGP-Hybrid is reported as the single best method on every one of 12 benchmarks with statistical significance in every column of Table 3, without a single baseline outperforming it anywhere. This pattern, combined with the fact that the switching threshold ρ_thresh=0.5 was "selected via cross-validation on held-out benchmarks" from the same small set of 12 benchmarks, raises concerns about potential threshold overfitting/leakage and selective reporting. Error bars (± SE) are given in most tables except the main comparison Table 3, where they are omitted, limiting the ability to assess true significance.
4. Several extensions rely heavily on existing techniques with limited new algorithmic content: CGP-Adaptive's doubling scheme is a standard bandit technique (à la LIPO/optimistic elimination), CGP-TR essentially imports TuRBO’s trust-region expand/contract heuristic with a certified-restart wrapper, and CGP-Hybrid's switching rule is a heuristic threshold with no formal regret/complexity guarantee for the “ρ<0.5” regime (Proposition 7.1(2) is qualitative/empirical rather than a proven rate).
5. Constants are stated as "not optimized" (Remark 4.4) and several bounds (e.g., allocation bound in Theorem 6.1) depend on generic constants cσ, cT that are not tied concretely to the paper's actual confidence schedule, making some of the finer high-probability guarantees less rigorously verifiable from the main text alone.
6. The claim that CGP-TR "scales to d=100" is empirically shown only on 3 specific high-dimensional benchmarks (Rover-60, NAS-36, Ant-100), each with only modest improvement margins (7–12%) over TuRBO/HEBO, which is a fairly narrow empirical basis for the strong scalability claim in the abstract.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized with clear notation (Table 2), consistent algorithm boxes, and appropriately structured theory-then-extensions-then-experiments flow. Minor readability issues exist (e.g., dense proof sketches embedded in the main text crowd out discussion of assumptions/limitations).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Several citations to "Shihab et al." (2025a/b/c, 2026) are used to support specific claims about Lipschitz bandit theory, certificate guarantees, and margin conditions, yet their apparent titles concern unrelated topics (RL/LLM alignment, sparse rewards, LLM compression), and one is dated 2026. Can the authors clarify the relevance of these references and correct any citation errors?
2. Given that Table 1 shows CGP's sample complexity is identical to existing zooming algorithms, what is the precise novel technical contribution beyond exposing the pruning mechanism explicitly? Please clarify what analysis or algorithmic step in CGP could not, even in principle, be extracted from the implicit active-arm sets already maintained by HOO/zooming/StoSOO.
3. The switching threshold ρ_thresh=0.5 in CGP-Hybrid was tuned via cross-validation on the same 12 benchmarks used for the main empirical comparison. Can the authors report leave-one-benchmark-out or held-out validation results to rule out threshold overfitting, and provide error bars for Table 3 (currently missing) to substantiate the reported significance markers?
4. Proposition 7.1(2) is stated qualitatively ("empirically yields faster convergence") rather than with a proven rate. Can the authors clarify whether any formal sample-complexity guarantee exists for the ρ<0.5 regime, or is this purely an empirical heuristic?
5. How sensitive are the CGP-TR allocation-bound guarantees (Theorem 6.1(3)) to the specific choice of constants cσ, cT relative to the actual confidence schedule used in experiments, and were these constants validated empirically?
review.limitations: The paper's conclusion section briefly acknowledges the requirement of Lipschitz continuity and dimensionality constraints (d≤15 for vanilla CGP, d≤100 for CGP-TR), and the impact statement notes that Lipschitz assumption violations could lead to incorrect pruning of optimal regions. However, the discussion of limitations does not address: (a) the potential overfitting of the ρ_thresh hyperparameter to the benchmark suite used, (b) the incremental nature of the theoretical contribution relative to prior zooming algorithms with identical sample-complexity rates, or (c) the reliability of self-reported near-uniform empirical dominance across all 12 benchmarks. I recommend the authors add a more candid discussion of these points, including a discussion of when explicit certificates provide genuinely new decision-making value versus when they simply restate quantities implicitly available from prior tree-based methods.

title: GIFT: Bootstrapping Image-to-CAD Program Synthesis via Geometric Feedback

review.summary: The paper introduces Geometric Inference Feedback Tuning (GIFT), a data-augmentation framework for image-to-CAD program synthesis. Building on the CAD-Coder pipeline (image → CadQuery code → B-Rep, verified with a CAD kernel), GIFT performs offline inference-time sampling from a pretrained model, verifies candidate programs against ground-truth geometry via IoU, and constructs two new supervised signals: (1) Soft-Rejection Sampling (GIFT-REJECT/SRS), which retains diverse high-IoU (0.9–0.99) alternative programs as additional valid targets for the same input image, and (2) Failure-Driven Augmentation (GIFT-FAIL/FDA), which renders near-miss programs (IoU 0.5–0.9) back into image space and pairs these synthetic 'noisy' images with the original ground-truth code, framed as a geometric denoising objective. The combined objective amortizes expensive test-time search into model weights via standard supervised fine-tuning. Experiments on the GenCAD-Code/DeepCAD dataset show that GIFT improves mean IoU by ~12% over an SFT baseline, narrows the amortization gap between pass@1 and pass@k, reduces inference-time compute needed to reach peak performance by ~80%, improves robustness to task complexity and sampling temperature, and remains competitive (though generally below) point-cloud/multi-modal specialized systems while using only single-view images. Extensive appendices provide ablations across base models, temperatures, complexity strata, OOD evaluation, dataset construction details, and a gradient/policy-gradient interpretation of the method.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper targets a practically relevant bottleneck (data scarcity for image-to-CAD alignment) and proposes a lightweight, non-RL alternative to reduce reliance on costly online RL pipelines that require CPU-bound CAD kernel execution in the training loop.
- The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for a workshop/short paper style contribution: multiple ablations (base model, temperature, task complexity, token/operation-count distributions, OOD real-world images, comparison against frontier VLMs zero-shot, and comparison to specialized point-cloud/multimodal systems) are provided, mostly in the appendix.
- The efficiency argument (matching baseline peak IoU with ~80% fewer test-time samples) is well supported by the pass@k curves (Figure 1, Table 2) and is a genuinely useful practical property if adopted in a deployed pipeline.
- The method is simple to implement (standard MLE fine-tuning on filtered/augmented data) which aids reproducibility relative to online RL baselines.

Weaknesses (Soundness):
- The core algorithmic idea — bootstrapping training data via rejection sampling of diverse correct outputs, and mining hard-negative/near-miss cases for further training — is essentially a domain-specific instantiation of well-established self-training paradigms (STaR, RAFT/RFT, ReST, best-of-n distillation), which the authors themselves acknowledge in Appendix A. The main novelty is the geometric verifier and the visual re-rendering of failures, which is useful but methodologically modest.
- The FDA mechanism has a potentially concerning conceptual issue: a near-miss program z (which encodes a genuinely different, incorrect 3D shape) is rendered into a synthetic image c̃ = φ(d(z)), and the model is trained to map this image of a DIFFERENT object back to the ORIGINAL ground-truth code z_gt. title: ALIEN: Analytic Latent Watermarking for Controllable Generation

review.summary: This paper proposes ALIEN, a watermarking scheme for latent diffusion models that embeds a secret residual δwm into the final denoised latent z0 by analytically deriving a time-dependent correction to the U-Net's noise prediction at each reverse diffusion step. The correction is obtained by applying Tweedie's formula under the VP-SDE framework: given a desired shift of the denoiser's clean-data estimate ẑ0 by δwm, the paper derives the corresponding shift of the score function and, consequently, of the predicted noise ε. This correction is injected into the noise-prediction target over a chosen timestep interval [Tstart, Tend] with strength λ, yielding two configurations (ALIEN-Q for quality, ALIEN-R for robustness). δwm itself is produced by a jointly trained secret encoder/decoder pair operating directly on the latent (added to z0), trained with BCE + LPIPS + MSE losses against the VAE-reconstructed (not original) image. The authors argue this approach avoids the semantic drift of initial-latent modification methods (Tree-Ring), the rigid subspace constraints of cryptographic sampling methods (Gaussian Shading, PRC), the heavy iterative optimization of latent-optimization methods (ROBIN, Zodiac), and the dependency on diffusion inversion (and hence reversible samplers) common to prior semantic watermarks. Extensive experiments on SD v1.5/2.1 compare fidelity (FID, PSNR, SSIM, SIFID, DreamSim, CLIP), stability across samplers/model versions/hyperparameters, robustness to image-processing/regeneration/adversarial/forgery attacks, and computational efficiency, reporting favorable results relative to Tree-Ring, Gaussian Shading, ROBIN, Zodiac, Stable Signature, AquaLoRA, and StegaStamp.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The central idea—translating a desired shift in the denoised latent estimate into a closed-form, time-dependent correction of the noise-prediction target—is a clean and practically useful derivation for watermarking. It removes the need for costly iterative latent optimization (as in Zodiac/ROBIN) and does not restrict the initial-noise sampling distribution (as constrained-sampling methods do), which is a genuine advantage for balancing efficiency, fidelity, and generative diversity.
- The empirical evaluation is broad: fidelity metrics, sampler-agnosticism (stochastic vs. deterministic samplers), model/hyperparameter robustness, standard image-processing and regenerative/rinsing attacks, adversarial embedding attacks, and three forgery attack types, plus runtime/preparation cost comparisons. This breadth is commendable and largely covers the threat models relevant to this sub-area.
- The ALIEN-Q/ALIEN-R split nicely demonstrates the quality-robustness trade-off directly controllable through the analytically-motivated λ and timestep interval, and the ablation in Table 6 supports this trade-off.
- Practical benefits such as sampler-agnostic detection and low per-image latency (0.079s/0.023s) are valuable and are backed by comparison against optimization-heavy baselines (e.g., Zodiac at 122s/image).

Weaknesses (Soundness):
- The theoretical derivation in Appendix A rigorously justifies the required correction for a single arbitrary timestep t under the assumption that the desired ẑ0 shift holds exactly at that instant, but the paper applies this correction repeatedly across many timesteps within [Tstart, Tend]. There is no proof (nor much discussion) of how compounding these per-step corrections over a discretized, stochastic trajectory guarantees—or even approximately guarantees—that the true terminal z0 satisfies the exact intended constraint z0 = z0_orig + δwm. title: Dual-Prototype Disentanglement: A Context-Aware Enhancement Framework for Time Series Forecasting

review.summary: The paper proposes DPAD (Dual-Prototype Adaptive Disentanglement), a model-agnostic auxiliary framework for time series forecasting. DPAD builds a Dynamic Dual-Prototype bank (DDP) consisting of a
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The framework is designed to be model-agnostic and is empirically validated across five diverse backbones (Transformer-, MLP-, CNN-based), which supports the claim of general applicability.
- The experimental scope is broad: long-term forecasting on 8 datasets, short-term forecasting on 4 PEMS datasets, zero-shot transfer experiments, comparisons against other enhancement strategies (RAFT, HCAN, FreDF), hyperparameter sensitivity studies, efficiency analysis, prototype visualization, and targeted case studies tied to the three motivating failure modes (distribution shift, intertwined patterns, rare events).
- The ablation studies (DDP components, DPC fusion strategy, DGLoss terms) are systematic and generally support the claimed necessity of each component, including the interesting finding that using only one prototype bank can hurt performance relative to the baseline, motivating the joint design.
- The efficiency table indicates the auxiliary module adds modest computational overhead, which is a practically relevant contribution for a plug-in module.

Weaknesses (Soundness):
- Several numerical entries appear anomalous or physically implausible. For example, Exchange dataset with TimesNet backbone shows MSE decreasing from 0.375 (336) to 0.101 (720), which is inconsistent with the near-universal trend of increasing error at longer horizons; this suggests either a transcription error or an unstable/underreported result. Similarly, iTransformer on PEMS04 has a baseline MSE of 0.912 (much higher than all other backbones on the same dataset, which cluster around 0.14-0.33), while DPAD reduces it to 0.199, an outsized ~78% relative improvement compared to more modest gains (10-40%) for other backbones on the same dataset. This raises the concern that the reported "improvement" is partly an artifact of an unstable or poorly-tuned baseline run rather than a genuine, generalizable gain, and undermines confidence in the average improvement claims (e.g., "9.3% MSE reduction for iTransformer").
- No multiple-seed/variance reporting is provided anywhere in the paper (main results, ablations, zero-shot), which is important given known instability of some backbones (as illustrated by the PEMS04 anomaly) and the relatively small margins of improvement in several cases (e.g., Solar, Weather).
- Equation (7)/(8) describing the Top-K and rare-selection routing is oddly notated ("arg top-K(ρ_i | 1 < i ≤ K)"), which appears to restrict the index range to unrelated to the actual prototype bank size M; this makes the routing mechanism difficult to verify precisely from the text.
- The similarity computation in DPC is based on φ(X) (a projection of the raw input) rather than the backbone's learned representation h, which seems to weaken the paper's own narrative about leveraging "context-aware" backbone representations for retrieval; the interplay between the routing similarity space and the final fused representation could be clarified.
- No parameter count comparison (only runtime/memory) is reported, which would help contextualize the overhead more completely, particularly for the
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can you clarify or correct the anomalous entries, in particular the Exchange/TimesNet 720-step MSE (0.101, which appears to be an outlier relative to the decreasing-then-increasing trend at other horizons) and the very large baseline MSE for iTransformer on PEMS04 (0.912 vs ~0.14-0.33 for other backbones)? Were these obtained with the same hyperparameters/training protocol as other backbones, and are they reproducible across multiple seeds?
2. Can you report results averaged over multiple random seeds (with standard deviation) at least for a subset of key experiments, given that some improvements (e.g., PEMS04 iTransformer) appear to be driven by fixing what looks like an unstable baseline run rather than a systematic, dataset-general effect?
3. In Eq. (7)-(8), please clarify the exact index set over which top-K selection and rare-prototype thresholding are performed; the current notation ("1<i≤K") is ambiguous relative to the described bank of size M.
4. The similarity/routing computation in Section 3.3 is based on φ(X) rather than the backbone representation h. Could you clarify why retrieval is not conditioned on the (possibly more contextual) representation of the backbone, and whether using h instead changes performance?
5. How many additional trainable parameters does DPAD introduce relative to each backbone (not just runtime/memory), and how does the routing computation cost scale with the number of variables C for very high-dimensional datasets like Traffic/PEMS?
review.limitations: The paper briefly mentions in the conclusion possible future work (interpretable routing, multi-modal prototypes) but does not explicitly discuss limitations of the current approach (e.g., reliance on hand-crafted GP kernel priors that may not transfer to arbitrary domains, potential instability/variance across runs, scalability of the routing mechanism to very high-dimensional or highly non-stationary datasets, or lack of theoretical guarantees for the disentanglement claims). There is no discussion of potential negative societal impact, though for a time series forecasting method this risk is likely minimal; a brief statement would still be appropriate. I recommend the authors add an explicit limitations paragraph addressing the above points, plus discussion of when the assumed common/rare pattern split may not hold (e.g., domains without a meaningful long-tail structure).

title: When Is Compositional Reasoning Learnable from Verifiable Rewards?

review.summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding when compositional reasoning problems can be learned via RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) using only outcome-level feedback, without supervision of intermediate chain-of-thought (CoT) steps. The authors model an LLM's CoT generation as a sequence of task selections, where at each step the model picks among a finite set of deterministic "skill" functions that each propose a next token, and where a linearized (NTK-style) model reallocates probability mass across these skills during REINFORCE-style training. The central technical contribution is the "task-advantage ratio," the ratio of the probability of verifier success when a task is selected at a given step to the probability of success when it is not. Theorem 5.2 gives an exact expression for the expected per-step logit update in terms of this ratio. Building on this, Theorem 5.4 shows that if the correct composition enjoys a uniform task-advantage (Assumption 5.3), RLVR converges to the correct composition with iteration complexity scaling quadratically in the CoT length S. Conversely, the authors show (via a parity-learning example) that when this structural advantage is absent, learning can require exponential time, and (via a simple two-step example) that RLVR can provably converge to a suboptimal composition depending on the quality (accuracy) of the base model at initialization. The paper connects these findings to empirically observed phenomena, such as RLVR's sensitivity to base model quality and its tendency to "sharpen" pre-existing skills rather than learn qualitatively new ones.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The task-advantage ratio is a clean, interpretable quantity, and Theorem 5.2 provides an exact (not just an upper/lower bound) characterization of the expected logit update, which is a nice technical result.
- The paper provides both positive (Theorem 5.4) and negative (parity hardness, base-model-dependence) results, giving a fairly complete and balanced picture of when RLVR without intermediate supervision succeeds or fails.
- The framework connects to and helps explain existing empirical observations in the RLVR literature (e.g., Yue et al. 2025's "sharpening" phenomenon, sensitivity of RL fine-tuning to the base model), lending some plausibility/relevance to the theory.
- The proofs in the appendix appear carefully constructed, with explicit tracking of concentration and induction arguments (e.g., Lemmas A.7–A.13) to convert expected per-step improvement into a global convergence guarantee.
- The paper is clearly structured, moving logically from setup to main theorem to illustrative case studies (parities vs. "inductive" compositions) to base-model dependence, aiding readability despite heavy notation.

Weaknesses (soundness/significance):
- The model architecture (Eq. 1) is highly stylized: it assumes the model's logits for the composition of tasks are linear combinations of fixed task-specific one-hot vectors weighted by inner products of orthonormal positional embeddings with a trainable parameter. Crucially, the coefficient governing task-selection probability at step s depends only on the step index s (via ⟨h_{s,j}, θ⟩), not on the specific content of the prefix beyond determining which task is "correct." This means the framework cannot capture context-dependent task selection (e.g., choosing different operations depending on the actual digits in an addition problem), which seems essential to real compositional reasoning. This is a significant idealization that the paper does not clearly acknowledge as a limitation.
- The link to real LLM fine-tuning rests on an NTK/lazy-training linearization argument, which is known in the broader literature to not hold well in realistic (non-infinitesimal learning rate, feature-learning) regimes; the paper's own discussion of this connection is brief and somewhat hand-wavy.
- Assumption 5.3 (uniform task-advantage) is essentially the desired property that guarantees learnability, and its plausibility is argued only through two stylized synthetic settings (parity vs. a hand-constructed "inductive" recovery model with i.i.d. λ_s per-step recovery probabilities). There is no empirical demonstration (even on a small-scale transformer or synthetic sequence model) that measured task-advantage ratios correlate with actual RLVR training success, which would substantially strengthen the paper's practical relevance.
- The examples in Sections 6.1 and 6.2, while illustrative, are quite minimal (two-token vocabulary, degenerate verifiers) and it is unclear how much insight transfers to more complex, realistic composition structures.
- The paper only analyzes training on positive samples with no KL regularization, which differs from typical RLVR implementations (e.g., that use advantage baselines or reference-model regularization); the impact of these design choices is not discussed.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized and the notation, while dense, is defined carefully in the main text, with proofs deferred properly to appendices. Related work section is reasonably thorough and situates the paper well relative to compositional generalization, PAC learnability, and CoT expressivity literature.

Originality: The task-advantage ratio and its exact characterization for outcome-only RLVR training appear to be a novel contribution, though the paper builds heavily on established tools (REINFORCE analysis, NTK linearization, hardness of parities under SQ-type arguments).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. The task-selection probability in the model (Eq. 1) depends only on the CoT step index s, not on the specific content of the prefix (beyond which task happens to be "correct"). How does this restriction affect the generality of the conclusions, given that real compositional reasoning typically requires context-dependent task selection (e.g., which arithmetic operation to apply depends on the actual digits)? Can the framework be extended to allow for this kind of contextual selection while retaining tractable analysis?

2. Can you provide any empirical validation—even on a small synthetic transformer trained with actual RLVR/REINFORCE—showing that measured task-advantage ratios predict success or failure of learning, beyond the toy logit-update simulation in Figure 4?

3. How sensitive are the results to the orthonormality assumption on positional embeddings {h_{s,j}}? In real transformers, features at different positions/heads are not orthogonal and can interfere; would relaxing this assumption change the qualitative conclusions (e.g., could cross-step interference create additional failure modes not captured here)?

4. Assumption 5.3 requires the advantage condition to hold not just at initialization but throughout the trajectory within Θ+. How can practitioners (or theorists) verify or estimate whether a given problem/base-model pair is likely to satisfy this assumption without already knowing the ground-truth CoT?

5. The iteration complexity bound in Theorem 5.4 requires batch size B scaling with 1/ε̃² and depends on α; could you clarify the total sample complexity (accounting for both T and B) and how it compares to the exponential blow-up in the parity example, to give a fuller picture of the tradeoffs?
review.limitations: The paper does not include a dedicated discussion of limitations, and the "Impact Statement" section appears to be empty/unfilled in the manuscript. The Discussion section does gesture at an open question (how task-advantage manifests in real LLMs), but this is framed as future work rather than an explicit acknowledgment of the paper's own limitations (e.g., the idealized model architecture, lack of context-dependent task selection, absence of empirical validation on real models, and the strength of Assumption 5.3). I recommend the authors add an explicit limitations discussion covering these points, and fill in the Impact Statement section (even a brief statement addressing potential misuse or societal implications of understanding/manipulating RLVR training dynamics would be appropriate for an ICML submission).

title: Semi-knockoffs: a model-agnostic conditional independence testing method with finite-sample guarantees

review.summary: This paper proposes "Semi-knockoffs," a conditional independence testing (CIT) framework designed to accommodate arbitrary pre-trained ML models while avoiding the train-test split that typically limits the power of model-agnostic CIT methods (e.g., HRT, CFI-based tests). The key idea is to construct two synthetic versions of a feature of interest: one obtained by imputing the feature from a regression on the remaining covariates only (ν), and another obtained by additionally conditioning on the response y (ρ). Under the null hypothesis of conditional independence, these two conditional expectations coincide, so the two constructed populations are exchangeable, enabling (i) valid finite-sample p-values via nonparametric paired tests (sign/Wilcoxon) when ν and ρ are known exactly (oracle setting), and (ii) FDR control via a knockoff-style thresholding procedure that exploits sign exchangeability of a newly defined test statistic. For the practical setting where ν and ρ must be estimated, the authors provide two supporting theoretical results: a stability bound for l2-regularized ERM estimators when trained with vs. without a null feature (Theorem 4.1), which is translated into a Wasserstein-distance bound on the induced loss distributions (Theorem 4.2), and a "double robustness" result (Theorem 4.3) showing that estimation errors in the imputer and the black-box model compound multiplicatively rather than additively under smoothness assumptions. The validity of the fully practical (estimated) procedure is empirically illustrated and conjectured rather than formally proven. Extensive simulations (linear settings with adjacent/masked correlated supports, heavy-tailed inputs) and a real dataset (Wisconsin Breast Cancer) compare Semi-knockoffs against numerous variable importance and variable selection baselines (Sobol-CPI/CFI variants, LOCO variants, dCRT, HRT, knockoffs), showing competitive or superior power while maintaining type-I error/FDR control across several black-box models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Neural Networks).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The core methodological idea—constructing two conditionally-imputed populations that are provably exchangeable under the null via a common conditional expectation, one incorporating the response and one not—is a genuinely creative way to sidestep both the stringent joint-exchangeability requirements of full knockoff variable construction and the need for train-test splitting required by HRT/CFI-style tests. This is a nontrivial and interesting contribution to the CIT literature.
2. The oracle-level theory (Theorem 3.3 type-I error control, Theorem 3.4 FDR control) is simple, correct, and clearly derived from the exchangeability of ν and ρ under the null; the associated proofs in the appendix are straightforward and easy to verify.
3. The stability result (Theorem 4.1) for regularized ERM trained with/without a null feature appears to be a novel and reusable technical tool, with a reasonably careful proof relying on standard high-dimensional probability tools (subgaussian/subexponential concentration).
4. The experimental section is extensive: multiple simulated regimes (adjacent support, masked correlation, heavy-tailed inputs), multiple black-box models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Neural Network, Lasso, Ridge), both p-value and FDR variants, a real dataset with an artificially inserted correlated null feature to estimate type-I error, and supplementary ablations on data-splitting regimes for the double-robustness illustration. This is a genuinely thorough empirical evaluation relative to typical CIT papers.
5. Related work is well surveyed and the positioning relative to LOCO, CFI/CPI, CRT/dCRT, HRT, and Knockoffs is clear and fair.

Weaknesses (soundness):
1. The central practical claim of the paper—that the algorithm used in experiments (which estimates ν and ρ) retains valid type-I error/FDR control—is not formally proven. Theorem 4.2 only shows W1-convergence of the two loss distributions at a rate depending on n, and Theorem 4.3 (double robustness) provides a bound on the decay of the loss difference under strong smoothness/differentiability assumptions on the black-box model, but neither result is combined into a formal probabilistic guarantee (even asymptotic) on the type-I error or FDR of the practical procedure. The authors explicitly state in Section 4.5 that preservation of the required sign symmetry for the *estimated* statistic is a "conjecture," supported only by qualitative arguments and empirical illustration (Figure 3, Appendix F.2). Given that the title advertises "finite-sample guarantees," this is a significant gap, since the finite-sample guarantee formally holds only for the oracle procedure, which is generally infeasible in practice.
2. Theorem 4.1's stability result (and hence Theorem 4.2) is proven only for l2-regularized ERM with restrictive assumptions (Lipschitz score, subgaussian design/score, bounded population covariance), essentially covering ridge-type linear/GLM imputers. In experiments, however, the same Semi-knockoffs pipeline is used with more flexible imputers (implicitly via the CPI-style regression-based sampler), and the paper only shows empirically (Figure 1) that Lasso behaves similarly; there is no theoretical extension to nonparametric or tree-based imputers, which are arguably more realistic choices in practice.
3. The requirement to estimate ρ = E[Xj | X-j, y] introduces a second, potentially harder estimation problem that could itself be a source of miscalibration if ρ is estimated with a much more/less flexible model than ν; the paper acknowledges this only briefly as a "limitation" in the discussion without a systematic sensitivity study (e.g., varying the flexibility mismatch between the two imputers).
4. The claimed computational advantage over LOCO/dCRT/HRT (from avoiding repeated refits or many resamples) is asserted in the introduction but not clearly substantiated in the experiments; the authors note the timing comparisons are "muted" because default hyperparameters were used, leaving the claimed efficiency benefit largely unverified.

Weaknesses (presentation/significance/originality):
5. The paper is dense, with much of the technical content and even key algorithmic descriptions relegated to a lengthy appendix; a reader following only the main text may not immediately realize that the practical (used-in-experiments) guarantee is only conjectured rather than proven, since this nuance is stated somewhat in passing (Section 4.5) with no explicit caveat in the abstract, introduction, or conclusion.
6. Real-data validation of type-I error relies on a single artificially injected null feature correlated at 0.6 with the real covariates; this is a reasonable but limited proxy for genuine finite-sample validity in a realistic (non-simulated) high-dimensional setting.
7. While the core idea is original, it builds substantially on existing components (CPI-style conditional permutation/regression imputers, knockoff thresholding, double-robustness arguments from Reyero-Lobo et al. 2025a); the novelty is the specific combination and the training-with/without-y trick, which is a meaningful but incremental methodological innovation rather than a fundamentally new technique.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can you provide any formal guarantee (even asymptotic, e.g., type-I error inflation vanishing as n→∞) for the fully practical Semi-knockoffs procedure that uses estimated ν̂ and ρ̂, rather than relying on the qualitative "conjecture" argument in Section 4.5? Would combining Theorem 4.2 (W1 control) with a quantitative version of Theorem 4.3 allow a formal (even if imperfect) finite-sample bound on the type-I error/FDR inflation?
2. Theorem 4.1's stability result is proven only for l2-regularized ERM imputers under fairly strong distributional assumptions. In your experiments, what specific models are used for ν̂ and ρ̂ when the black-box model mb is Random Forest/Gradient Boosting/Neural Network? Do you have any theoretical or empirical evidence that the stability property still holds when ν̂/ρ̂ themselves are nonparametric/complex models rather than regularized linear predictors?
3. How sensitive is the validity (type-I error/FDR control) of the practical procedure to a mismatch in flexibility between the ν and ρ imputers (e.g., using a highly flexible model for ρ but a simple one for ν, or vice versa)? Could an overly flexible ρ (which incorporates y) overfit and create spurious asymmetries even under the null, inflating false positive rates?
4. Can you clarify precisely what, if any, assumptions on the marginal/joint distribution of X are required for the FDR control of Semi-knockoffs (Theorem 3.4, oracle case), given that standard model-X knockoffs require a known/estimable joint distribution while your method only needs the conditional-mean equality under the null? Does this hold regardless of the distribution of X (e.g., heavy-tailed, as in your Appendix F.5.2 experiments)?
5. Could you provide a more direct empirical comparison of wall-clock computation time between Semi-knockoffs and the baselines (LOCO, dCRT, HRT) under matched, non-default hyperparameter settings, to substantiate the computational-efficiency claim made in the introduction?
review.limitations: The paper includes a short discussion of one limitation (that using a simple imputer for ρ may fail to capture richer relationships and break symmetry under the alternative, potentially reducing power) and proposes this as future work. However, the more critical limitation—that the practical (estimated) version of the method's finite-sample validity is not formally proven and relies on a conjecture supported by partial theory and empirical illustration—is only implicitly acknowledged (via careful wording such as "we conjecture") rather than explicitly flagged as a limitation in the discussion or abstract. I would suggest the authors explicitly state this gap as a limitation in the main paper (not just in Section 4.5) to avoid overstating the "finite-sample guarantees" claim in the title/abstract relative to what is actually proven for the deployed algorithm. The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not discuss potential negative societal impacts (e.g., risks of false scientific discoveries if the conjectured validity does not hold in practice, or misuse in high-stakes domains like genomics/clinical decision-making); a brief discussion of these risks would strengthen the paper.

title: JEPA-VLA: Video Predictive Embedding is Needed for VLA Models

review.summary: This paper studies which pretrained visual representations best support Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation. The authors argue that VLAs require two forms of visual knowledge that current backbones (DINO-family, CLIP/SigLIP-family) do not adequately provide: (i) environment understanding, i.e., precise encoding of task-relevant state while discarding nuisance factors, and (ii) policy priors, i.e., anticipatory knowledge of how the environment evolves during successful task execution. Through probing experiments on LIBERO/LIBERO-plus (regressing/predicting robot-arm and object states, as well as lighting/background nuisances from frozen visual features), the authors show that V-JEPA 2, a video-based joint-embedding predictive architecture, better captures task-relevant states/dynamics and is less sensitive to irrelevant factors than DINOv2 and SigLIP. Building on this analysis, the paper proposes JEPA-VLA, which integrates a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into existing VLA architectures via two fusion strategies: simple token concatenation for VLAs trained from scratch, and gated cross-attention (Flamingo-style) for VLAs pretrained on large-scale robot data. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-plus, RoboTwin2.0, a real-robot pick-and-place task, and CortexBench show consistent performance gains from adding V-JEPA 2 representations, including in low-data regimes.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper articulates a clear, sensible conceptual framework (environment understanding vs. policy priors) for diagnosing why current visual backbones may be suboptimal for VLA policies, which is a useful lens even beyond this paper.
- The probing analysis in Section 2 is a nice attempt to empirically ground the motivation rather than relying purely on intuition, comparing task-relevant/-irrelevant state regression and future-state prediction across representations.
- The proposed integration method is lightweight and practical (frozen encoder, minimal architectural change), which increases the likelihood of adoption/reproducibility if code is released.
- The empirical evaluation is broad: LIBERO, LIBERO-plus, RoboTwin2.0, a real-robot task, and CortexBench, with a data-efficiency angle (1/10 and 1/5 training data) that strengthens the sample-efficiency claim.
- Reported gains are large and mostly consistent in sign across benchmarks, including domain-randomized RoboTwin2.0 settings and real-world layout/lighting shifts.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- Table 7 contains an apparent inconsistency: two rows are both labeled "BASELINE+DINOV2" with different scores (26.0 and 31.2); this is either a typo (e.g., one should be DINOv3, as DINOv3 is cited elsewhere) or a data-entry error, and undermines confidence in the reported ablation.
- In Table 3, the reproduced OpenVLA-OFT baseline (90.30%) is notably below the official reported number (95.35%), and JEPA-VLA's final number (96.40%) is only marginally above the official baseline. Since batch size (and possibly other training conditions) differ from the official protocol, it is unclear how much of the reported "+6.1%" gain reflects V-JEPA 2 fusion versus reproduction/training variance. A controlled re-run of the exact baseline recipe would strengthen this claim.
- No variance/error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere (LIBERO, LIBERO-plus, RoboTwin2.0, real-world with only 10 trials). Several RoboTwin2.0 "Hard" numbers are very small in absolute value (e.g., 0.0%, 13.0%, 21.0%), making it hard to assess whether reported deltas are meaningful or within noise given presumably limited rollouts per task.
