The platform has three components: (1) a modular tool-environment layer that exposes enterprise applications (CRM, HR, ticketing, version control, etc.) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with a dynamic tool registry, stateful Docker-based execution, and an observation normalizer; (2) an automated trajectory-synthesis pipeline that builds a tool dependency graph from environment schemas, performs constraint-aware depth-first traversal to collect valid tool sequences, and uses an LLM to turn these into low-level and high-level natural-language tasks, followed by de-duplication/diversity/grounding filtering; and (3) an integrated training stack supporting SFT, DPO, and an "Agentic GRPO" variant of GRPO that computes trajectory-level rewards from environment execution and masks tool-output tokens during optimization. The authors instantiate the platform as EnterpriseArena, a benchmark with 15 containerized MCP servers, 140+ tools, and 500 expert-curated tasks spanning IT, HR, sales, engineering, and communication domains, validated by nine domain experts. They fine-tune Qwen3-8B (and briefly Qwen2.5-4B) with fewer than 1K synthesized trajectories and report that the resulting models are competitive with or exceed GPT-4o on EnterpriseArena, EnterpriseBench, and CRMArena, and are competitive on τ-Bench, while reducing per-token inference cost by roughly 8–10×. Additional experiments examine data-scale ablations, robustness to environment schema changes (with incremental retraining), synthetic-data quality (diversity/complexity/correctness), and comparisons of Agentic GRPO against token-level GRPO and DPO.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Addresses a practical and timely problem: unifying tool integration, data synthesis, and training for enterprise agent specialization, which is currently fragmented across separate tools/benchmarks.
- The EnterpriseArena instantiation is fairly comprehensive (15 MCP servers, 140+ tools) and was validated by nine domain experts via a structured survey, lending some credibility to task realism.
- The platform supports multiple training paradigms (SFT, DPO, Agentic GRPO) in the same loop, enabling apples-to-apples comparison of adaptation strategies (Table showing Agentic GRPO > token-level GRPO > DPO).
- Useful practical analyses: cost comparison (inference cost table), robustness to environment/schema drift with incremental fine-tuning recovering most of the performance, and basic synthetic-data quality diagnostics (Self-BLEU, turn complexity, dual-layer correctness checks).
- Extensive appendix with full tool catalogs, prompts, and algorithmic details, aiding reproducibility for those with access to similar infrastructure.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The central empirical claim ("8B models match GPT-4o") is only partially supported: on EnterpriseArena the Agentic GRPO model (0.43) is actually slightly *below* GPT-4o (0.45), and across all four benchmarks Claude-3.5-Sonnet and especially Gemini-2.5-Pro substantially outperform both GPT-4o and the platform-trained models (e.g., Gemini reaches 0.71 on EA vs. 0.43 for the trained 8B model). The framing selectively compares to GPT-4o while downplaying that stronger proprietary baselines are not matched at all.
- The comparison is not apples-to-apples: the platform-trained 8B model is specialized (fine-tuned) on the target benchmark's own environment, while GPT-4o/Claude/Gemini are evaluated with only 2-shot prompting and no fine-tuning. A natural, fairer ablation—fine-tuning GPT-4o on the same synthetic data via the provider's fine-tuning API—is not attempted, making it hard to disentangle "platform enables good SLM specialization" from "any model fine-tuned on benchmark-specific data will outperform an unadapted few-shot model."
- The reported "+10%" improvements over GPT-4o on EnterpriseBench/CRMArena in the abstract seem to refer to relative percentage gains (e.g., 0.51 vs. 0.47, ~8.5% relative; 0.35 vs. 0.32, ~9% relative) rather than absolute 10-point gains, which is not made explicit and could mislead readers.
- Baseline tool-selection and execution accuracies for frontier models are surprisingly low (e.g., GPT-4o tool-selection accuracy of 0.21–0.31), raising questions about whether the evaluation harness (ReAct prompting vs. native function calling, tool-schema exposure, parsing strictness) is equally well-tuned for proprietary vs. open models.
- No variance/seed information is reported for any results, which is particularly concerning for RL-based training (Agentic GRPO) that is known to be high-variance; single-run point estimates limit confidence in the reported gains.
- The core technical novelty is modest: the trajectory-synthesis approach (tool graph construction + two-stage low/high-level instruction generation) closely follows prior work (OS-Genesis, ToolACE, Graph2Eval), and "Agentic GRPO" is essentially GRPO with trajectory-level (group-relative) rewards and tool-output token masking, both ideas already present in cited prior agentic-RL/ARTIST work. The paper's contribution is primarily the engineering integration into a platform rather than a new algorithmic idea.
- Model diversity is narrow: main results use Qwen3-8B; a Qwen2.5-4B ablation appears only in the appendix with a different evaluator, and no other model family (e.g., Llama) is tested for the core Agentic GRPO pipeline, limiting generalizability claims.

Weaknesses (presentation/significance):
- The paper claims broad generalizability across enterprise domains, but training and test sets are drawn from the same underlying schema/environment for each benchmark, so it's unclear how well trained agents generalize to genuinely novel enterprise tool sets not seen during synthesis.
- The synthetic-data quality analysis (Self-BLEU, correctness) is conducted only on EnterpriseBench trajectories, not across all four evaluated environments, limiting the generality of these quality claims.
- Minor overclaiming in the abstract/conclusion (e.g., "match GPT-4o's performance") is not fully consistent with Table 1 results.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. GPT-4o's reported scores (e.g., 0.32 on CRMArena, 0.21 tool-selection accuracy on EnterpriseBench) seem unusually low for a frontier model on tool-use tasks. Was native function calling used as described in Section 2.3 for the reported baseline numbers, and were identical tool schemas/prompt budgets given to all models? Can you report variance across seeds/runs?
2. Have you tried fine-tuning a proprietary model (e.g., via OpenAI's fine-tuning API) on the same <1K synthesized trajectories, to isolate whether the gains come from the platform's synthetic data quality versus simply the effect of task-specific specialization regardless of base model?
3. Please clarify how the "+10%" figures for EnterpriseBench/CRMArena in the abstract are computed (absolute point difference vs. relative percentage), since the raw numbers in Table 1 suggest smaller absolute gaps.
4. Given that Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-3.5-Sonnet substantially outperform both GPT-4o and your trained 8B models on nearly every benchmark, how should readers interpret the claim that EnterpriseLab provides "a practical path to...agents without compromising operational capability" relative to the strongest available proprietary models?
5. How many independent training runs (seeds) were used for the Agentic GRPO results, and what is the variance in execution accuracy across runs, given RL training instability?
review.limitations: The paper includes a dedicated Limitations section (Appendix A.8) acknowledging scope restrictions (tool-based vs. UI-based environments, dependence on reasonably capable base models for RL, and that some frontier models retain an edge on complex scenarios), plus a brief Impact Statement focused on positive societal effects (data sovereignty, cost reduction, lower energy use). However, the discussion of potential negative impacts is minimal; the paper would benefit from explicitly discussing risks specific to deploying autonomous agents with write access to enterprise systems (e.g., HR, CRM, finance), such as prompt-injection vulnerabilities, unintended cross-application side effects from the stateful backend, and security/access-control implications of MCP-based tool exposure in production settings.

title: Expert Threshold Routing for Autoregressive Language Modeling with Dynamic Computation Allocation and Load Balancing

review.summary: This paper introduces Expert Threshold (ET) routing for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. Instead of Token-Choice (TC) routing (each token picks fixed top-G experts, requiring auxiliary/loss-free balancing losses) or Expert-Choice (EC) routing (each expert picks its top-k tokens within a batch, which achieves perfect load balance but breaks causality for autoregressive generation), ET routes each token to an expert if its router score exceeds an expert-specific threshold that is estimated online via an exponential moving average (EMA) of the batch's k-th largest logit. Because the threshold depends only on past statistics, routing is fully causal at both train and inference time, while approximately preserving load balance in expectation. The paper frames ET conceptually as EC in the infinite-batch limit, includes a theoretical appendix bounding future-information leakage of EC under finite- vs infinite-precision cutoffs, and empirically validates ET on 575M and 2.4B parameter GPT-2-style (nanochat) models trained on FineWeb-Edu. Results show ET outperforms TC (with auxiliary loss or loss-free balancing) in both cross-entropy loss and CORE benchmark score, and nearly matches large-batch EC (with a causal ET-inference protocol) without requiring batch-size coordination. Extensive analyses cover cutoff-vs-usage tradeoffs, dynamic compute allocation, expert specialization, batch-size scaling for EC, train/inference gap, and routing consistency across checkpoints, plus ablations on warmup, shared experts, and normalization.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The core idea—maintaining a globally-estimated, EMA-tracked per-expert threshold to causalize Expert-Choice-style routing—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained with a good conceptual bridge between TC, EC, and ET (Section 2–3, Figure 2).
- The framing of ET as the infinite-batch limit of EC is intuitive and is empirically supported by the batch-size scaling experiment (Section 4.3.4), which shows EC performance improving with batch size and saturating near ET's performance.
- The experimental protocol is reasonably thorough for an academic-scale pretraining study: two model scales (575M/195M active, 2.4B/561M active), multiple TC/EC baselines with different balancing strategies and batch sizes, and consistent evaluation (CE loss, CORE benchmark).
- Several useful diagnostic analyses are included: cutoff-vs-usage tradeoff (Fig. 3), qualitative dynamic computation allocation examples on GSM8K/HumanEval (Fig. 4–5), expert specialization heatmaps, and routing consistency across checkpoints via weighted Jaccard/joint JSD (Fig. 8, 14). These add useful qualitative insight beyond the headline numbers.
- Appendix A's formal treatment of future-information leakage in EC (finite- vs. infinite-precision cutoffs) is an interesting theoretical contribution that clarifies why threshold-based causal EC does not
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How many seeds were used for each configuration (TC, EC at various batch sizes, ET)? Given that some deltas (e.g., EC 512k at 2.843 vs ET at 2.844 CE) are very small, how confident are you that the reported ET vs EC/TC gaps are statistically distinguishable from run-to-run noise?
2. For the TC baselines, were the auxiliary-loss coefficient α and loss-free update rate u tuned via a sweep, or fixed to commonly used defaults? Could under-tuned TC baselines be inflating the apparent ET advantage?
3. Can you clarify how sensitive ET's performance is to the EMA decay β and the 4k-step EC warmup length? Is there a principled way to set these hyperparameters as model/batch size scale, or were they tuned specifically for this setup?
4. Given that expert capacity constraints (C=0.5) are still applied during ET training (Appendix F.1), how does the choice of capacity factor affect the reported near-perfect load balance and the train/inference gap? Would a tighter or looser capacity factor change the picture?
5. Do you have any results or projections at larger scale (e.g., >10B params or >100B tokens) to support that the ET advantage over TC persists or grows, rather than being specific to this modest-scale, short-training regime?
review.limitations: The paper includes a brief Impact Statement but it is generic and does not discuss any specific limitations of the method (e.g., dependence on capacity factors to avoid OOM, sensitivity to EMA hyperparameters and warmup schedule, applicability only tested on a single mid-scale architecture/dataset, single-seed results). The authors should explicitly discuss: (1) scaling limitations of the current empirical evidence (2.4B/561M active parameters, ~11B tokens), (2) sensitivity of the threshold mechanism to non-stationary token distributions or domain shifts at inference time, (3) hardware/systems implications of variable expert load (e.g., possible under-utilization or padding overhead in production serving), and (4) any potential negative societal impacts, even if minimal, rather than stating that none need to be highlighted.

title: Whole-Brain Connectomic Graph Model Enables Whole-Body Locomotion Control in Fruit Fly

review.summary: The paper introduces FlyGM, a neural controller for embodied reinforcement learning whose computational graph is derived directly from the complete synaptic connectome of the adult Drosophila brain (FlyWire dataset). The connectome is represented as a directed, signed (excitatory/inhibitory) message-passing graph with afferent, intrinsic, and efferent neuron partitions; observations are injected into afferent neurons, propagated via the fixed synaptic weight matrix combined with trainable per-neuron intrinsic descriptors, and decoded into motor commands for a biomechanical fly model (flybody) in MuJoCo. The model is trained via a two-stage pipeline (imitation learning from an MLP expert followed by PPO fine-tuning) and evaluated on walking, gait initiation, turning, and flight tasks. The authors compare FlyGM against an Erdős–Rényi random graph, a degree-preserving rewired graph, and an MLP baseline, reporting faster convergence and lower error for the connectome-based model, and further show qualitative visualizations of gait patterns and emergent functional segregation in learned neural representations.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The central idea—instantiating an entire measured whole-brain connectome as a functioning RL policy for embodied whole-body control—is novel and creative, extending prior connectome-constrained models (which target single subsystems or simplified behaviors) to full-body, multi-task control.
- The method section is detailed, providing a principled way to convert a static wiring diagram into a dynamical message-passing controller, including signed synaptic weighting via neurotransmitter polarity.
- The paper evaluates across multiple, qualitatively different locomotor tasks (gait initiation, straight walking, turning, flight), which is a reasonably comprehensive testbed.
- The ablations against random and degree-preserving rewired graphs, as well as an MLP, are a sensible attempt to isolate the contribution of biological topology.
- The neural representation analysis (PCA-reduced activity, spectral neuron reordering) is an interesting attempt to connect the model's internal dynamics to neuroscience literature.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- A significant confound undermines the central causal claim: the connectome-based model uses real, signed synaptic weights (Nexc − Ninh), while the ER-random and degree-preserving rewired baselines are explicitly unweighted (unit-strength edges). Thus, the reported advantage of FlyGM cannot be cleanly attributed to "topology" alone, since it also encodes substantial additional biological information (synapse counts, transmitter polarity) that the baselines lack. A topology-only ablation (connectome structure with unit weights) is needed to make the inductive-bias claim rigorous.
- The RL-based quantitative evaluation (Table 1) omits the MLP baseline entirely; MLP comparisons are only shown via imitation-learning training curves (Fig. 3), not final task performance under RL fine-tuning. This leaves the central claim of "superior performance" over MLPs for actual embodied control largely unsubstantiated.
- Gait initiation and flight tasks are evaluated only qualitatively (snapshot figures), without any quantitative metrics (e.g., time-to-stable-gait, trajectory tracking error, energy expenditure), limiting rigor of the claimed generalization across tasks.
- No statistical significance testing is reported; only mean ± std over an unspecified (and possibly small) number of runs is given, and it is unclear how many independent random-topology instantiations were used for the ER-random/rewired baselines.
- The neural representation analysis is descriptive and qualitative; claims of "functional segregation" and consistency with neuroscience literature are not backed by quantitative clustering or comparison metrics.
- Computational cost (parameter count, wall-clock time, memory) of the very large connectome graph (likely >100k neurons) versus baselines is only mentioned qualitatively as a limitation, without concrete numbers, making it hard to assess practical trade-offs of "sample efficiency" measured in training steps vs. real compute.

Presentation:
- The paper is generally clearly written and organized, with helpful diagrams (Fig. 1, 2) and an algorithm box. However, important experimental details (e.g., number of seeds/runs, MLP baseline exclusion from Table 1, exact node/edge counts of the full connectome) are missing or deferred, and some figures duplicate information without adding new quantitative substance (e.g., snapshot images without corresponding numeric metrics).

Significance:
- The work is interesting to the intersection of neuroscience and ML, potentially opening a novel direction for bio-inspired architecture design. However, given the current evaluation gaps, it is unclear how strongly this establishes broad significance for the ML community versus being a compelling but preliminary demonstration.

Originality:
- To my knowledge, using a full measured connectome (rather than a stylized or partial one) as the exact computational graph of an embodied RL policy for whole-body, multi-task control is original and distinguishes this work from prior connectome-constrained models limited to single subsystems.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Baselines (ER-random, rewired) use unweighted unit-strength edges while FlyGM uses signed, magnitude-weighted synaptic connections. Can you provide an ablation with connectome topology but unit-weighted edges (and vice versa: baselines with matched weight statistics) to isolate the contribution of topology from the contribution of real synaptic weights/polarity? 
2. Why is the MLP baseline excluded from Table 1 (the RL-based task performance comparison)? Can you provide quantitative RL performance metrics for the MLP baseline on the same speed/yaw conditions, and for gait initiation and flight tasks?
3. How many independent random seeds/topology instantiations were used for the ER-random and rewired-graph baselines, and were results statistically tested (e.g., via t-test or non-overlapping confidence intervals)?
4. What are the actual parameter counts and wall-clock training/inference times for FlyGM versus the MLP and graph baselines? Does the "higher sample efficiency" claim hold when measured in wall-clock time rather than gradient steps, given the much larger connectome graph?
5. Can you provide quantitative evidence (e.g., clustering scores, mutual information) supporting the claimed "functional segregation" emerging in neural representations, beyond visual inspection of heatmaps?
review.limitations: The authors briefly discuss limitations (connectome completeness/richness, higher computational/memory cost relative to MLPs, and restriction to locomotion tasks) and include a short impact statement noting potential to reduce animal experimentation, with no significant negative societal risks claimed. However, the limitations section does not address the important methodological confound between weighted (biological) and unweighted (random/rewired) baseline comparisons, nor does it discuss the lack of statistical rigor (single-run or small-sample reporting) or the absence of quantitative metrics for two of the four evaluated tasks (gait initiation and flight). These points should be added for a more complete and self-critical limitations discussion.

title: Robust Privacy: Inference-Time Privacy through Certified Robustness

review.summary: This paper proposes "Robust Privacy" (RP), a notion that repurposes certified-robustness guarantees (specifically randomized smoothing) as an inference-time privacy mechanism. The core claim is that if a model's output is provably invariant within an ℓp-ball of radius R around an input x, an observer of the output cannot distinguish x from any point in that ball, and hence releasing the prediction does not leak fine-grained information about x. Building on this, the authors define "Attribute Privacy Enhancement" (APE), which translates input-level output invariance into an expansion of the set of sensitive-attribute values consistent with an observed output. They instantiate RP with Cohen et al.'s randomized smoothing and evaluate two applications: (1) a synthetic recommendation task where a two-layer network is engineered to depend primarily on BMI, showing that smoothing shifts the positive-prediction boundary leftward (expanding the inference interval by up to ~1.0 BMI unit); and (2) mitigation of the label-only model inversion attack of Kahla et al. (2022) on CelebA/FaceNet, showing that increasing the smoothing noise scale σ reduces attack success rate (ASR) from 73% to as low as 4% (with accuracy degradation) or to 44% (with no accuracy loss).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The core idea of repurposing certified robustness (a well-established adversarial-robustness tool) as an inference-time privacy mechanism is a novel and intuitively appealing analogy, and is clearly motivated by a concrete example (insulin recommendation revealing BMI).
- The paper is well organized: it carefully specifies threat models for two distinct scenarios (attribute inference and model inversion), gives formal definitions (Def. 1, Def. 2), and discusses practical issues such as abstention handling and privacy-utility-cost tradeoffs (Section 7).
- The empirical demonstration on model inversion is a reasonable proof of concept, using an established attack (Kahla et al., 2022) and standard benchmark (CelebA/FaceNet), and shows a clear trend of ASR reduction with increasing σ.
- The discussion contrasting RP with Differential Privacy (Section 7.3) is useful for situating the contribution.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The paper never establishes a rigorous, quantitative link between the certified radius R and a meaningful privacy metric (e.g., bound on posterior odds, likelihood-ratio, or mutual information). APE is defined purely as a set-expansion notion; it says nothing about how much an adversary's estimation error, expected loss, or Bayesian posterior actually improves for the attacker (or degrades for the defender). This is a substantial gap for a paper claiming to introduce a new "privacy notion."
- The magnitude of the demonstrated protection is very small: the empirically observed interval expansion is on the order of 0.4–1.0 BMI units (Figure 1, Table 1), which is a negligible fraction of the meaningful BMI range (typically spanning tens of units). The paper does not discuss whether such small expansions provide any practically meaningful protection against a realistic adversary who also has priors over the population BMI distribution.
- No baselines are compared. The APE effect (blurring a decision boundary near a threshold) could plausibly be achieved by much simpler techniques (e.g., adding calibrated noise directly to the sensitive attribute before thresholding, generalization/binning, or randomized response), and the paper does not show RP provides any advantage over such simpler alternatives, nor does it justify why the heavier machinery of randomized smoothing (N=1000 queries per inference) is needed.
- Section 5's "attack" is not an actual adversarial procedure but simply a sweep over BMI to observe where positive predictions occur; there is no adaptive attacker whose actual inference accuracy/error is measured (e.g., mean absolute error of a point estimate, or attack success at guessing a bucket). This weakens the empirical evaluation of the attribute-inference protection compared to the more concrete evaluation done for model inversion.
- In the model-inversion experiments, the reported "accuracy" (Figure 3, Table in Section 6) is computed on a curated set of 1000 images chosen as the single highest-confidence image per identity under the *undefended* model, which is a favorable/easy sample that could inflate the apparent accuracy retention under smoothing; the paper does not report accuracy on a representative or random test sample, nor variance across multiple seeds/attack runs.
- The paper's own Section 7.2 documents that different abstention-handling protocols are used for the two experiments to obtain "favorable" measurements (retaining ⊥ in one case, suppressing it in the other) — while the authors provide a rationale, this ad hoc protocol switching raises reproducibility and fairness-of-comparison concerns.
- RP is only instantiated for classifiers via randomized smoothing; the practical relevance to real recommendation/regression/generative systems (where outputs are often continuous or richer than hard labels) is unclear, and the added query cost (N up to 1000 per prediction) for certification is not benchmarked against real deployment latency constraints.
- Only a single synthetic tabular dataset (BMI/insurance) is used for the attribute-inference evaluation, and the classifier is deliberately engineered (via ℓ1 penalty) to depend almost exclusively on BMI, limiting external validity.

Presentation: The paper is generally clearly written, well-structured with formal definitions and threat models, and includes helpful illustrative figures (e.g., Fig. 2's schematic). Minor issues: some sections restate the same conclusions multiple times (e.g., contribution list vs. intro vs. conclusion), and Table/Figure captions are dense.

Significance: The idea of connecting certified robustness to privacy is interesting but the demonstrated empirical gains are narrow (single small-scale synthetic task) and of small magnitude for the attribute-inference use case; the model-inversion mitigation results are more convincing but lack baselines and variance reporting.

Originality: Repurposing certified robustness for privacy is a reasonably original framing, though the underlying mechanism (adding noise to blur a decision boundary or attack gradient signal) is conceptually related to well-known ideas in privacy/robustness literature (e.g., randomized response, noise-based defenses against black-box attacks), so the technical novelty beyond the reframing is modest.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can you provide a formal, quantitative relationship between the certified robust radius R and a standard privacy/leakage metric (e.g., bound on adversary posterior shift, likelihood-ratio bound, or mutual information reduction), rather than relying solely on the deterministic interval-expansion notion in Definition 2?
2. How does RP compare empirically against simpler baselines for the attribute-inference task, such as adding calibrated noise directly to the sensitive attribute or randomized response before classification, or simply shifting/generalizing the decision threshold by a fixed margin?
3. In Section 6, the reported accuracy is measured on a set of images selected as the highest-confidence sample per identity under the undefended model. Can you report accuracy (and its variance) on a random/representative test sample, and provide error bars/repeated trials for ASR and accuracy in Figure 3?
4. Have you evaluated Robust Privacy against an adaptive, optimization-based attribute-inference attacker (rather than a static sweep) to quantify realistic reductions in adversary success (e.g., expected estimation error), analogous to the evaluation done for model inversion?
5. Given that N up to 1000 forward evaluations per query are needed for certification/prediction, what is the practical latency/throughput overhead of deploying RP in a real-time recommendation system, and have you considered more query-efficient certification schemes?
review.limitations: The paper discusses some practical limitations (privacy-utility-cost tradeoffs, abstention handling, comparison to DP) in Section 7, but does not adequately address: (1) the lack of a formal connection between the certified radius and standard information-theoretic/statistical privacy guarantees; (2) the very small magnitude of the demonstrated attribute-privacy protection relative to the meaningful range of the sensitive attribute; (3) potential fairness/societal impacts of accuracy degradation under smoothing across subpopulations; (4) generalizability of the framework beyond classification-style models with hard-label outputs (e.g., regression, ranking, or generative outputs common in real recommender systems); and (5) the query-cost/latency overhead of randomized smoothing certification in real deployment settings. The authors should expand the limitations discussion to cover these points.

title: Benchmarks Are Not That Out of Distribution: Word Overlap Predicts Performance

review.summary: This paper studies whether zero-shot benchmark performance of pretrained language models is largely explained by simple statistical overlap between the pretraining corpus and the benchmark, rather than by more abstract generalization. The authors propose a word-level unigram cross-entropy metric (KL divergence between marginal word-frequency distributions of pretraining corpus and benchmark, computed via whitespace tokenization to avoid subword tokenizer biases) and complementary word-frequency/coverage statistics. They pretrain LLaMA-style models (400M–3.36B parameters) on subsets (8.5B–60B tokens) of four corpora (FineWeb-Edu, DCLM, C4, OpenWebText) and evaluate on ten zero-shot benchmarks. They report that, for most benchmarks, the ranking of corpora by unigram cross-entropy matches the ranking of downstream accuracy, and that increasing token count while roughly holding cross-entropy fixed also improves performance, attributed to stronger frequency-driven learning signal. A theoretical appendix argues why unigram (rather than higher-order n-gram) cross-entropy cleanly isolates marginal distributional overlap. The paper also identifies benchmarks (BLiMP, MathQA, multilingual tasks) where the cross-entropy proxy fails to explain performance, and discusses implications for interpreting benchmark gains and potential “benchmark hacking” by synthetically increasing benchmark-relevant word frequency in pretraining data.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Investigates a timely and important question: what drives benchmark performance gains from different pretraining corpora, and whether observed gains reflect genuine generalization or superficial distributional overlap.
- Fairly broad empirical sweep: 4 corpora, 3 token scales, 3 model scales, and 10 benchmarks, with additional ablations (5 independent subsets per corpus) intended to check robustness to sampling noise.
- The word-level (rather than token-level) formulation is a sensible design choice to avoid subword-tokenization confounds, and the KL-divergence decomposition (Appendix A) gives a clear, if standard, information-theoretic justification for using unigram over higher-order n-gram statistics.
- Commendably transparent in reporting counter-examples (BLiMP, MathQA, multilingual tasks) where the proposed metric fails to explain performance, and in cautioning against interpreting cross-entropy as a measure of benchmark difficulty.

Weaknesses (Soundness):
- The central empirical claim — that cross-entropy ranks predict performance ranks — is evaluated, for any given benchmark, across only 3 (sometimes 4) pretraining corpora. With n=3–4 points, an “ordering match” is extremely weak statistical evidence and easily could arise by chance or from confounds; no correlation coefficients, significance tests, or aggregate statistics across the full grid of benchmark×corpus combinations are reported to substantiate the “robust” language used throughout the paper.
- FineWeb-Edu and DCLM are curated with quality/topical filters that plausibly make their content more educational/encyclopedic in nature, which would independently explain better performance on knowledge-heavy benchmarks (ARC, MMLU, SciQ) without needing a “word-overlap” framing; the paper does not disentangle corpus quality/topical relevance from pure marginal word-frequency overlap (e.g., via controlled corpus mixtures or matched-quality corpora differing only in vocabulary alignment).
- There is an internal inconsistency: Table 4 (1.33B model, 26B tokens) reports that BLiMP does *not* follow the cross-entropy trend, while Appendix Table 15 (3.36B model, 60B tokens) shows BLiMP performance *does* follow the trend (DCLM lowest entropy and highest score). This contradiction is only noted in passing in a table caption and is never reconciled or discussed in the main text, undermining confidence in the “exceptions” analysis in Section 5.
- The synthetic “benchmark hacking” idea (Section 6.1) is purely speculative — no experiment is run to validate it, weakening the practical implications drawn from the paper.
- The theoretical contribution (Appendix A) is a standard cross-entropy/KL decomposition; while a clean derivation, it does not constitute a novel theoretical advance and the associated claims about n-gram sample complexity are asserted rather than empirically demonstrated.

Presentation:
- The paper suffers from numerous grammatical errors and awkward phrasing (e.g., “these empirical evidences,” “we raise a question regarding the the relationship,” “dowmstream” typo in a table caption, “Bigger word count leads score improvements”), which detract from clarity and suggest the manuscript would benefit from careful proofreading.
- Figures are generally interpretable, but claims of a “stable inverse relationship” rely on visual inspection across very few data points per plot rather than quantitative summary statistics.

Significance:
- The topic is relevant to ongoing debates about pretraining data curation and benchmark validity, but the main finding — that stylistically/topically similar pretraining data improves performance on similarly-styled benchmarks — is not particularly surprising and is arguably already assumed by practitioners; the paper does not clearly establish that this is due to superficial marginal word overlap per se, as opposed to general topical/domain relevance, which limits the novelty of the practical implications.

Originality:
- The word-level unigram cross-entropy metric and its explicit connection to benchmark performance is a reasonably original framing, distinguishing itself from other data-quality studies that rely on token-level or n-gram statistics, even though the underlying intuition ("training loss correlates with benchmark score") is well established in prior work the authors themselves cite.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can you provide quantitative correlation statistics (e.g., Spearman/Pearson correlations with significance tests, aggregated across all benchmark×corpus combinations) rather than relying on qualitative visual pattern matching across only 3–4 corpora per benchmark?
2. Table 4 (1.33B/26B) reports that BLiMP does not follow the cross-entropy trend, while Appendix Table 15 (3.36B/60B) shows the opposite (BLiMP does follow the trend). Can you clarify and reconcile this discrepancy, and explain how it affects the claims in Section 5.1?
3. To what extent could the observed cross-entropy–performance correlation be confounded by general corpus quality/topical relevance (e.g., FineWeb-Edu/DCLM being curated for educational content) rather than pure marginal word-overlap? Could you test with corpora matched in curation quality but differing specifically in benchmark vocabulary overlap?
4. Have you considered testing with a larger number of pretraining corpora or continuous mixtures (e.g., interpolations between C4/DCLM/FineWeb-Edu) to assess whether the cross-entropy–performance relationship holds as a continuous trend rather than an ordinal match over 3–4 points?
5. How sensitive are the reported results to the specific choice of "word" definition (whitespace splitting, no normalization)? Would results change materially under alternative tokenization/normalization choices for computing word frequencies?
review.limitations: The paper acknowledges some limitations by presenting counter-example benchmark categories (grammar, math, multilingual) where the proposed metric fails to explain performance, and includes a caveat that cross-entropy should not be treated as a universal difficulty scale across benchmarks. However, it does not discuss the statistical limitations of drawing strong conclusions from comparisons across only 3–4 pretraining corpora, does not address the potential confound between corpus curation quality and word-overlap, and does not discuss any societal impact (e.g., implications of the proposed "benchmark hacking" strategy for gaming leaderboards, or risks of encouraging data curation strategies that optimize superficial overlap rather than genuine capability). Adding a dedicated limitations section addressing these points, along with resolving the noted internal inconsistency in the BLiMP results, would strengthen the paper.

title: From Perception to Action: An Interactive Benchmark for Vision Reasoning

review.summary: The paper introduces CHAIN (Causal Hierarchy of Actions and Interactions), an interactive 3D, physics-driven benchmark intended to move VLM evaluation away from static, single-turn VQA toward closed-loop physical problem solving. CHAIN consists of two task families: (1) interlocking mechanical puzzles (32 instances across easy/medium/hard, built in Unity with a color-hinted interaction interface) that require multi-step disassembly/assembly under kinematic and contact constraints, and (2) 3D spatial packing/stacking (77 instances, procedurally generated with a DLX-based exact-cover solver) that require reasoning about geometry, support, and remaining free space over multiple placement steps. The authors define a suite of metrics covering task success (Pass@1), plan efficiency (AvgSteps, Dist2Opt, NormDist), and token/dollar cost efficiency. They benchmark a large pool of closed- and open-source VLMs (GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Pro, Claude models, Qwen3-VL variants, Kimi, GLM, etc.) under a unified interaction protocol, finding that models perform far worse on puzzles than on stacking, that success degrades sharply with difficulty, that interactive settings substantially outperform one-shot solving, and that reward-model-based action reranking offers limited gains over simple multi-sample selection. As a side study, they also probe several video/diffusion “world models” (Sora 2, Wan 2.6, Veo 3.1, Kling 2.6, HunyuanVideo 1.5) on generating physically valid disassembly sequences of a Luban lock and report systematic catastrophic failures (physics violations, hallucinated/corrupted geometry). The appendix provides a detailed procedural-generation pipeline for stacking puzzles with solvability, connectivity, and (optional) linear-assembly guarantees, plus qualitative case studies of successful/failed stacking trajectories.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing VLM evaluation is dominated by static VQA-style benchmarks that do not test closed-loop, constraint-aware action selection; CHAIN’s emphasis on iterative perception-action loops with feedback is a valuable shift.
- Reasonably comprehensive empirical study spanning many contemporary closed- and open-source VLMs under a controlled, unified protocol (fixed temperature/top-p, fixed step budget, fixed history window), which aids comparability.
- Thoughtful metric design that goes beyond binary success to capture plan efficiency and cost/token efficiency, which is useful for practitioners assessing deployment trade-offs.
- The one-shot vs. interactive comparison (Table 3) and difficulty-stratified analysis (Table 2) are informative ablations that support the paper's central claim that closed-loop interaction is necessary and that the benchmark cannot be trivially “solved” by static single-view reasoning.
- The procedural stacking-puzzle generation pipeline (Appendix A.5) is rigorous, using an exact-cover DLX solver with connectivity, size-bound, and linear-assembly-feasibility constraints, plus canonicalization-based de-duplication — a solid engineering contribution that could be reused by others.
- The world-model failure analysis (Section 3.3), while limited, is an interesting addition that broadens the benchmark's relevance to video/diffusion generative reasoning.

Weaknesses (Soundness):
- The benchmark scale is modest: 32 puzzle instances and 77 stacking instances (109 total). For the puzzle subset specifically, nearly every model in Table 1 scores exactly 0.0 or 3.1% (i.e., 0 or 1 out of 32 solved), which is a very coarse, nearly binary signal that undermines the statistical resolution of cross-model comparisons on this subtask, despite the paper's framing that “Puzzle success is consistently far below Stacking” as a robust finding.
- No repeated trials or variance estimates are reported for the main Table 1 results (only Pass@1 is used as the primary metric due to cost, per Appendix A.1). The brief robustness check in Section 3.6 (Avg@4 vs Pass@1) is done only for a single model (Kimi-k2.5) and a single generator, which is insufficient to establish that the main leaderboard rankings are not driven by noise, especially given the small instance counts noted above.
- The world-model evaluation (Section 3.3) is entirely qualitative (visual inspection of Figure 4) on only two puzzle configurations (2-beam and 6-beam Luban lock) with no quantitative or automated scoring metric, limiting the rigor of claims about “catastrophic failure.”
- Difficulty stratification for Puzzle (Table 2) shows 0.0% across all evaluated models on Mid/Hard, which is presented as evidence of a fundamentally different difficulty regime, but could equally suggest floor effects that make comparative claims about puzzle difficulty hard to substantiate empirically.
- Design choices such as the fixed 5-turn history window and 30–60 step budget are not ablated, so it is unclear how much of the observed puzzle failure is attributable to information/context bottlenecks rather than genuine reasoning limitations.
- Limited discussion/comparison with prior interactive/embodied benchmarks (e.g., ALFRED, Behavior-1K, ManiSkill2, EmbodiedEval) in terms of concrete quantitative or qualitative differentiation, despite several being cited; the related-work section is largely descriptive rather than comparative.

Presentation:
- Overall structure is clear and the pipeline figure (Fig. 2) aids understanding, but there are minor lapses (e.g., Section 2.3 numbering lists "(i) task success, (ii) plan efficiency, and (iv) cost efficiency" skipping (iii), a likely typo) and some redundant phrasing in the introduction repeating the same sentence about early actions constraining future feasible action spaces.
- Tables are dense but mostly interpretable; Figure 3’s cost/token trade-off plot is a nice touch for visualizing multi-metric comparison.

Significance/Originality:
- The high-level idea of interactive, physics-grounded evaluation is not entirely new (relates to embodied AI and manipulation benchmarks), but the specific combination of interlocking mechanical puzzles with rule-based verification and procedurally generated exact-cover stacking puzzles, evaluated uniformly across a broad set of contemporary VLMs and extended to video/world models, is a reasonably original and useful contribution to the physical/embodied reasoning evaluation literature.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Why does Puzzle Pass@1 collapse to almost exactly 0.0% or 3.1% (i.e., 0/32 or 1/32) for nearly every evaluated model? Is this a genuine difficulty floor, or could it reflect overly strict/binary rule-based verification, environment implementation issues, or a specific single puzzle instance being uniquely easy? Have you investigated which specific instance(s) are being solved?
2. Given the small instance counts (32 puzzles, 77 stacking tasks) and that only Pass@1 is reported for most models, how confident are you that the cross-model rankings in Table 1 are not dominated by sampling noise? Can you provide variance/error bars or repeated-run results for at least a subset of top models to substantiate the main claims?
3. How sensitive are results to the fixed 5-turn interaction history window and the 30–60 step budget? Could puzzle failures be partly attributable to context/history truncation rather than fundamental reasoning limitations, especially for hard puzzles requiring long-horizon dependency tracking?
4. For the world-model evaluation (Section 3.3), is there a plan to introduce a quantitative or automated metric (e.g., physical plausibility scoring, object permanence checks) to complement the qualitative failure analysis, and could the evaluation be extended beyond two configurations to strengthen the generality of the

title: Physics as the Inductive Bias for Causal Discovery

review.summary: This paper proposes a framework for causal discovery in dynamical systems that combines partially known ODE-based physics with data-driven graph learning. The key modeling idea is to represent the system as a stochastic differential equation (SDE) where the drift term encodes known ODE dynamics and the (state-dependent, diagonal) diffusion term captures unknown cross-variable causal couplings not explained by the known physics. The paper (i) motivates and formalizes a notion of "causal coupling beyond known dynamics" defined via nonzero diffusion coefficients, (ii) derives a tractable quasi-likelihood objective (via Euler–Maruyama discretization) with an ℓ1 penalty for graph/parameter estimation (the SCD algorithm), and (iii) develops finite-sample identifiability guarantees for graph recovery under a local restricted strong convexity argument, extending Lasso-type nonconvex M-estimator theory (à la Loh & Wainwright) to a setting with multiplicative SDE noise, without imposing acyclicity or additive-noise assumptions. Guarantees rely on SDE well-posedness, Lyapunov-stability-type conditions, sparsity, and an incoherence condition on the population Fisher information. Empirically, the method is evaluated on simulated DAG and directed-loop-graph datasets (varying dimension p, stable/unstable regimes, partial physics settings) and compared against DYNOTEARS, PCMCI, SCOTCH, and Neural-GC using SHD/TPR/FDR, showing consistent improvements. Supplementary results include robustness to ODE (drift) misspecification and a small "real-world-inspired" biological (Hes1) illustrative example.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. Originality of framing: Casting physics-informed causal discovery for dynamical systems via an SDE whose drift encodes known ODE structure and whose (multiplicative) diffusion encodes unknown causal couplings is a fresh and reasonably compelling idea, and the paper explicitly departs from acyclicity/stationarity/additive-noise assumptions common in prior SDE-based causal discovery work (NGM, SCOTCH, GCLMs).

2. Non-trivial theory: The identifiability analysis handles a genuinely harder setting than standard high-dimensional Lasso analyses — the loss is nonconvex, the noise is multiplicative and state-dependent (leading to non-Gaussian, non-i.i.d. residuals), and the process is non-stationary. The authors introduce a stabilization constant to obtain a local restricted strong convexity property and carry out a careful primal-dual witness argument. This is a solid, if dense, technical contribution.

3. Reasonably thorough experiments: multiple graph families (DAGs, directed loop graphs), stable/unstable regimes, varying dimension, an ODE-misspecification stress test, and comparison against four relevant baselines with three standard metrics (SHD/TPR/FDR). The reported gaps versus baselines are large and the explanations for baseline failure modes (stationarity mismatch, diagonal-diffusion assumption in SCOTCH, Granger-style temporal precedence in Neural-GC) are plausible and consistent with known baseline limitations.

Weaknesses:

1. Questionable causal semantics of the core modeling choice. The paper defines the "causal graph" purely via the nonzero pattern of a matrix A that multiplies the state inside a diagonal diffusion term (Eq. 3), rather than via the drift/deterministic coupling. This is a strong and somewhat unusual choice: it implicitly assumes that any unmodeled inter-variable causal influence manifests exclusively as multiplicative process noise rather than as deterministic (drift-level) feedback. The derivation in §S1.4 that arrives at this structure relies on an admittedly ad hoc substitution (ẋ(t) ≈ x(t)) described as a "surrogate feature choice," which is not rigorously justified beyond convenience, and it is unclear how well the resulting notion of causal coupling maps onto interventional causal semantics used in the broader SCM literature (e.g., via do-operator or the Hansen–Sokol postintervention SDE framework the paper itself cites). This could materially affect how much of the strong empirical results are attributable to a favorable alignment between the (synthetic) data-generating process and the specific diffusion-based estimator, rather than to a generally applicable notion of physics-informed causal discovery.

2. Purely synthetic evaluation. All quantitative experiments are on simulated data generated from the same family of models the estimator assumes (linear ODE + diagonal multiplicative-noise SDE with Erdős–Rényi/loop graphs). There is no evaluation on real or semi-real benchmark datasets (the Hes1 example in §S1.2 is illustrative only, not used for quantitative evaluation). This limits confidence that the reported gains transfer beyond the paper's own generative assumptions, which happen to match the estimator's functional form closely.

3. Limited baseline fairness discussion. Several baselines (DYNOTEARS, PCMCI, Neural-GC) are designed for discrete-time lagged/contemporaneous SVAR-type or Granger settings and are known to be poorly suited to continuous-time, nonstationary, cyclic data; the paper acknowledges this but the resulting comparison may partly reflect a fundamental mismatch in problem setting rather than a fair apples-to-apples comparison of causal discovery quality. Threshold tuning for baselines (e.g., manually shrinking DYNOTEARS's thresholds to avoid degenerate empty graphs) raises some concern about baseline optimization effort relative to the proposed method.

4. Practical significance and scalability are only lightly explored. Experiments only go up to p = 20 variables; the paper claims scalability but provides no wall-clock/complexity comparison against baselines, and no discussion of computational cost of the sparsity-inducing MLE relative to alternatives.

5. Presentation could be improved: the exposition of the theoretical machinery (Section 5 and the appendix) is very dense with many lemmas and constants, and could benefit from more high-level intuition connecting the technical assumptions (Lyapunov stability, incoherence, beta-min) to concrete, checkable properties of real physical systems. The claim of being "the first causal discovery framework for nonstationary time series that does not rely on a DAG assumption" is a strong claim that would benefit from a more careful positioning relative to closely related non-DAG approaches (e.g., GCLMs, which the paper itself cites as also not requiring acyclicity).

6. The choice of tuning parameters (c=0.1, λ=5) is described as found empirically to work well, without much guidance on how a practitioner should set these values in line with the theoretical bounds (which involve several unknown constants, e.g., K, B, L_H, α).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Why should unmodeled causal coupling be represented exclusively through the (diagonal, multiplicative) diffusion term rather than through additional deterministic (drift-level) feedback? Can the authors clarify the causal/interventional interpretation of edges defined via A in Eq. (3), e.g., relative to the do-calculus or the Hansen–Sokol postintervention SDE framework cited in the related work?
2. The derivation in §S1.4 uses the surrogate ẋ(t) ≈ x(t) to obtain a closed diffusion parameterization. How sensitive are the theoretical guarantees and empirical results to this approximation when the true unmodeled dynamics deviate substantially from this surrogate (beyond the additive drift-misspecification experiment in §S1.5, which perturbs the drift, not this specific surrogate assumption)?
3. Could the authors provide any evaluation on non-synthetic or semi-realistic benchmark data (e.g., simulated from a well-known nonlinear physical system such as Lotka–Volterra with truly unmodeled deterministic feedback, rather than diffusion-generated ground truth) to assess robustness when the data-generating process does not exactly match the diagonal multiplicative-noise SDE assumption?
4. How does SCD's computational cost/runtime scale with p compared to the baselines, particularly DYNOTEARS and SCOTCH which also use continuous optimization?
5. Can the authors clarify how a practitioner would set λ and c in practice, given that the theoretical bounds depend on several unknown problem-specific constants (K, B, L_H, α, Cmin)?
review.limitations: The paper includes a brief "Impact Statement" focused on positive framing (trustworthiness, interpretability, responsible deployment) but does not discuss concrete methodological limitations in the main text in a dedicated section, beyond the future-work discussion in the appendix. The appendix (§S1.10) does list some genuine limitations/future directions (theory restricted to stable SDEs, restrictive diffusion parameterization for the diffusion term, only ODE-level mechanistic knowledge considered). I would suggest the authors move a concise version of these limitations (e.g., the strong assumption that causal coupling manifests only through diffusion, reliance on synthetic-only evaluation, and reliance on stability/incoherence/beta-min conditions that may not hold in practice) into the main paper, and add explicit discussion of potential failure modes when the SDE model class is misspecified relative to real physical systems (e.g., deterministic feedback loops not captured by diffusion coupling).

title: Formalizing the Sampling Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models via Adaptive Solvers and Wasserstein-Bounded Timesteps

review.summary: This paper proposes SDM, a training-free framework for accelerating diffusion model sampling that combines two components: (1) a curvature-based adaptive solver allocation strategy, where a closed-form expression for the second-order derivative (acceleration) of the probability-flow ODE is derived under EDM/VP/VE parameterizations, showing that curvature is small in the high-noise regime and grows sharply near the data manifold; this motivates a convex mixture of first-order (Euler) and second-order (Heun) updates that is scheduled (via step/linear/cosine functions of a cheaply-computed proxy curvature) to progressively favor Heun updates later in sampling; and (2) a Wasserstein-bounded adaptive timestep scheduler, which derives a sufficient condition on step size that keeps the local 2-Wasserstein transport error below a tunable tolerance η, together with a total-error bound (extending AdaFlow to score-based diffusion) and an N-step resampling procedure to project the adaptive schedule onto a fixed NFE budget. Both components are training-free and can be combined. Experiments on CIFAR-10, FFHQ, AFHQv2, and ImageNet (unconditional and conditional, VP/VE parameterizations) using pretrained EDM/ADM checkpoints show FID improvements over EDM and COS baselines with comparable or reduced NFE, along with ablations on the curvature threshold, Λ(t) schedule choice, and Wasserstein tolerance parameters.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper provides a fairly rigorous derivation of the second-order PF-ODE dynamics across three standard parameterizations (EDM, VP, VE), unifying prior curvature intuitions (e.g., from EDM) into explicit closed forms; this is a genuine, non-trivial technical contribution, and the empirical validation of the predicted noise-curvature correlation (Fig. 2) is a nice sanity check.
- The Wasserstein-bounded scheduling formalism is theoretically motivated and connects reasonably to prior optimal-transport-based scheduling work (AdaFlow, COS), extending the total-error bound to the score-based diffusion setting.
- The framework is training-free and modular: the adaptive solver and adaptive scheduler can be applied independently or jointly, and the paper demonstrates complementary gains from combining them.
- Reasonably thorough ablations are provided for the threshold τk, the choice of Λ(t), and the η/resampling hyperparameters.

Weaknesses (soundness/significance-related):
- The core competing training-free acceleration methods repeatedly cited in the related work (DPM-Solver++, UniPC, DEIS, Align-Your-Steps, AutoDiffusion) are never included as empirical baselines; only EDM and COS (a schedule-only baseline using the same Euler/Heun solvers) are compared. Given that these higher-order/exponential-integrator solvers are the dominant practical choice for fast (5–15 NFE) sampling, the absence of this comparison significantly weakens the
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) In Algorithm 1, the predictor-corrector line search requires additional trial evaluations of the velocity field before committing to a final step; is this overhead included in the NFE numbers reported in Table 1/4, or are these tables reporting only the number of "final" steps taken? Please clarify precisely how NFE is counted for the adaptive-scheduling variants.
2) Why were DPM-Solver++, UniPC, and DEIS—prominently discussed in the related work as the dominant training-free acceleration approaches—excluded from the empirical comparison? How does SDM compare to these methods at matched NFE, particularly in the very-low-NFE regime (5–15 steps) where such solvers are most commonly used and where the practical impact of sampler design is greatest?
3) The abstract and introduction state that SDM can be "plugged into existing pre-trained diffusion models (e.g., EDM, Stable Diffusion)," but no experiments on Stable Diffusion or any latent/text-conditioned diffusion model are shown. Can you provide such results, or otherwise temper this claim?
4) The hyperparameters τk, ηmin, ηmax, p, and q are tuned per-dataset via grid search (Tables 2–3). How sensitive is performance to these choices on unseen datasets/architectures, and doesn't this reintroduce dataset-specific heuristic tuning that the paper otherwise argues against?
5) Given that many reported FID gains over EDM/COS are small (e.g., 1.96→1.93, 2.04→1.98), were multiple sampling runs/seeds used to assess variance, and is the improvement statistically distinguishable from noise in the FID estimator?
review.limitations: The paper's "Impact Statement" is boilerplate and does not discuss any concrete limitations of the proposed method (e.g., computational/implementation overhead of the line-search-based adaptive scheduler, the introduction of several new hyperparameters requiring per-dataset tuning, or the fact that all experiments are restricted to small-to-medium resolution pixel-space diffusion models rather than the latent/text-to-image setting mentioned in the introduction). I recommend the authors add an explicit limitations discussion covering: (a) the extra computational cost of the adaptive scheduling line search, (b) the current reliance on tuned per-dataset hyperparameters, and (c) the absence of validation on large-scale/latent diffusion or text-to-image models despite motivating claims about such applicability.

title: DDP-WM: Disentangled Dynamics Prediction for Efficient World Models

review.summary: The paper proposes DDP-WM, a latent-space world model that decomposes visual dynamics prediction into two components: (1) sparse "primary dynamics" localized via a dynamic localization network and processed by a dedicated, more expensive ViT predictor, and (2) "context-driven background updates" that are modeled cheaply via a single-layer, unidirectional cross-attention module (the Low-Rank Correction Module, LRM) that queries the newly predicted foreground tokens. The motivation stems from an empirical observation that in DINOv2-based dense world models (e.g., DINO-WM), most background tokens change little across predictor layers, while ground-truth feature differences between consecutive frames are highly sparse. The authors argue that naive sparse prediction (simply copying background tokens) creates a rugged, non-smooth MPC cost landscape that hurts closed-loop planning even though it may achieve competitive open-loop error, and that the proposed LRM restores landscape smoothness by encoding a low-rank correction for background tokens. Experiments across five simulated environments (PointMaze, Push-T, Wall, Rope, Granular) show that DDP-WM matches or exceeds DINO-WM in success rate/Chamfer distance while achieving substantial reductions in FLOPs, throughput improvements, and MPC decision-loop speedups (up to ~9x on Push-T). Ablations isolate the contributions of the LRM, the Sparse MPC Cost Mask, and the localization network's precision, and additional analyses (PCA of background updates, 1D/2D cost landscape visualizations) are provided to support the paper's central hypothesis.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The core motivating observation (Fig. 1: PCA analysis showing minimal background feature change vs. sparse but nonzero ground-truth deltas) is a clear and intuitive way to motivate sparse computation for world models, and the paper backs this up with a systematic architecture rather than ad-hoc heuristics.
- The identification that naive sparse (copy-paste) prediction can match open-loop accuracy but catastrophically fail in closed-loop MPC due to a rugged cost landscape (Section 4.4, Fig. 5) is an interesting and non-obvious finding that adds genuine insight beyond simply reporting a new SOTA number.
- The efficiency gains are substantial and are reported through multiple complementary metrics (theoretical FLOPs, single-step throughput, full MPC decision latency), which strengthens the practical claim of real-time applicability.
- Reasonably comprehensive ablations (Tables 5, 7, 8) isolate the roles of the LRM, sparse MPC cost mask, and localization precision.
- The task suite spans a useful range of difficulty (rigid navigation, contact-rich manipulation, deformable/rope dynamics, and multi-body granular dynamics), which is a nontrivial testbed for generalization of the disentanglement idea.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The paper never explains how ground-truth supervision for the Dynamic Localization Network (the "changed region" labels used to train Psub and the binary mask M) is obtained. This is a critical missing methodological detail: is it thresholded ground-truth feature difference, pixel difference, or something else? Without this, reproducibility and understanding of a core module is compromised.
- The central theoretical claim that background updates are "inherently low-rank" is supported only by a PCA cumulative-variance curve (Appendix A) that shows fast saturation. This is fairly weak evidence, since low-dimensional simulated environments (Push-T, PointMaze, etc.) could produce such curves for many different modeling choices, not uniquely validating a
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How are the ground-truth labels for the Dynamic Localization Network (Psub / mask M) constructed during training? Is this derived from feature-difference thresholds, pixel-difference thresholds, or another criterion, and how sensitive is downstream performance to this choice?
2. The overall speedup (9x) is task-specific to Push-T; other tasks show only 2.7-3.1x speedup. Can you clarify what structural/task properties determine the achievable speedup, and would speedups degrade further in visually richer, real-world scenes with more background texture/tokens?
3. Can you report variance/confidence intervals over multiple seeds or repeated MPC rollouts for the success rate numbers in Table 1, given the relatively small absolute differences (e.g., 90% vs 98%, 96% vs 98%)?
4. Why is the "Sparse Imagination" baseline missing CD values for Rope and Granular in Table 1, and how was it adapted/tuned for a fair comparison?
5. Since the stepwise (non end-to-end) training pipeline trains localization, primary predictor, and LRM sequentially, how sensitive is final performance to errors introduced by upstream modules (e.g., a poorly localized mask propagating errors to LRM training)? Have you tried joint fine-tuning after the stepwise pretraining?
review.limitations: The paper does not include a dedicated discussion of limitations or negative societal impact. Given that the method is evaluated exclusively on simulated, visually simple environments (2D navigation, rigid tabletop pushing, rope/granular simulation), the authors should explicitly discuss whether the low-rank/sparsity assumptions are expected to hold in visually cluttered or photorealistic real-world scenes, and whether real robot deployment (with sensor noise, lighting variation, etc.) was tested or is expected to transfer. A brief discussion of potential negative impacts of more efficient, real-time robotic world models (e.g., increased feasibility of autonomous systems operating in safety-critical or adversarial settings) would also strengthen the submission per ICML's broader impact expectations.

title: SPA: A Simple but Tough-to-Beat Baseline for Knowledge Injection

review.summary: This paper introduces SPA (Scaling Prompt-engineered Augmentation), a knowledge-injection baseline that expands a small domain corpus into a large synthetic corpus using a fixed set of 7 human-curated prompt templates (grouped under Concept Learning, Critical Thinking, and Generative Learning) applied repeatedly at scale, followed by continued pretraining on the synthetic corpus. The authors compare SPA against several more complex methods, including RL-based augmentation (SEAL, PaST) and multi-stage prompting pipelines (EntiGraph, Active Reading, SoG), across three benchmarks: SQuAD (Wikipedia QA), QuALITY (long-document comprehension), and MultiHop-RAG (multi-hop reasoning). Under token-matched, controlled comparisons, SPA matches or exceeds these baselines, especially at larger synthetic data scales. The paper further analyzes why prior methods underperform at scale: RL-based methods (SEAL) reportedly exhibit diversity collapse as the corpus grows, while multi-stage pipelines (Active Reading) can produce lower average-quality intermediate strategies compared to SPA's fixed human-curated prompts. Additional ablations examine the contribution of individual prompts and the effect of task-specific prompt-set tuning, along with diversity metrics (compression ratio, self-repetition, self-BLEU, CR-POS) to support the diversity-collapse claim.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Broad, systematic evaluation across three qualitatively distinct benchmarks (single-document QA, long-document comprehension, multi-hop reasoning) and multiple base model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Meta-Llama-3-8B), which supports claims of generality.
2. Token-matched comparisons against a good set of contemporary and relevant baselines (SEAL, PaST, EntiGraph, Active Reading, SoG), which is methodologically important for fair evaluation of synthetic-data augmentation methods.
3. The diversity-collapse analysis for RL-based methods (via CR, Self-Rep, Self-BLEU, CR-POS) provides a plausible mechanistic account for why SEAL saturates at scale, and is a useful empirical contribution beyond simply reporting accuracy numbers.
4. Reasonable transparency about implementation/evaluation choices (e.g., truncating model outputs for judging, hyperparameter search spaces, generator ablations across GPT-4-Turbo/gpt-oss-120b/GPT-4o), and code availability, which aids reproducibility.
5. The framing as a 'tough-to-beat baseline' is a valuable contribution to the field's research hygiene: many recent knowledge-injection papers may be under-comparing against well-tuned simple methods, and this paper provides evidence for that concern.

Weaknesses (soundness/originality concerns):
1. Originality is limited: the core idea—prompting an LLM with several human-crafted strategies (rephrasing, QA generation, discussions, etc.) to expand a corpus—is very close to prior work already cited (Maini et al. 2024's Rephrase/QA baselines, EntiGraph, Active Reading). The main novel element is the particular curated 7-prompt set and its cognitive-science framing, and simply using much more scale than prior papers. The 'contribution' is largely an engineering/empirical one rather than a methodological/algorithmic one, which is fine for a 'strong baseline' paper but limits originality.
2. The connection to cognitive science/educational psychology is somewhat superficial — the mapping from learning theories (concept learning, critical thinking, generative learning) to specific prompt templates is intuitive but not rigorously justified or ablated against alternative prompt sets constructed without this framing (e.g., a randomly chosen set of 7 diverse prompts). It is unclear whether the specific theoretical grounding matters versus simply having diverse, well-written prompts.
3. Effect sizes at the largest budgets are sometimes fairly small (e.g., 91.27% vs 90.25% for Active Reading on SQuAD, 57.03% vs 56.22% for EntiGraph on QuALITY), yet the abstract and results text describe these as 'clear margins' or 'consistently outperforms.' No variance/error bars or multiple seeds are reported, so it is hard to assess whether these differences are statistically meaningful given the closeness of many results.
4. The QuALITY comparison to EntiGraph uses a different generator (gpt-oss-120b vs GPT-4-Turbo), and while the authors attempt to control for generator strength via Table 2 (27M-token, small-scale check), the large-scale (455M token) comparison in Table 1/Figure 3 mixes generators, which weakens the head-to-head claim of SPA 'beating' EntiGraph at scale.
5. Several baseline numbers (PaST, SoG) are taken directly from the original papers rather than reproduced under the same controlled pipeline, which introduces confounds in comparing methods trained/evaluated under potentially different codebases and hyperparameters, despite the appendix's attempt to show cross-codebase consistency for EntiGraph.
6. Prompt-set tuning experiments (Section 6.1/6.3) show that the optimal subset of prompts differs between SQuAD and QuALITY and that a tuned configuration on one task can underperform the full 7-prompt set on another. This actually weakens (rather than supports) the claim that the default 7-prompt SPA set is a well-motivated universal design, and suggests the reported gains could be sensitive to which exact prompt configuration/parameters are chosen — an important caveat that could be discussed more critically.
7. Some presentational issues are apparent: the extracted manuscript shows what appears to be duplicated/overlapping text blocks in Section 5.3/6.1/6.2 (two versions of the MultiHop-RAG discussion with different rounding of the same numbers, and duplicated Table 3/4 content), suggesting the submitted draft may contain leftover duplicate content or was not fully proofread before submission.
8. The evaluation methodology involves several ad hoc modifications (e.g., considering only the first paragraph/sentence of model outputs during LLM-judged evaluation) that, while reasonably justified, could differentially affect different methods' scores depending on their output verbosity/structure, and it is not clear whether this evaluation choice was validated to be neutral across all compared methods.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. For the QuALITY comparison at 455M tokens (Table 1, Figure 3), EntiGraph uses GPT-4-Turbo while SPA uses gpt-oss-120b. Can you provide a large-scale, same-generator comparison (e.g., SPA with GPT-4-Turbo at 455M tokens) to more directly validate the claim that SPA outperforms EntiGraph, beyond the small-scale (27M token) generator-controlled experiment in Table 2?
2. Many of the reported gains (e.g., SQuAD 91.27% vs 90.25%, QuALITY 57.03% vs 56.22%) are within a few points. Have you run multiple seeds/training runs to report variance, and are these gaps statistically significant?
3. In Section 6.1/6.3, the optimal prompt subset differs across SQuAD and QuALITY, and a tuned subset can underperform the full set on a different task. Doesn't this undermine the argument that the specific cognitive-science-motivated 7-prompt design is well-justified, as opposed to simply having any sufficiently large and diverse prompt pool? Have you compared against a similarly-sized set of prompts not grounded in the three learning-strategy levels (e.g., randomly diversified paraphrase styles) to isolate the contribution of the cognitive-science framing itself?
4. Could you clarify/fix the apparent duplicated content in Section 5.3/6.1/6.2 of the submitted manuscript (the MultiHop-RAG results and diversity-analysis text appear twice with slightly different numbers/wording)? Was this a formatting/rendering artifact, or does it reflect an issue with the submitted draft?
5. For SEAL and PaST comparisons, were these methods retrained/fine-tuned under the exact same computational budget and optimization effort as SPA, or are the numbers taken from the original papers under potentially different training conditions? If the latter, how confident are you that the comparison is fully apples-to-apples?
review.limitations: The paper includes a reasonable 'Discussion' section (Section 7) acknowledging that broader/more challenging scenarios (e.g., numerical reasoning, rapidly evolving knowledge) are not covered, and explicitly states that SPA is intended as a baseline rather than a final solution. However, the paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts (e.g., risks of synthetic data hallucination despite grounding constraints, compute/energy costs of large-scale data generation, or misuse for injecting misleading domain content). A brief discussion of these points, as well as more explicit discussion of the limits of statistical significance given the closeness of many reported results, would strengthen the limitations section.

title: SpatialAnt: Autonomous Zero-Shot Robot Navigation via Active Scene Reconstruction and Visual Anticipation

review.summary: The paper proposes SpatialAnt, a zero-shot Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) framework intended to close the gap between idealized, human-crafted 3D scene reconstructions (as used by prior pre-exploration-based zero-shot agents) and the noisy, incomplete point clouds a real robot can build for itself with a monocular RGB camera. The system has three stages: (1) an active scene discovery module that combines frontier-based DFS exploration with a visibility-aware traveling-salesman path planner to collect view-continuous RGB/IMU data; (2) a physically-grounded scene reconstruction pipeline that uses SLAM3R for regional point-cloud reconstruction, then aligns the ambiguous monocular scale to real metric units by comparing rendered depth to Depth-Anything-2 predicted depth, followed by global pose integration to merge regional point clouds; and (3) an anticipation-guided navigation module that renders candidate future views from the noisy point cloud via Gaussian splatting and reformulates action selection as sub-path selection, letting an MLLM (GPT-5.1) perform counterfactual reasoning by comparing anticipated views against the instruction. The paper reports results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE (sampled validation-unseen episodes) where SpatialAnt outperforms previous zero-shot baselines and approaches supervised methods, plus real-world deployment on a Hello Robot achieving 52% SR. Ablations examine robustness to noisy vs. idealized point clouds, the effect of the visual anticipation mechanism and its field of view, and scalability across different MLLM backbones.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper targets a genuinely important and under-addressed practical problem: prior pre-exploration zero-shot VLN agents assume access to idealized, dataset-quality point clouds, which is unrealistic for real robot deployment. Framing the contribution around this reality gap is well motivated.
- The physical grounding (scale-recovery) strategy and visual anticipation mechanism are reasonably novel combinations of existing tools (SLAM3R, Depth-Anything-2, Gaussian splatting) applied in a new way to convert noisy point clouds into counterfactual visual evidence rather than treating them as ground-truth maps.
- The empirical evaluation spans both simulation (R2R-CE, RxR-CE) and real-world deployment (Hello Robot), which is commendable, and the ablation comparing human-curated vs. agent-reconstructed point clouds nicely supports the core claim that SpatialAnt degrades far less than the strongest zero-shot baseline (SpatialNav) when moving from idealized to noisy scenes.
- The backbone scalability experiment (Figure 3) and the anticipation-horizon ablation (Table 4) are useful analyses that support the claimed model-agnostic and design-choice robustness of the framework.

Weaknesses (soundness/significance related):
- Evaluation sample sizes are small: only 100 and 195 episodes are sampled from R2R-CE/RxR-CE validation-unseen splits, and only 25 real-world paths are used. No confidence intervals, variance, or multiple seeds are reported, which weakens the statistical reliability of the reported gains (e.g., +2% SR on R2R-CE over the previous best zero-shot method is within noise range for n=100).
- The scale-alignment procedure (Section 4.2) estimates a single global scale factor per regional reconstruction from one best-matching frame's SSIM-based comparison with a monocular metric-depth model (Depth-Anything-2).
