title: UAOR: Uncertainty-aware Observation Reinjection for Vision-Language-Action Models

review.summary: The paper proposes UAOR (Uncertainty-aware Observation Reinjection), a training-free, plug-and-play mechanism for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The key idea is to (1) define a layer-wise "Action Entropy" uncertainty metric computed via a logit-lens style projection of intermediate FFN outputs onto action/condition tokens, and (2) when this uncertainty exceeds a threshold γ at layer ℓ, reinject observation features (visual + proprioceptive, treated as key-value memory) into the FFN of the next layer (ℓ+1) via an attention-like retrieval and blend with weight α. The authors motivate the design with empirical observations that uncertainty rises and observation attention decays in early transformer layers, and back the method with four theorems (grounded in mutual information / information bottleneck arguments) purporting to show that UAOR increases hidden-state/observation mutual information, reduces conditional entropy over actions, improves the IB objective under certain conditions, and that entropy-gated triggering is preferable to indiscriminate injection. Empirically, UAOR is applied to four heterogeneous VLA backbones (OpenVLA-OFT, π0, CogACT, LLaVA-VLA) across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and CALVIN benchmarks, as well as four real-world Franka manipulation tasks, showing consistent (generally modest, +1 to +4 point) success-rate improvements with low (~5%) inference overhead. Extensive ablations examine injection mechanism (residual vs. blending), feature extraction (mean pooling vs. attentive retrieval), trigger policy (all-layer/random/entropy-based), injection timing/location (current vs. next layer, FFN vs. self-attention), the choice of reinjected modality (vision/proprio/instruction), and sensitivity to γ and α.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Practical framing: a genuinely training-free, architecture-agnostic module that can be applied post-hoc to already-trained VLA checkpoints without extra data collection, auxiliary encoders, or fine-tuning is a valuable and underexplored direction.
- Broad empirical coverage: results are reported across three simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, SIMPLER, CALVIN) and four structurally different VLA backbones (single-system discrete-token, single-system continuous, dual-system diffusion, dual-system with different scale), plus real-world experiments on two backbones and four tasks. This diversity is a meaningful soundness strength.
- Thorough ablations: the paper carefully isolates the contribution of each design choice (injection mechanism, feature extraction method, trigger policy, injection timing/location, and modality selection), which substantiates the design rationale better than most "plug-in" papers.
- Reasonable complexity/overhead analysis (both theoretical FLOPs and measured latency/throughput) supporting the "negligible overhead" claim.
- The empirical evidence motivating the method (Figures 1–2: rising early-layer uncertainty correlating with dropping attention to observation tokens) is a clear, intuitive, and testable premise.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The four "theorems" are largely restatements of standard information-theoretic inequalities (data-processing inequality, chain rule) under strong, unverified assumptions (A1 non-degenerate reinjection, A2 near-invertible mixing with vanishing ε, A3 deterministic backbone). These assumptions are not empirically validated for real deep transformer hidden states, so the theorems establish plausibility rather than rigorous guarantees; in practice they reduce to "if the injected content is informative and mixing doesn't destroy information, then things improve," which is close to tautological. The claimed "rigorous theoretical analysis" is oversold relative to what is actually shown.
- The threshold γ and blending factor α are tuned per task suite (Table 7 shows quite different values across benchmarks and even across different LIBERO suites for the same backbone, and a very different regime for π0 vs. OpenVLA-OFT). This undercuts the "training-free"/plug-and-play framing to some extent, since per-task or per-backbone hyperparameter search is still required, which is a hidden practical cost not fully acknowledged.
- Reported gains are frequently small relative to the reported standard deviations across seeds (e.g., Table 1, OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO-Object: 98.4±0.4 vs. 98.2±0.2), raising concerns about statistical significance of some individual improvements, even though the aggregate trend across many settings is consistently positive.
- Baselines are already close to ceiling (>94–98% on LIBERO, >90% average length ratio on CALVIN), which limits how informative the absolute improvements are and makes it hard to assess whether the method would generalize to harder/more open-ended tasks where headroom is larger.

Weaknesses (originality):
- The core mechanistic ingredients—FFN as key-value memory (Geva et al., 2021), and injecting/retracing information into FFN based on retrieval to mitigate model failure modes (already explored in "memory-space visual retracing" for hallucination mitigation in MLLMs, Zou et al., 2024, cited in the paper)—are not new. The main novel contributions are the specific "Action Entropy" metric tailored to VLA action/condition tokens and the domain transfer to VLA models. This is a reasonable but somewhat incremental combination of existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the paper does not directly compare against the closest prior work (Zou et al., 2024) empirically.

Weaknesses (presentation):
- Overall writing and organization are clear and the figures are informative, but the theoretical section (Section 3.4 and Appendix A) is presented with more mathematical formalism than substance, which could mislead readers into overestimating rigor. Some notation (e.g., strong-DPI bounds with unspecified κ, η functions) is introduced without concrete instantiation, making it hard to assess practical tightness.
- The real-world evaluation, while a nice addition, uses only 4 tasks with 20 rollouts each and only two backbones; more statistical detail (variance across trials, seeds) would strengthen these claims.

Significance: The method could be practically useful given its low overhead and generality across backbones, but the reliance on per-task hyperparameter tuning and modest absolute gains on largely saturated benchmarks somewhat limits the perceived impact.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. The uncertainty threshold γ and blending factor α are tuned per benchmark suite and even differ substantially across backbones (e.g., γ=0.20 for π0 vs. 0.75–0.80 for OpenVLA-OFT on the same LIBERO tasks, per Table 7). Doesn't this per-task/per-model tuning undermine the "training-free, plug-and-play" claim? Have you tested whether a single fixed (γ, α) pair generalizes reasonably well across all tasks/backbones without substantial performance loss?
2. Several reported gains (e.g., Table 1, OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO-Object, +0.2) are within or close to the reported standard deviation across seeds. Can you provide a statistical significance test (e.g., paired t-test across seeds/rollouts) to substantiate that these smaller gains are not due to noise?
3. The theoretical analysis rests on assumptions (A1: non-degenerate reinjection; A2: near-invertible mixing with vanishing ε) that are not empirically verified for actual VLA hidden representations. Can you provide any empirical evidence (e.g., estimated mutual information or reconstruction error under ψ) that these assumptions approximately hold in your experiments, to justify that the theorems are not merely vacuous under worst-case conditions?
4. How does UAOR compare quantitatively (success rate, overhead) to Memory-Space Visual Retracing (Zou et al., 2024), the closest prior work applying a similar FFN-reinjection idea for hallucination mitigation, when adapted to VLA settings?
5. The Action Entropy metric depends on a logit-lens style projection of intermediate hidden states through the final LM head. How reliable is this projection at very early layers (e.g., layers 2–4), where representations may not yet be well aligned with the final output vocabulary space? Have you validated that the entropy computed at these early layers is a faithful uncertainty signal (e.g., via calibration analysis) rather than an artifact of premature projection?
review.limitations: The paper includes only a generic "Impact Statements" section stating no notable societal impact, without substantive discussion. The paper does not discuss key practical limitations such as: (1) the need for per-task/per-backbone hyperparameter tuning of γ and α, which partially offsets the "training-free" framing; (2) the reliance on strong theoretical assumptions that are not empirically verified; (3) the relatively narrow real-world evaluation (4 tasks, small rollout counts); and (4) potential failure modes when observation reinjection is applied to tasks requiring strong instruction-following (the paper itself notes in Table 5 that reinjecting instruction features can hurt performance, hinting at a deeper limitation of current VLA instruction-following that is not explored further). I recommend the authors add a dedicated limitations section addressing these points.

title: FHAIM: Fully Homomorphic AIM For Private Synthetic Data Generation

review.summary: This paper introduces FHAIM, a system that trains a marginal-based differentially private synthetic data generator (based on the AIM algorithm) directly on data encrypted with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). The motivation is to provide "input privacy" (the service provider never sees the plaintext data) in the common single-data-holder/single-service-provider outsourcing scenario, which existing MPC- and FL-based approaches (CAPS, FLAIM) do not adequately address. The authors design FHE protocols for the three data-dependent steps of AIM (compute, select, measure), introduce a column-wise SIMD packing scheme for one-hot-encoded tabular data that keeps multiplicative depth independent of dataset size and only dependent on marginal degree, and replace AIM's L1-norm quality score with a squared L2-norm to avoid unstable polynomial approximations of the absolute value function under FHE. They provide sensitivity proofs for the modified quality score and empirically evaluate utility (workload error, downstream classification accuracy/F1) and computational cost (runtime, memory) on three small tabular datasets (breast cancer, COMPAS, diabetes), showing that FHAIM-L2 nearly matches plaintext AIM while incurring runtimes of roughly 11–30 minutes.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The problem setting (input privacy for SDG-as-a-service with a single data holder and single provider) is well-motivated and clearly distinguished from MPC- and FL-based alternatives (Table 1), and to the authors' knowledge no prior work tackles FHE-based SDG training.
- The engineering contributions are concrete: a column-wise SIMD packing strategy that keeps multiplicative depth dependent only on marginal degree (not N or |Ω|), and the substitution of the unstable L1-norm approximation with an exact, single-level squared L2 norm, backed by a sensitivity proof (Theorem D.1) and expected-penalty proof (Theorem D.2).
- The end-to-end system design (DE/CE/GE/CSE) and workflow are clearly diagrammed, and the trust model is explicitly stated.
- Empirical results show that FHAIM-L2 closely tracks plaintext AIM-L2 both with and without DP noise, while FHAIM-L1 suffers from approximation-induced utility loss, supporting the core design choice.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The threat/trust model claims "1 computing party" (Table 1) as an advantage over MPC's non-collusion requirement, yet the system still requires two computing entities (CE and CSE) that are explicitly assumed not to collude (Sec. 4, "Trust Model"). This undercuts the paper's central selling point that FHAIM avoids the non-collusion assumptions of MPC-based approaches; the paper does not clearly justify why a CE/CSE non-collusion assumption is meaningfully weaker or more credible than a 2-or-3-party MPC non-collusion assumption.
- In Protocol 2 (πSELECT), the noisy quality score for every candidate query w ∈ QC is individually decrypted (line 11, inside the loop) before the arg max is taken, rather than only decrypting/releasing the identity of the arg max. Standard analyses of "Report Noisy Max"/exponential-mechanism-via-Gumbel guarantee the stated ε only when solely the arg max (not all perturbed scores) is revealed; revealing every noisy score to the CSE is a strictly larger release of information and may require different (weaker) accounting than what is claimed. The paper does not discuss or prove that this leakage is consistent with the stated (ε, δ)-DP guarantee.
- Concrete FHE security parameters (N, Q, security level λ) used in the experiments are not reported, and the extremely low peak memory footprints reported (11–32 MB total) seem surprisingly small for CKKS ciphertexts operating at realistic security levels (RLWE degree 2^12–2^16), raising questions about whether the experimental setup used cryptographically meaningful parameters or a lighter-weight/simulated configuration.
- Evaluation is limited to three small datasets (228–4120 training records after split, low dimensionality), which is far from the scale of realistic healthcare/finance datasets the paper motivates itself with; no experiments directly vary N or d to empirically validate the claimed linear/near-constant scaling behavior.
- There is a minor data inconsistency: the intro/appendix states COMPAS has 7,214 samples, but Table 3 reports N=4120.
- No baseline comparison against CAPS or FLAIM is provided empirically (even a rough comparison would strengthen the significance claims), and results lack repeated trials/error bars to assess variance from DP and FHE approximation noise.

Presentation:
- Overall the paper is well organized with clear figures (system diagram, workflow, protocols) and readable notation, though dense in places. Some empirical claims (e.g., "FHAIM-L2 achieves parity with the plaintext model") are somewhat overstated relative to the actual numbers in Table 3, where several F1 scores show noticeable gaps even for the L2 variant (e.g., diabetes ε=1 F1: AIM-L2 0.278 vs FHAIM-L2 0.218).

Significance and Originality:
- The core idea of combining FHE with a DP marginal-based SDG algorithm is novel and represents a genuine first attempt at input-private SDG for the single-holder/single-provider scenario, which is a reasonably important use case. However, due to the small-scale evaluation and unresolved concerns about the trust model and privacy accounting, the immediate practical impact and generality of the results are limited.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. In Protocol 2 (πSELECT), all per-candidate noisy quality scores are decrypted before computing the arg max, rather than only the identity of the winning candidate. Does this match the privacy accounting used by AIM's exponential mechanism/Report-Noisy-Max proof (which typically assumes only the arg max is released)? Please clarify what exactly is revealed to the CSE and justify why this preserves the stated (ε, δ)-DP guarantee.
2. The trust model requires CE and CSE to be non-colluding, yet Table 1 lists FHAIM as needing only 1 computing party, in contrast to MPC approaches that are criticized for requiring non-collusion among multiple parties. Can you clarify/justify this distinction, since FHAIM also relies on a non-collusion assumption between two entities?
3. What concrete FHE parameters (polynomial degree N, ciphertext modulus Q, security level λ) were used in the experiments? How do you reconcile these with the reported peak memory usage of only ~11-32 MB, which seems unusually low for CKKS at standard security levels?
4. Can you provide any results (even simulated/theoretical) showing how runtime and memory scale as N and/or d grow well beyond the small datasets tested (largest is ~4-7K records), given that the motivating use cases (healthcare, finance) often involve much larger datasets?
5. There is a discrepancy between the reported COMPAS dataset size (7,214 samples in the intro/appendix vs. N=4120 in Table 3) — could you clarify this?
review.limitations: The paper includes a brief impact statement acknowledging the higher energy footprint of FHE relative to plaintext approaches, but it does not discuss the practical implications of the CE/CSE non-collusion trust assumption (which is a notable limitation given the paper's framing against MPC-based non-collusion requirements), nor does it discuss the scalability limits suggested by the very small evaluation datasets used. I would suggest the authors explicitly discuss these limitations, along with the potential privacy leakage nuance raised in the SELECT protocol.

title: HeiSD: Hybrid Speculative Decoding for Embodied Vision-Language-Action Models with Kinematic Awareness

review.summary: This paper studies inference acceleration for autoregressive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models via Speculative Decoding (SD). The authors observe that drafter-based SD gives high-quality but costly drafts, while retrieval-based SD is cheap but often produces poor-quality drafts. Through a kinematic trajectory analysis on LIBERO, they show that segments where VLA-inferred and retrieved trajectories overlap correspond to coarse, high-curvature-radius/large-displacement motions, whereas non-overlapping segments correspond to fine-grained, low-radius motions. Based on this, they propose HeiSD, a hybrid SD framework that (1) improves retrieval-based SD via an adaptive verify-skip mechanism (skipping verification when hidden-feature similarity between the current and historical trajectory points is high) and a sequence-wise relaxed acceptance strategy (grouping kinematically-correlated action dimensions into sequences and allowing bounded index bias for acceptance, using tree-based decoding over Top-K retrieved candidates); and (2) automatically switches between retrieval-based and drafter-based SD using a fused kinematic metric (curvature radius + cumulative displacement) computed over a sliding window. The system is implemented with database offloading to CPU to fit consumer GPU memory constraints. Experiments on four LIBERO suites and a real-world tabletop manipulation setup with an AgileX PIPER arm show speedups of up to 2.45× in simulation and 2.06×–2.41× in the real world, generally outperforming pure drafter-based SD, pure retrieval-based SD, and the SpecVLA baseline, with modest success-rate degradation. Ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity studies (window size w, fusion weight α) are also reported, along with extensive appendix material on database construction, normalization, and real-world data collection/fine-tuning procedures.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The problem (VLA inference latency) is practically important, and the paper provides a clear, empirically grounded rationale (Fig. 2, Tab. 1-2) for why neither pure drafter-based nor pure retrieval-based SD alone suffices, motivating the hybrid design.
- The technical contributions are reasonably well matched to identified failure modes: verify-skip addresses spurious rejections, sequence-wise relaxed acceptance (grouping kinematically correlated DoFs) addresses persistent retrieval errors, and the kinematic fused metric offers an interpretable, lightweight way to decide the SD boundary without needing to see full trajectories in advance.
- The evaluation is fairly extensive: four LIBERO suites with 50 trials/task, real-world experiments across three task categories with a physical robot, ablations isolating each component's contribution, and hardware/system considerations (CPU-GPU offloading, latency breakdowns). The appendix provides substantial engineering detail on database construction, normalization schemes, and real-world data collection, which supports reproducibility.
- Comparison against a recent SOTA baseline (SpecVLA) as well as naive pure-drafter and pure-retrieval variants strengthens the empirical case.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The verify-skip and sequence-wise relaxed acceptance mechanisms intentionally break the standard SD guarantee of matching the target model's output distribution (unlike classical lossless SD). The paper explicitly states in the Scope section that

title: AI Empathy Erodes Cognitive Autonomy in Younger Users

review.summary: This is a position/vision paper arguing that affective sycophancy in RLHF-aligned conversational AI is developmentally harmful for younger (adolescent) users, because reward models trained on adult preference judgments systematically favor emotional validation over the 'productive friction' that (per the Desirable Difficulties literature) is needed for cognitive/emotional skill acquisition. The authors review sycophancy and cognitive-offloading literature, argue that Constitutional AI only partially solves the problem, and propose 'Stoic Architectures': (1) a sycophancy penalty based on cosine similarity between input/output sentiment embeddings, (2) an RLAIF procedure guided by a hand-authored 'Developmental Constitution' (Objectivity and Agency principles) instead of human preference labels, and (3) a dynamic valence-gating mechanism that switches between 'Rapport' and 'Stoic' system prompts based on a classifier of user arousal. They also propose an extensive (but entirely unimplemented) five-part evaluation framework and close with policy recommendations for regulating AI systems aimed at minors. No experiments, implementations, or empirical results are presented; the entire technical content is prescriptive/hypothetical.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Timely and socially important topic: sycophancy and cognitive offloading in AI companions for young users is an underexplored, high-stakes concern.
- The paper engages thoughtfully with counterarguments (therapeutic alliance, harm reduction, engagement incentives) in Section 4, which strengthens the position-paper framing.
- The proposed sycophancy-penalty formalization (a hinge loss on affective cosine similarity) is at least a concrete, falsifiable technical object, and the overall architecture diagram (Fig. 2) communicates the pipeline clearly.
- Reasonably comprehensive literature synthesis spanning ML alignment (RLHF, RLAIF, Constitutional AI, sycophancy) and developmental/clinical psychology (Bjork's desirable difficulties, CBT, attachment theory).

Weaknesses (soundness):
- There is no empirical validation of any kind: no experiments, no ablations, no user studies, no actual training runs, not even a toy demonstration of the sycophancy penalty. Every proposed mechanism is described with 'we propose', 'would', 'could'. For an ICML submission this is a severe limitation — the entire evaluation section (Section 6) is itself a proposal for future evaluation, not a report of results.
- Figure 1 presents a specific bar chart (83/63/42) and a correlation statistic (r=-0.68, p<0.001) attributed to Gerlich (2025) as though directly reproduced, but it is unclear whether these particular numbers are faithfully sourced or reconstructed/approximated by the authors; presenting synthesized or approximate figures as if they were verbatim empirical data from a cited source is a soundness concern that should be clarified or corrected.
- The proposed sycophancy penalty (cosine similarity between input and output sentiment embeddings via a generic Twitter sentiment model) is a very coarse proxy for the sophisticated construct the paper wants to capture (validating false beliefs vs. appropriate empathetic tone). It would likely penalize legitimate empathetic acknowledgment ('I hear that you're upset') at the same rate as harmful validation of a cognitive distortion, undermining the paper's own goal of preserving 'informational utility'. No justification or pilot analysis is given for the chosen τ=0.3, λ=0.1 hyperparameters beyond 'theoretical baseline'.
- The causal narrative (adult annotators → sycophantic reward model → developmental harm in adolescents) is plausible but supported mainly by loosely related, non-causal evidence (correlational studies on general AI usage and critical thinking, unrelated ELIZA anecdotes, attachment-theory papers about adult chatbot users). The chain from RLHF annotation bias to specific adolescent cognitive/emotional harm is asserted rather than demonstrated.
- The Objectivity Principle (challenging user cognitive distortions) raises safety concerns that are only superficially addressed; the paper acknowledges the risk of missing genuine crises (Section 7) but does not specify how the safety override would be operationalized or validated, which is concerning given this is explicitly targeted at vulnerable young users.
- Considerable textual redundancy: the abstract, the 'Position Statement' subsection, and parts of the introduction essentially repeat the same content nearly verbatim, adding little beyond required position-paper formatting.

Presentation: The paper is generally well-organized and readable, with a clear thesis and logical section flow (crisis → mechanics → alternative views → proposed architecture → evaluation → implications → call to action). Formula and figure presentation are reasonably clear, though the empirical figure’s provenance should be clarified.

Significance: The topic is significant and underexplored, but because the contribution is purely conceptual/prescriptive with no working system or empirical support, its immediate significance to ML practice is limited; it functions more as a discussion/opinion piece than a technical advance that others can build upon or reproduce.

Originality: The framing of sycophancy specifically through a developmental-psychology lens for younger users, and the specific 'Stoic Architecture' proposal (sycophancy penalty + developmental constitution + valence gating) is a reasonably original synthesis, even though each individual component (RLAIF, Constitutional AI, sentiment-based rewards, arousal classifiers) is drawn from existing techniques.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Is Figure 1 a direct reproduction of statistics reported in Gerlich (2025), or an approximation/illustration constructed by the authors? Please clarify the exact source of the r=-0.68 statistic and the three bar values.
2. How would the sycophancy penalty distinguish between appropriate empathetic acknowledgment of emotion (e.g., 'that sounds really hard') and harmful validation of a cognitive distortion, given that both could produce similar sentiment-embedding similarity scores?
3. Do you have any preliminary results—even a small pilot with human or LLM judges—showing that Stoic-Architecture-style responses are rated by experts as more developmentally appropriate without being perceived as invalidating, or is this entirely a proposal for future work?
4. How would the dynamic valence-gating classifier and Objectivity Principle be prevented from misclassifying genuine crisis disclosures (e.g., self-harm ideation) as ordinary 'catastrophic generalization' to be challenged, beyond the general statement of 'safety overrides'?
5. Given the reliance on Western CBT and Stoic philosophical frameworks, how do the authors propose empirically validating or adapting the Objectivity/Agency principles across different cultural contexts before deployment, rather than only flagging this as a risk?
review.limitations: The paper does dedicate Section 7 to risks (psychological reactance/attrition, sociopathic failure modes in crisis detection, cultural imposition of Western rationalist norms), which is commendable. However, the discussion remains at the level of acknowledging these risks rather than proposing concrete mitigations or evaluation plans beyond generic 'safety overrides' and 'cultural sensitivity panels.' The lack of any empirical work means potential negative impacts of deploying an untested 'stoic' system with vulnerable minors (e.g., missed crises, perceived coldness causing disengagement from needed support) are discussed only hypothetically. I would suggest the authors more concretely specify fail-safe mechanisms and a plan for staged, ethically-reviewed pilot testing with adolescents before any real-world deployment recommendation.

title: RC-GRPO: Reward-Conditioned Group Relative Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Tool Calling Agents

review.summary: This paper studies a specific failure mode of the standard SFT→GRPO pipeline for training multi-turn tool-calling LLM agents: when SFT produces a highly peaked ('golden-path') policy, GRPO rollouts within a group become nearly identical, causing the group-normalized advantage to collapse and updates to vanish. To address this, the authors propose RC-GRPO, a two-stage method. Stage 1 fine-tunes a 'Reward-Conditioned Trajectory Policy' (RCTP) on a 50/50 mix of expert and failure trajectories, prepending discrete reward tokens (<|high_reward|>/<|low_reward|>) to the prompt so the model learns to generate qualitatively different trajectories on demand. Stage 2 runs GRPO but samples a reward token per rollout within each group (matching the proportion used in Stage-1 training) and conditions generation on it, explicitly injecting between-mode reward variance to keep group-normalized advantages informative. They provide a small theoretical analysis (vanishing-advantage proposition for peaked policies and a variance lower bound under reward-conditioned sampling via the law of total variance) and evaluate on the BFCLv4 multi-turn benchmark with LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, showing consistent gains over SFT+GRPO, SFT+RC-GRPO, and RCTP-FT+GRPO ablations, additional training-dynamics analyses (entropy, entropy-reward correlation, advantage spread) to argue the gains are not merely due to increased randomness, and a comparison against several closed API models on the same benchmark.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The identified failure mode (variance collapse of group-normalized advantage from a peaked SFT policy) is a real and practically important issue, and is well-motivated with references to related vanishing-gradient analyses (Razin et al., 2024).
- The proposed fix—decoupling within-group diversity from sampling temperature/entropy by conditioning rollouts on discrete reward-goal tokens—is an intuitive and reasonably novel combination of return-conditioned generation (Decision Transformer/UDRL) with GRPO group construction.
- The ablations (Q1, Q2) cleanly isolate the separate contributions of RCTP initialization versus reward-conditioned sampling during RL, and show that RCTP-FT initialization is necessary for the RC mechanism to help (Table 3), which is informative and reasonably convincing internally.
- The training-dynamics analysis (entropy trajectories, entropy-reward correlation, advantage spread) is a nice attempt to rule out the trivial explanation that the method just behaves like a higher-temperature/entropy-bonus exploration heuristic.
- Detailed appendices (data curation, reward function definition with worked examples, hyperparameters) support some reproducibility.

Weaknesses (soundness/significance):
- Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (BFCLv4 multi-turn) with an extremely small test split (80 examples; Table 7). Reported accuracies (e.g., 46.25% vs 48.75%, or 85.00% vs 73.75%) correspond to differences of only a few examples out of 80, and no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or variance estimates are reported for the main results in Table 1. This substantially undermines confidence in the significance of the reported gains.
- The headline claim that RC-GRPO on open-weight 7B models 'surpasses all closed-source API models' is potentially misleading: the open-weight models are extensively task-specific fine-tuned (SFT/RCTP-FT + RL) on data drawn from the same simulated BFCLv4 environments/categories used for evaluation, whereas the API models are evaluated zero-shot/general-purpose. This is an apples-to-oranges comparison that inflates the perceived significance of the contribution; a fairer comparison would include API models with in-context few-shot examples from the same domain, or fine-tuned API baselines, or should be framed more carefully as 'specialized vs generalist' rather than an unqualified capability claim.
- A highly relevant and simple baseline is missing: dynamic/rejection sampling that filters out degenerate (all-0 or all-1 reward) groups before computing advantages (used e.g., in DAPO-style approaches) directly addresses the same failure mode without requiring an additional SFT stage with reward-token conditioning. Without this comparison, it is hard to judge whether the added complexity of RCTP-FT + conditioned sampling is necessary versus a much simpler fix.
- The correlation-based statistical claims in Table 4 (Pearson ρ with p-values across training steps) do not appear to account for the strong autocorrelation inherent in time-series training logs, which can produce spuriously significant p-values; details of how significance was computed are not given.
- The theoretical contributions (Propositions 4.2 and 4.3) are correct but fairly elementary applications of KL-probability bounds and the law of total variance; they formalize an intuitive point rather than offering deep new theoretical insight.
- Only two similarly-sized (7-8B) base models are tested; no evidence of the method's behavior at larger scale or on other multi-turn tool-use benchmarks (e.g., API-Bank, ToolBench multi-turn splits, AgentBench) is provided, limiting claims of general applicability.
- Minor: writing contains a number of typos ('Berkley' for 'Berkeley', 'agvantage', 'consistantly'), suggesting incomplete proofreading; some redundant material (Algorithm 1 essentially restates Sec. 3 in pseudocode without much new information).

Originality: moderate—combines known ideas (return-conditioned generation à la Decision Transformer/UDRL, GRPO) in a new way targeted at a specific pathology, but each component individually is well established.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized with a clear pipeline diagram, but suffers from typos and could be more concise in places (e.g., extensive raw hyperparameter tables in the appendix, redundant algorithmic restatement).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Given the 80-example test split, how variable are the reported accuracies across different random seeds (both for training and rollout sampling)? Can you report mean ± std over multiple runs, and/or use a larger or additional benchmark to substantiate the magnitude of the gains?
2. How does RC-GRPO compare against a simple dynamic/rejection-sampling baseline that filters degenerate (all-0/all-1) groups before GRPO update, which directly targets the same vanishing-advantage problem without requiring the RCTP-FT stage?
3. Can you clarify how 'reward conditioning' is even meaningful for the SFT+RC-GRPO baseline in Table 3(A), given that the plain SFT model was never trained to associate the <|high_reward|>/<|low_reward|> tokens with distinct behavior? Doesn't sampling conditioning tokens for an SFT model amount to conditioning on effectively meaningless/out-of-distribution tokens, which would trivially explain the negligible effect?
4. Given that the fine-tuned open models are trained on data drawn from the same BFCLv4 categories used for evaluation, while the API baselines are evaluated presumably zero-shot, do you think the 'surpasses all closed-source API models' claim is a fair characterization, or would it be more accurate to frame this as specialization vs. generalization?
5. How were the p-values in Table 4 computed, and were autocorrelation effects in the training-step time series accounted for?
review.limitations: The paper includes a brief Impact Statement acknowledging dual-use risk of more capable tool-using agents, but does not discuss important technical limitations such as the small evaluation set size, the single-benchmark scope, or the fairness of the comparison against generalist closed-source API models fine-tuned. I recommend the authors explicitly discuss these methodological limitations (dataset size/variance, single-domain evaluation, fine-tuned vs. zero-shot comparison fairness) in a dedicated limitations section.

title: Structurally Aligned Subtask-Level Memory for Software Engineering Agents

review.summary: This paper addresses a granularity mismatch problem in memory-augmented SWE (software engineering) agents. The authors argue that existing memory mechanisms operate at the instance/episode level, retrieving prior trajectories based on global task similarity, which can mislead agents when surface-similar issues require different subtask-level reasoning (and miss reusable skills when globally dissimilar tasks share subtask-level logic). To address this, the paper proposes Structurally Aligned Subtask-Level Memory, which decomposes agent trajectories into functional subtask categories (ANALYZE, REPRODUCE, EDIT, VERIFY), stores memory entries as (category, description, experience) triples, and performs two-stage retrieval (hard category filtering followed by semantic similarity matching on subtask intent). Memory is updated online after each subtask by an LLM-based extractor that abstracts transferable insights from the raw trajectory. The method is evaluated on SWE-bench Verified across four backbone LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro, Claude 3.7/4.0 Sonnet), showing consistent Pass@1 gains over a vanilla agent and an instance-level memory baseline (a reproduction of ReasoningBank), plus a set of ablations (structured prompting only, no category filter, raw trajectory vs. abstracted insight) and analyses (temporal dynamics, task complexity stratification, memory usage distribution, functional specialization of retrieved memories, and a qualitative case study).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper identifies a plausible and well-motivated failure mode of instance-level memory (surface similarity vs. stage-specific reasoning needs), illustrated clearly with intuitive examples.
- The proposed method is simple to describe, has a clean formalization (subtask tuple, memory triple, two-stage retrieval), and integrates naturally into an agent's reasoning loop with minimal architectural overhead.
- The empirical evaluation spans four diverse backbone LLMs (two Gemini, two Claude variants) with fairly consistent gains, which strengthens claims of generalizability across model families.
- The ablation studies (structured prompting only, category filter removal, raw trajectory vs. abstracted experience) are well-designed and isolate the contribution of individual components reasonably convincingly.
- The analysis section (temporal dynamics, complexity stratification, memory usage long-tail, functional specialization by phase, qualitative case study) provides useful mechanistic insight into why/where the method helps.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The paper compares against only a single instance-level memory baseline (a reproduction of ReasoningBank), yet related work lists several other directly relevant methods explicitly targeting stage/step-aligned memory or SWE-specific experience reuse (e.g., TRAD's step-wise thought retrieval, StructuThink's task-transition knowledge, SWE-Exp, ExpeRepair's dual memory, Agent KB). None of these are used as empirical baselines, despite being conceptually very close to the proposed idea. This weakens the strength of the
review.limitations: endation"

title: Elucidating the Design Space of Flow Matching for Cellular Microscopy

review.summary: This paper presents a systematic empirical study of the flow-matching design space for generative modeling of cellular microscopy images. The authors: (1) provide a lightweight theoretical decomposition of virtual-screening error into a 'base generative model' term and a 'perturbation encoder' term; (2) run an extensive set of ablations on the RxRx1 benchmark covering conditioning strategies, source/target flow construction (control-to-perturbed vs. noise-to-data), minibatch optimal transport coupling, interpolant choice, and architecture/training stability, finding that several techniques used by prior state-of-the-art methods (CellFlux, CellFluxV2) are unnecessary or harmful; (3) scale up a diffusion-transformer-based 'Microscopy Transformer' (MiT) architecture and pretrain on a large proprietary dataset (Phenoprints), achieving roughly 2x FID and 10x KID improvements over prior state-of-the-art on RxRx1; and (4) fine-tune the resulting foundation model with different molecular embeddings (one-hot, unconditional, Morgan fingerprints, MolGPS) on BBBC021 to evaluate virtual screening of unseen molecules, achieving state-of-the-art results with MolGPS conditioning. The paper closes with a discussion arguing that domain-specific tricks are often unnecessary, that molecular representation quality is the main bottleneck for unseen-perturbation generalization, and that current public benchmarks may be saturating.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The ablation study is unusually thorough and well documented (detailed appendices with hyperparameters, FLOP estimates, stabilization ablations, interpolant comparisons, and guidance-strength sweeps), which aids reproducibility and community trust.
- The paper produces genuinely useful negative results: showing that control-to-perturbed flows and minibatch OT couplings—both intuitively appealing and used in prior/contemporaneous work—do not help and can hurt performance. This kind of 'what doesn't work' finding is valuable and analogous in spirit to Karras et al.'s EDM paper for natural images.
- Care is taken to validate the evaluation pipeline against prior work's released generations (reproducing CellFlux's reported FID/KID closely), increasing confidence in the comparisons.
- The paper reports both an 'undertrained' variant of its best ADM configuration and full runs, which helps partially disentangle compute increases from methodological changes (flow direction) in the ablation table.
- Reasonably comprehensive empirical coverage: two datasets (RxRx1, BBBC021), a seen/unseen molecule split, several molecular embeddings, and a qualitative biological plausibility case study (Aurora kinase inhibitor AZ841).
- Honest discussion of benchmark saturation and diminishing returns from large-scale pretraining, which is a valuable and unusually candid observation for a paper touting a 'foundation model' framing.

Weaknesses:
- Soundness of the theoretical section (§3) is fairly weak: Proposition 3.1 is a straightforward triangle-inequality argument under strong, unverified assumptions (existence of e*, global Lipschitz constant U, and a well-defined ϵ_G). None of ϵ_base, ϵ_G, or U are estimated or connected quantitatively to the empirical results; the theory functions mainly as a motivating narrative for the two-stage empirical study rather than a tool that yields actionable, falsifiable predictions.
- Some of the ablation comparisons still confound multiple factors. For example, moving from Config A (C→P) to Config B (N→D) also coincides with a jump in total training compute (4.70 to 15.7 ExaFLOPs, more than 3x), since Config A was stopped early due to overfitting. While the 'undertrained' Config B variant partially controls for this, a cleaner compute-matched design (e.g., stopping Config B and Config A at identical FLOP budgets throughout the sweep) would strengthen the causal claims about flow construction being the primary driver of improvement.
- The scaling/pretraining argument is undercut by the authors' own finding that two additional orders of magnitude of pretraining compute (Phenoprints, ~1 ZettaFLOP) yields only a marginal FID improvement (9.07 → 9.00) on RxRx1, raising the question whether the
review.limitations: placeholder

title: VLM-Guided Experience Replay

review.summary: The paper introduces VLM-RB, a plug-and-play prioritization mechanism for experience replay in off-policy RL that uses a frozen, pre-trained Vision-Language Model (specifically Perception-LM-1B) to assign a binary semantic-relevance score to short rendered clips (sub-trajectories) of agent experience. These scores are propagated to individual transitions and mixed with uniform sampling via an annealed interpolation coefficient λt, forming the prioritized sampling distribution. The VLM scoring is performed asynchronously so it does not block the RL learner, and for continuous-control tasks the authors further combine the VLM score with TD-error to refine prioritization. The method is evaluated on MiniGrid/DoorKey (discrete, three grid sizes) and OGBench/Scene (continuous manipulation, three task difficulties) across four base algorithms (DQN, IQN, SAC, TD3), and compared against UER, PER, and three additional prioritization baselines (AER, ERO, ReLo). The authors report consistent gains in both asymptotic success rate (11-52% aggregate, up to 241.7% on the hardest single task) and sample efficiency (19-45%), along with analyses showing that VLM scores anticipate learned critic values and that performance degrades when the VLM's visual input is semantically corrupted (sprite-swap/abstract-texture ablations), supporting the claim that gains stem from genuine semantic grounding rather than incidental visual cues. Ablations on the mixing schedule and VLM model size, plus throughput/overhead measurements, are also provided.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The idea of using a frozen VLM to prioritize replay buffer sampling (rather than to shape rewards, provide plans, or act as a policy component) is a novel and underexplored angle, clearly motivated relative to existing LLM/VLM-RL literature.
- The empirical evaluation spans two task families with multiple difficulty tiers and four distinct base algorithms (discrete and continuous), and includes comparisons against a reasonably comprehensive set of baselines (UER, PER, AER, ERO, ReLo).
- The "Modified Game" ablation (sprite-swap and abstract-texture renderings) is a well-designed control that isolates whether gains come from genuine semantic understanding versus incidental visual statistics, and the results (degradation to PER-level performance under abstract textures) meaningfully support the causal claim.
- The correlation analysis between frozen VLM scores and evolving critic value estimates (Fig. 3) is an interesting qualitative validation that the VLM anticipates useful learning signal before the critic converges.
- Engineering considerations (asynchronous scoring, lightweight 1B model, single VLM instance serving multiple environments) are sensible and the overhead analysis (Table 6, ~12% throughput cost) is a useful practical contribution.
- The appendix is extensive, providing algorithm pseudocode, environment details, prompts, and hyperparameters, which aids reproducibility.

Weaknesses:
- Task diversity is narrow: essentially two task families (DoorKey and Scene) with parametric variations in difficulty, despite the abstract's broad claim of "game-playing and robotics, discrete and continuous domains." No evaluation on Atari, DeepMind Control, or other manipulation benchmarks with visual pixel-based policies, limiting confidence in generality.
- The comparison arguably confounds information access: VLM-RB is given a rendering channel and internet-scale visual-semantic pretraining that baselines (UER, PER, AER, ERO, ReLo) never receive. While this is the point of the method, the fairness of using "extra information" is not explicitly discussed as a caveat; a fairer comparison might include a VLM-based reward-shaping baseline using the same visual channel to isolate the specific benefit of buffer prioritization versus other uses of the same VLM signal.
- The binary thresholding of the VLM's yes/no probability (Section 3.1,
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How is the prioritized distribution q^P handled during the cold-start phase of training when no clips have yet received a positive VLM score (all transitions score 0)? Does the mixture collapse entirely to uniform sampling in this regime, and if so, for how long empirically?
2. Can you report the empirical precision/recall (or agreement with human/ground-truth semantic milestones) of the frozen VLM's binary success classification on your tasks? This would help quantify how noisy or reliable the "semantic" priority signal actually is.
3. The clip length L=32 frames is used uniformly across grid sizes from 8x8 to 16x16 with very different episode horizons. Was L tuned per task, and how sensitive are the reported gains to this choice?
4. Since VLM-RB and baselines differ not only in prioritization strategy but also in access to a visual rendering channel plus internet-pretrained semantic priors, could you include a baseline that uses the same VLM/rendering channel for reward shaping (rather than replay prioritization) to disentangle where the benefit specifically comes from?
5. Can you provide any preliminary results on a third, qualitatively different domain (e.g., a locomotion or Atari-like task) to substantiate the claimed generality of the approach beyond DoorKey and Scene?
review.limitations: The authors explicitly discuss two limitations: (1) reliance on the assumption that task progress is visually observable (excluding non-visual domains), and (2) the ~12% throughput overhead from VLM inference, noting it is implementation-dependent. These are reasonable but incomplete. The paper does not discuss: (a) the cold-start problem when no experience yet exhibits VLM-detectable success, (b) potential unfairness from giving the method exclusive access to a visual rendering channel and pretrained semantic priors relative to baselines, (c) lack of calibration/error analysis of the VLM's binary judgments (false positives/negatives), and (d) risks of over-reliance on the specific VLM's biases (e.g., could systematically mis-prioritize experiences involving underrepresented visual concepts). The impact statement is only a single generic sentence and does not meaningfully engage with potential negative societal impacts (e.g., biases inherited from the pretrained VLM being baked into agent behavior, dual-use concerns for robotics). I recommend the authors expand this discussion.

title: AffordanceGrasp-R1:Leveraging Reasoning-Based Affordance Segmentation with Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Grasping

review.summary: The paper introduces AffordanceGrasp-R1, a three-module framework (MLLM reasoning, SAM2-based segmentation, and a grasp generation module) for language-conditioned robotic grasping via affordance segmentation. The MLLM (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) is post-trained with a two-stage strategy: (1) supervised fine-tuning on a curated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) dataset built from RAGNet with a self-consistency box-point verification procedure, and (2) GRPO-based reinforcement learning with format, non-repeat, and accuracy rewards. The MLLM outputs bounding-box and point prompts that are fed to a LoRA fine-tuned SAM2 to produce affordance masks. For grasping, the authors argue that existing pipelines (e.g., AffordanceNet) crop the point cloud with the predicted mask before grasp generation, which is misaligned with the grasp model's full-scene pretraining distribution; instead, they generate 6D grasp candidates from the full scene point cloud first and then filter/rank them using a 3D-IoU matching against the affordance-conditioned subcloud. Experiments on RAGNet's sub-benchmarks (HANDAL, GraspNet, 3DOI, and their reasoning-based variants) show consistent state-of-the-art gIoU/cIoU scores compared to several segmentation and reasoning-segmentation baselines, and real-world grasping experiments on a KUKA arm demonstrate higher success rates than AffordanceNet under easy and hard instructions. An ablation study quantifies the incremental contributions of CoT-SFT, GRPO, and SAM2-LoRA fine-tuning.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper targets a concrete and practically relevant mismatch in existing affordance-to-grasping pipelines (crop-then-generate vs. generate-then-filter), and the proposed reordering combined with 3D IoU-based candidate filtering is a sensible, well-motivated design choice supported by both benchmark and real-robot experiments.
- The evaluation is extensive: multiple RAGNet sub-datasets covering in-domain, category-level zero-shot, domain-level zero-shot, and explicitly reasoning-based subsets, alongside a real-world robot deployment with two difficulty levels of language instructions.
- The ablation table (Table 4) clearly isolates the contribution of CoT-SFT, GRPO, and SAM2-LoRA, showing incremental but consistent gains.
- The CoT dataset construction pipeline, including box/point prompt extraction with IoU-based self-consistency filtering and multi-stage generation/verification of reasoning traces, is described in good detail and is a useful engineering contribution.
- Real-world experiments (10 trials/task across 10 objects, easy/hard instructions) show clear improvement over the AffordanceNet baseline and include qualitative failure mode analysis.

Weaknesses:
- Originality is limited: the core techniques (CoT cold-start + GRPO RL for reasoning segmentation, decoupled MLLM+SAM prompt-based segmentation, LoRA fine-tuning) closely follow established recipes (DeepSeek-R1, Seg-Zero, SAM-R1, LISA-family). The main novel elements are the box+point prompt formulation (already similar to Seg-Zero) and the

title: Transport Clustering: Solving Low-Rank Optimal Transport via Clustering

review.summary: This paper studies low-rank optimal transport (LR-OT), which constrains the nonnegative rank of a transport plan to reveal latent structure between two distributions, at the cost of NP-hardness. The authors propose "transport clustering" (TC), which reduces the LR-OT problem to a generalized K-means clustering problem via a "Monge registration" step: compute a full-rank (permutation/OT) map between the two datasets, use it to permute/align the cost matrix, and then solve a single generalized K-means problem on the registered cost to obtain one low-rank factor, with the other factor obtained automatically via the permutation. They prove constant-factor approximation guarantees for this reduction — (1+γ) for negative-type metrics and (1+γ+√(2γ)) for kernel costs, where γ is the ratio between optimal full-rank and low-rank OT costs — and show these bounds are essentially tight via explicit constructions. They further show that using off-the-shelf (1+ε)-approximate K-means/K-medians solvers for initialization preserves the approximation guarantees, and provide a mirror-descent algorithm (GKMS) and an SDP-based alternative for solving the generalized K-means subproblem. Empirically, TC is compared against LOT, FRLC, and LatentOT on synthetic benchmarks (2-Moons/8-Gaussians, shifted Gaussians, stochastic block model), a CIFAR-10 co-clustering task, large-scale single-cell transcriptomics alignment (up to ~130K cells), and Wasserstein-distance estimation on the fragmented hypercube benchmark, generally showing lower OT cost and better co-clustering metrics (AMI/ARI/CTA) than baselines.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The core idea — reduce LR-OT's co-clustering structure to a single generalized K-means instance via registering the cost matrix with the optimal full-rank (Monge) plan — is a clean and, to my knowledge, novel reduction. It nicely eliminates auxiliary variables (Q, R, g) that other methods must jointly optimize.

2. The paper gives, apparently for the first time, worst-case constant-factor approximation guarantees for the LR-OT problem (which is NP-hard), rather than just local-stationarity guarantees as in prior LR-OT solvers (LOT, FRLC). This is a meaningful theoretical advance for the sub-area, and the derivations (via triangle-inequality doubling, CND-metric intra/inter-cluster bounds, and a Young's-inequality trick for the kernel case with an optimized parameter t) are non-trivial and mostly carefully done.

3. The authors verify the approximation ratios are essentially tight with explicit adversarial constructions in R^2 (Proposition 4.2), which strengthens confidence in the theoretical analysis and shows the authors did due diligence beyond just deriving an upper bound.

4. The initialization result (Theorem 4.3), showing that solving K-means/K-medians separately on X and Y and choosing the better Monge-registered initialization already gives a constant-factor guarantee (requiring only a local-descent subroutine thereafter), is a practically useful and cheap-to-implement corollary.

5. Empirical evaluation spans synthetic data, an image co-clustering benchmark (CIFAR-10) matching an existing K-means SDP protocol, and a genuinely large-scale, high-dimensional real dataset (single-cell mouse embryogenesis, up to 131,040 cells), where competing methods (particularly LOT) fail to scale. Showing that low-rank OT tooling can be pushed to genuinely large n is valuable.

6. Reasonably thorough ablations (entropy regularization scale in the registration step, using TC's initialization to warm-start FRLC, and Kantorovich (unequal marginal) registration) are included in the appendix and support robustness claims to a degree.

Weaknesses:

1. Theorem 4.1's approximation ratio depends on γ = OPT_n / OPT_r (ratio of optimal full-rank to optimal rank-K cost), which is a property of the (unknown) optimal solution, not something computable a priori or guaranteed small in general — the claim
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can you clarify precisely how γ = OPT_n/OPT_K behaves as a function of K and n in the reported experiments (synthetic and real)? Since the guarantee's tightness hinges on γ being small, an explicit computation or estimate of γ (even approximately, via lower-bounding OPT_K) for at least one dataset would substantially strengthen confidence that the theoretical guarantees are operative in your experimental regime rather than vacuous.

2. Theorem 4.1 requires the *exact* optimal Monge/Kantorovich plan. In your implementation, this is approximated via Sinkhorn or Hierarchical Refinement with finite regularization/iterations. Proposition/ablation in Appendix B.6 (Table 4) shows solution quality substantially degrades as ε grows, but does not explicitly connect this to the theory (i.e., is there a formal statement bounding the approximation ratio degradation as a function of ε or as a function of a (1+δ)-approximate Monge map)? If not currently available, do you have intuition for how large the degradation could be for realistic ε?

3. For the CIFAR-10 and single-cell experiments, how sensitive are the reported gains (in OT cost, AMI/ARI, CTA) to the choice of random seed, GKMS hyperparameters (step size, iteration count, λ mixing weight), and K-means initialization? Only single runs appear to be reported for these experiments (unlike the 5-seed synthetic experiments), which makes it hard to assess whether the improvements over LOT/FRLC (which are often modest, e.g., OT cost 231.2 vs 234.7 on CIFAR-10) are statistically meaningful.

4. Wall-clock runtime for TC versus LOT and FRLC on the large-scale single-cell datasets (Table 6 in the appendix) shows TC taking roughly 5-15x longer than FRLC. Could you comment on whether this runtime gap is dominated by the Monge registration step (Hierarchical Refinement) or the GKMS clustering step, and whether there are opportunities to close this gap, given that scalability is one of the claimed practical advantages of the method?

5. Corollary A.11 / Proposition A.10 establish relative smoothness under a floor assumption (Q_ij ≥ ε, (Q^T 1_n)_k ≥ δ) enforced via entropic regularization or explicit flooring — how is this floor enforced in the actual GKMS implementation described in Appendix B.1, and does it affect the hard-assignment structure needed for the K in Theorem 4.1's guarantees, or is there a rounding step at the end that could reintroduce a gap between the theoretical guarantee and the practical algorithm's output?
review.limitations: The paper includes a brief, generic societal-impact statement ("work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning... no [consequences] we feel must be specifically highlighted") but does not substantively discuss limitations of the method itself. Concrete limitations that could be addressed but are not clearly discussed include: (1) the dependence of approximation quality on the a priori unknown quantity γ, and the lack of guidance on when γ is expected to be small versus close to 1 in practice; (2) the reliance on an (near-)exact full-rank OT/Monge solution as a subroutine, whose own approximation error is not formally propagated into the stated guarantees; (3) the additional computational cost of computing a full-rank transport plan before clustering, which is nontrivial for large n despite recent near-linear-time solvers, and the empirically observed higher runtime relative to FRLC; and (4) applicability being currently restricted to metric/kernel/triangle-inequality cost structures — costs outside these classes (e.g., some Gromov-Wasserstein-type costs) are not covered by the guarantees. I would recommend the authors add a short, substantive limitations paragraph addressing these points rather than relying on the boilerplate societal impact statement.

title: AdaVBoost: Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs via Token-Level Adaptive Visual Attention Boosting

review.summary: This paper studies training-free visual attention boosting methods for mitigating hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). The authors first present a motivating analysis showing that existing methods, which apply a single predefined scaling factor to visual token attention across all generation steps, produce a trade-off: the fixed scaling factor resolves some hallucinations but is too weak for others (under-boosted) and simultaneously introduces new hallucinations for other tokens (over-boosted). Based on this observation, the paper proposes AdaVBoost, which (1) introduces Visual Grounding Entropy (VGE), a token-level hallucination risk estimator that combines predictive entropy with a visual grounding score computed once during pre-filling, and (2) uses this risk score to adaptively scale visual attention boosting and textual (input) attention suppression at each generation step. The method requires no additional training or extra forward passes. Experiments are conducted on three LVLMs (LLaVA-NeXT-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL3.5-8B) and four hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, SHR, POPE, AMBER), comparing against three visual-attention-boosting baselines (PAI, VAF, VGA). The paper also provides ablations on method components and suppression scope, sensitivity analyses of the introduced hyperparameters, and an inference-time efficiency comparison.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The motivating analysis (Figures 1–3) is a nice illustration of the core problem (uniform boosting strength is sometimes too weak, sometimes too strong) and provides good intuition for why token-level adaptivity is needed.
- The proposed VGE signal is a reasonable and lightweight combination of two complementary, readily available signals (predictive entropy and grounding derived from visual-token logits during pre-fill), and the paper shows empirically (Figure 4) that it correlates better with hallucinated tokens than entropy alone.
- Evaluation spans four established hallucination benchmarks and three different LVLM backbones, with consistent gains over three recent visual-boosting baselines (PAI, VAF, VGA) on the generative tasks (CHAIR, SHR, AMBER generative metrics).
- The method is efficient (single forward pass, no additional training), and the paper reports an inference-time comparison showing overhead comparable to the vanilla model and much lower than PAI.
- Reasonably thorough ablations (visual boosting vs. text suppression contribution, suppression scope) and sensitivity analyses over α, γ, mmax_vis, mmax_txt are provided in the appendix.

Weaknesses (soundness):
- The paper’s central motivating claims and part of its evaluation (SHR benchmark) rely heavily on GPT-5-mini as a hallucination judge, including a secondary GPT-5-mini-based classification (“derived” vs. “new” hallucinated tokens, Appendix A.2) that is used to define over-boosted vs. under-boosted tokens. No human validation, inter-rater agreement, or sanity check of GPT-5-mini’s own reliability as a hallucination judge is reported, despite the paper acknowledging that LLM judges can themselves hallucinate. Given that essentially the entire motivation and one full benchmark's numbers depend on this judge, this is a significant soundness concern.
- The proof-of-concept analysis in Section 1/Figure 1 is based on only 200 sampled images from a single benchmark (AMBER) and a single model (LLaVA-NeXT-7B), which is a fairly small and narrow basis for the paper's central claims, even though Figure 2 shows qualitative examples on other models.
- Gains on discriminative tasks (POPE, AMBER discriminative split) are modest, and the explanation given (single-token predictions leave little room for adaptive intervention) is plausible but somewhat post-hoc; it slightly undercuts the generality of the claimed benefit.
- Hyperparameters (α, γ, mmax_vis, mmax_txt, and layer ranges) are tuned per-model, and the chosen values differ substantially across backbones (e.g., mmax_vis=1.1 for LLaVA-NeXT vs. 1.3 for Qwen3-VL/InternVL3.5) without a principled explanation of why; this raises concerns about the practical burden of retuning for new models, partially undermining the “training-free, practical deployment” framing.
- The computational cost of computing the grounding vector G (Eq. 1), which requires a softmax over the full vocabulary for every visual token and an elementwise max across all visual tokens, is not analyzed in detail; for LVLMs with many visual tokens (e.g., high-resolution image splits) and large vocabularies, this could be non-trivial, yet the paper only reports one aggregate efficiency plot (Figure 5) without a breakdown of this specific operation's cost.
- No statistical significance testing / variance reporting is provided for the main benchmark tables, making it harder to assess whether the (sometimes fairly small, e.g., <1 point) improvements over baselines like VAF/VGA are robust.

Weaknesses (originality/significance):
- Technically, the paper builds incrementally on the existing visual-attention-boosting paradigm (PAI/VAF/VGA); the main novel contributions are (i) the VGE risk signal and (ii) making the boosting/suppression strength a function of this signal rather than a fixed constant. This is a reasonable and useful advance but not a fundamentally new mechanism.
- The paper does not compare against TARAC, a directly relevant recent baseline, due to lack of public code; while understandable, this leaves the empirical comparison somewhat incomplete relative to the closest recent related work.

Presentation:
- The paper is generally clearly written, with helpful figures (Figures 1–5) and a clear algorithm box (Algorithm 1). Some notational density in Section 3 (e.g., overloaded use of t for both current step and risk index, multiple hyperparameters) could be streamlined, and the appendix material on GPT-5-mini judging methodology (which is central to the paper's motivation) could be more prominently integrated or summarized in the main text rather than relegated entirely to the appendix.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How reliable is GPT-5-mini as a hallucination judge for the claims in Figures 1-4 and the SHR benchmark results? Have you validated its judgments against human annotations on even a small subset, and can you report inter-annotator/judge agreement?
2. How sensitive are the main conclusions in Figure 1 (proportions of over-boosted/under-boosted/unfixable tokens) to the choice of judge model or to sampling additional images beyond the 200 used?
3. Can you clarify and quantify the computational/memory cost of computing the grounding vector G ∈ R^V (Eq. 1) at pre-fill time, particularly for models with large numbers of visual tokens and/or large vocabularies, and confirm this is included in the efficiency comparison in Figure 5?
4. The hyperparameters (α, γ, mmax_vis, mmax_txt) differ substantially across the three backbones. Can you provide guidance or an automated procedure for selecting these per new model, rather than relying on benchmark-specific tuning?
5. Why do sensitivity results in Tables 8-9 show relatively flat performance across a wide range of α and γ — does this suggest the
review.limitations: The paper includes a brief Impact Statement acknowledging that the method operates only at inference time (no additional training data) and discusses potential benefits for factual reliability in real-world VQA/captioning applications. However, the discussion of limitations is fairly shallow: it does not explicitly discuss (a) the reliance on an LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) whose own hallucination tendencies could bias both the motivating analysis and part of the evaluation, (b) the need for per-model hyperparameter tuning, or (c) potential failure modes when hallucination risk is systematically mis-estimated by VGE (e.g., confidently wrong grounding scores). I would suggest the authors add explicit discussion of these points, along with any human-validation results for the LLM-judge-based evaluations, in a revised limitations section.

title: Mitigating Safety Tax via Distribution-Grounded Refinement in Large Reasoning Models

review.summary: This paper studies the "safety tax" phenomenon in large reasoning models (LRMs), where safety alignment via SFT on distilled safety datasets degrades general reasoning capability. The authors hypothesize that this degradation stems from a distributional mismatch between the safety data (often distilled from external, stronger LRMs) and the target model's own output distribution. To address this, they propose Distribution-Grounded Refinement (DGR): a two-stage pipeline where (1) the target model is prompted to rephrase/re-express existing safety reasoning traces and answers in its own words, and (2) a quality-control filter removes "overthinking" (excessive, unterminated reasoning) and "meta-thinking" (instructional/self-referential) samples, falling back to the original sample when filtering fails. They evaluate DGR against Vanilla SFT on three safety datasets (DirectRefusal, STAR-1, R1-ACT) using s1.1-7B, showing improved reasoning retention while maintaining comparable safety scores. They further present correlation analyses between distribution-shift metrics (BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, embedding similarity, BERTScore) and reasoning degradation, ablations on prompt templates, QLoRA efficiency, and model scale (s1.1-32B), and an analysis suggesting safety alignment behaves as a latent-knowledge activation mechanism (10 samples suffice for refusal behavior), alongside an over-refusal analysis tied to template diversity.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The core insight—that OOD safety data distilled from an external LRM can be re-expressed by the target model itself to reduce distribution shift—is a simple, low-cost, and practically appealing intervention (essentially self-distillation applied to safety data), and the paper provides a reasonably thorough empirical investigation of this idea across three datasets and multiple axes (reasoning, safety, over-refusal, scale, PEFT).
2. The correlation analysis between distribution-shift metrics and reasoning degradation (Figure 2, Figure 3) is a nice complementary piece of evidence supporting the causal story, going beyond just showing an improvement in Table 1.

review.key_questions_for_authors: 1) Statistical significance and variance: Are the reported numbers from a single run per configuration? Given the extreme swings (e.g., MATH500 from 81.4% to 10.2%), how sensitive are these numbers to random seed, and what is the variance across repeated fine-tuning runs? 2) Model diversity: All experiments use s1.1-7B (and s1.1-32B for one ablation). Does DGR generalize to other model families (e.g., Qwen-based reasoning models, DeepSeek-R1-Distill models) that might have different self-refinement quality or susceptibility to overthinking/meta-thinking? 3) Refinement cost and quality-control statistics: What fraction of samples are filtered as overthinking or meta-thinking per dataset, and what is the added computational/inference cost of the two-stage refinement relative to Vanilla SFT? Could imperfect refinements (hallucinations, semantic drift from the original safety reasoning) introduce new safety risks not captured by the current benchmarks? 4) Correlation vs. causation: Since DGR simultaneously changes both the distribution (via self-rephrasing) and other properties of the data (e.g., naturalness, sentence structure, possibly shorter length after filtering), how confident are the authors that distributional similarity to the base model - rather than some other confound (e.g., text length, fluency, filtering itself) - is the primary driver of the observed improvement? Have the authors tried a control where paraphrasing is done by a similarly-capable but different model (still OOD) to isolate the effect of self-consistency versus general paraphrasing/denoising? 5) Why does R1-ACT's Not_Overrefusal rate drop so drastically (81.2% to 43.8%) with only 10 samples restricted to harmful-only, and is this an artifact of the specific 10 samples chosen rather than a general property—did the authors test multiple random 10-sample subsets to check variance in this specific finding?
review.limitations: The authors include a limitations section acknowledging (1) that DGR has not been extended to RL-based alignment pipelines, and (2) that most experiments were conducted at 7B scale with only limited verification at 32B. These are reasonable but somewhat narrow; the paper does not discuss more fundamental limitations such as reliance on a single base model family (s1.1), lack of variance/statistical significance reporting, the subjective nature of the keyword-based meta-thinking filter, or potential risks that self-rephrased safety content could subtly drift from the intended safety semantics (a form of safety-relevant information loss) despite passing surface based filters. title: VETime: Vision Enhanced Zero-Shot Time Series Anomaly Detection

review.summary: This paper proposes VETime, a zero-shot time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) framework that combines 1D temporal and 2D visual modalities. The authors argue that 1D temporal foundation models excel at detecting point anomalies but miss long-range context anomalies, while 2D vision-based approaches capture global context but suffer from coarse localization due to fixed-resolution image conversion. VETime addresses this via four components: (1) a Reversible Image Conversion module that encodes trend/remainder/original signal into RGB channels and folds the sequence adaptively before resizing to standard ViT input size; (2) a Patch-Level Temporal Alignment module that maps visual patch features back onto the original temporal axis to enable fine-grained cross-modal correspondence; (3) an Anomaly Window Contrastive Learning mechanism with intra-window (point anomaly) and inter-window (context anomaly) contrastive objectives to sharpen discriminative features; and (4) a Task-Adaptive Multi-Modal Fusion module that dynamically routes/fuses temporal, visual, and anomaly-enhanced features for both an anomaly-classification head and an auxiliary reconstruction head. The model is trained end-to-end (with LoRA fine-tuning of a pretrained Time-RCD backbone and a frozen MAE visual backbone) on a large synthetic time-series corpus, then evaluated in a zero-shot fashion on 11 univariate and 5 multivariate TSB-AD benchmark datasets. Extensive comparisons against zero-shot TSFMs, full-shot deep models, and vision/VLM-based baselines, together with ablation studies on each module, vision backbone choice, and image conversion strategy, are reported, along with efficiency comparisons (VETime is claimed to be ~100x faster than vision/VLM baselines).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper targets a well-motivated and practically important gap: unifying pointwise precision and global context awareness for zero-shot TSAD, an area under-explored relative to time-series forecasting multimodal work (e.g., Time-VLM).
2. Experimental breadth is substantial: 11 univariate and 5 multivariate datasets, comparisons against 7 zero-shot TSFMs, 5 full-shot models, and 4 vision/VLM-based baselines, plus efficiency measurements.
3. The ablation studies are thorough, isolating the contribution of each proposed component (RIC, PTA, AWCL, TMF), the choice of vision backbone, and different image-conversion strategies, which strengthens the empirical case for the design choices.
4. The proposed patch-level temporal alignment addresses a genuine limitation of prior vision-for-time-series approaches (loss of temporal indexing after 2D conversion), and the intra-/inter-window contrastive design is a reasonable way to differentiate point vs. context anomalies.
5. Efficiency gains over VLM-based baselines are compelling and practically relevant for real-time deployment.

Weaknesses (Soundness):
1. There appears to be a data inconsistency between Table 1's zero-shot and full-shot sections: for the same model (VETime), same metric (Standard-F1), and same dataset (WSD), the reported values differ (46.55 in the zero-shot block vs. 56.55 in the full-shot block), even though VETime is stated to be evaluated identically (strictly zero-shot) in both blocks. This raises concerns about the correctness/consistency of the reported numbers and undermines confidence in the tables.
2. The framing of
